topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: What is machine learning? Give the two classic definitions.
plain: Machine learning is getting a computer to improve at a job from data instead of from hand written rules. The older definition, from 1959, says it gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. A chess program full of hand coded rules is explicit programming. A chess program that studies many games and adjusts itself to pick better moves is learning. Tom Mitchell of Carnegie Mellon tightened this: a program learns from experience E on a class of tasks T, measured by performance P, if its performance on T as measured by P improves with E.
deep: Samuel's 1959 definition (learning without explicit programming) separates learning from writing rules by hand. Mitchell's definition makes learning testable: fix the task $T$ and the metric $P$, vary the experience $E$, and check that performance rises as $E$ grows. If more data does not move $P$, the system has not learned. For a game player, the experience is games played, the task is playing, and the performance measure is win rate. Both definitions are operational: they say nothing about neural networks or any particular model family, only about improvement from data.
say: Machine learning is getting a computer to improve at a task from data instead of from hand written rules. The older definition, from 1959, says it gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. Tom Mitchell's definition is sharper: a program learns from experience E on tasks T, measured by performance P, if its performance on T improves with E. Take a chess player: the task is playing games, the performance measure is win rate, and the experience is the games it has seen. The useful consequence is a test. If you add more experience and the measure does not move, the system has not learned anything.
must_mention: experience E, task T, performance P

followups.q: What counts as experience for a modern language model?
followups.a: Web text, human labeled examples, synthetic data from other models, and the thinking tokens the model writes while reasoning.

followups.q: How would you tell that a system is not learning?
followups.a: More experience does not improve the performance measure on the task.

traps: Defining machine learning as neural networks or as AI in general. The definition is about improving from data, not about a model family.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: How does Mitchell's experience, task and performance definition apply to modern systems like language models?
plain: Each part of the definition has widened since it was written. Experience used to mean a labeled table of examples. Now it also includes web scale text, data written by people, data generated by other models, and the tokens a model produces while it thinks. A task used to be one narrow job such as predicting house prices, while one model can now be asked to solve a huge range of problems. The performance measure still tells training which direction to move: accuracy for a classifier, win rate for a game player, a reward score for a chat model.
deep: Experience $E$: labeled pairs for supervised learning, unlabeled corpora for pre training, trajectories collected by interaction for reinforcement learning, and synthetic or model generated data such as reasoning traces. Task $T$: older systems solve one task (ImageNet classification, price regression); a general purpose model is given the task at use time through a prompt. Performance $P$: it has to be computable or approximable because it drives optimization, either a differentiable loss for gradient descent or a reward for RL. The three part frame still holds, but experience can now be data the model produced itself, which is what makes self improvement loops possible.
say: Each part of Mitchell's definition has widened. Experience is no longer just a labeled table: it includes web text, human written data, synthetic data from other models, and the tokens a model writes while reasoning. A task used to be one narrow problem like price prediction, and now one model can be prompted to handle a huge range of problems. The performance measure is still the piece that tells training which direction to move, whether that is accuracy, a win rate, or a reward score. So the frame survives, but experience can now be data the model generated itself.
must_mention: experience includes synthetic data and thinking tokens
model can generate its own experience

followups.q: Why does the performance measure have to be computable?
followups.a: Because training optimizes it, either as a differentiable loss or as a reward signal.

traps: Saying experience only means a static labeled dataset.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: Do you still need classical machine learning now that large language models exist?
plain: Yes, because the way models are trained has barely changed even though the way people use them has. Not long ago, using machine learning at a company meant building a pipeline: collect data, train and tune a model, deploy it. Today you often write a query to a pretrained model instead. But that pretrained model was still built with a loss function, gradients, an optimizer and held out data to check generalization. Knowing those pieces lets you configure, debug and judge the model instead of treating it as magic.
deep: The lecturer's position is that the methodology for training models is still very similar to the past, and that what changed is usage: a query or a skill given to a pretrained model replaces a hand built pipeline. The course therefore focuses on the fundamental technology behind configuring models. Examples of classical pieces inside modern systems: supervised fine tuning is supervised learning, language model pre training is next token classification with a cross entropy loss, and reinforcement learning from human feedback is policy optimization. Even the 1959 definition of machine learning still holds. In an interview, name where each classical idea lives in a modern stack.
say: Yes, because what changed is how models are used, not how they are trained. A few years ago, using machine learning at a company meant building a pipeline: gather data, train a model, tune it, deploy it. Now you often just write a prompt to a pretrained model. But that pretrained model was still built with a loss function, gradients, an optimizer and held out data, and supervised fine tuning is literally supervised learning. If you understand those pieces you can configure these models, debug them, and judge their outputs, instead of treating them as a black box.
must_mention: usage changed from pipelines to prompts
loss, gradients, optimizer, held out data

followups.q: Give one classical idea that shows up inside LLM training.
followups.a: Next token prediction is a classification problem trained with cross entropy, and fine tuning on examples is supervised learning.

traps: Claiming prompting makes the underlying training theory irrelevant.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: Name the three main paradigms of machine learning and say how they differ.
plain: Supervised learning gets inputs paired with the right answers and learns to predict the answer for new inputs, such as house features paired with sale prices. Unsupervised learning gets inputs only and looks for structure, such as grouping similar customers. Reinforcement learning has an agent that takes actions, receives feedback and learns to make good sequences of decisions, such as a robot learning to walk. The boundaries are blurry in practice: supervised fine tuning, for example, is one step in building an agent that is later trained with reinforcement learning.
deep: Supervised: data $\{(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}$, learn a function from $x$ to $y$ that is accurate on new inputs. Unsupervised: data $\{x^{(i)}\}$ only, find structure such as clusters, low dimensional representations, or a generative model of the data. Reinforcement learning: an agent chooses actions, receives rewards, and maximizes cumulative reward; its data is collected by the agent itself. The lecturer notes there is no agreed taxonomy, that the paradigms intersect more than before, and that today they are better viewed as tools than as end goals, since the real goal is usually a general learning agent that uses all three.
say: Supervised learning has inputs paired with correct answers and learns to predict the answer for new inputs, like house features and prices. Unsupervised learning has inputs only and looks for structure, like clusters of similar customers. Reinforcement learning has an agent that takes actions, gets rewards, and learns a good sequence of decisions, like a robot learning to walk. The key difference is the training signal: labels, none, or rewards. The categories overlap in practice. For example, supervised fine tuning is one stage in building an agent that is later improved with reinforcement learning.

followups.q: Where does a language model's pre training fit in this taxonomy?
followups.a: It uses unlabeled text, so it is unsupervised in its data, but the next token loss looks like supervised classification.

followups.q: Give an example of the paradigms combined.
followups.a: Supervised fine tuning of a language model, followed by reinforcement learning against a reward model.

traps: Presenting the taxonomy as sharp and universally agreed.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: Set up the supervised learning problem using house prices. What are x, y and the dataset?
plain: You have a dataset of examples, and each example is an input x paired with the correct output y. For houses, x is the square footage and y is the sale price, so each house is one point on a plot. Training means finding a rule that maps x to y well. At test time you receive a new x, such as 800 square feet, and the model predicts y. You could fit a straight line through the points, or a curve if a quadratic fits better. Adding more inputs, such as plot size, turns x into a list of numbers.
deep: Dataset $\{(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ with $x^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$. The goal is a function $h$ with $h(x)\approx y$ on new data, not only on the training points. Three design choices define a learning algorithm: the model family (a line, a quadratic, a neural network), the loss function that says how wrong a prediction is, and the optimizer that finds good parameters. The lecture previews these as the content of the next lectures. Adding features such as plot size, floors or zip code makes $x$ a vector and the picture a surface in higher dimensions.
say: In supervised learning I have a dataset of pairs, an input x and the correct output y. For house prices, x is the square footage and y is the sale price, so each house is a point on a plot. Training finds a function that maps x to y well, say a line or a quadratic. At test time I get a new x and predict y. What matters is accuracy on houses the model has not seen, not on the training points. In practice x has many features, like plot size and zip code, so it becomes a vector, but the setup is the same.
must_mention: dataset of input and output pairs
learn a function from x to y

followups.q: What changes when there are many features?
followups.a: x becomes a vector, and the fitted function becomes a surface or a higher dimensional map.

traps: Evaluating only on the training points.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: What is the difference between regression and classification?
plain: If the output is a continuous number, like a price in dollars, the task is regression. If the output is a discrete label, like single family home versus townhouse, or flamingo versus cat in a photo, the task is classification. The input can be anything in both cases. A quick test is to ask whether the answer can sit anywhere on a number line or must be one of a fixed list of choices. A classifier can be pictured as a boundary that splits the input space into regions, one region per label.
deep: Regression: $y\in\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^k$), usually trained with squared error. Classification: $y\in\{1,\dots,K\}$, with a model that scores or gives a probability for each class and a decision boundary in input space. The learning setup is the same and only the output space and loss differ. In the lecture's picture, houses and townhouses are circles and triangles on a plane of plot size against area, and the classifier is a line with houses on one side. Borderline case: a bounding box is four continuous numbers (two corners), so localization is regression on four outputs.
say: If the output is a continuous number, like a price, it's regression. If the output is one of a fixed list of labels, like house versus townhouse or cat versus flamingo, it's classification. The input can be anything in both cases, and the learning setup is the same: pairs of x and y. Only the output space and the loss differ. For classification I picture a boundary in input space with a different label on each side. A quick test is whether the answer can be any number on a line or has to be one of a few choices.

followups.q: Is predicting a bounding box regression or classification?
followups.a: Regression, because it outputs four continuous coordinates, often paired with a class label for the object.

traps: Choosing by the input type instead of the output type.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: Why is next word prediction in a language model a classification problem?
plain: A language model must choose the next token from a fixed vocabulary, and choosing one item from a fixed list is classification. The vocabulary holds tens of thousands of entries, roughly 50 thousand up to 250 thousand, so every prediction is a classification with that many classes. The input is the text so far, and the label is the token that actually came next. Every piece of text supplies its own labels this way, which is why such models can train on enormous unlabeled corpora.
deep: The model outputs a distribution $p_\theta(\text{token}\mid\text{context})$ over a vocabulary of size $V$ (the lecture quotes about $5\times 10^{4}$ to $2.5\times 10^{5}$) through a softmax, and training minimizes cross entropy against the observed next token. This is a $V$ way classification. Generating text repeats the classification and then samples from the distribution. That sampling step is stochastic and not differentiable, which is why gradients do not flow through generated text and why reinforcement learning enters at later training stages.
say: Because the model has to pick the next token from a fixed vocabulary, and picking one item from a fixed list is classification. The vocabulary is tens of thousands of tokens, maybe 50 thousand to 250 thousand, so each step is a classification with that many classes. The input is the text so far and the label is the token that actually followed. That's what makes pre training scalable: any text gives you labels for free. At generation time I sample from the predicted distribution, which is a stochastic step, and that matters later for reinforcement learning.
must_mention: choose one token from a fixed vocabulary
label is the actual next token

followups.q: What loss trains it?
followups.a: Cross entropy between the predicted distribution and the observed next token.

followups.q: Why does generation complicate gradients?
followups.a: Sampling a token is not differentiable, so you cannot backpropagate through generated text.

traps: Calling it regression because the output is text.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: Give supervised learning examples beyond price prediction and say what x and y are in each.
plain: In image classification, x is the raw pixels and y is a label such as flamingo or Egyptian cat. In object localization, x is still the pixels, but y is four numbers: the coordinates of the bottom left and top right corners of a bounding box. In machine translation, x is a sentence in one language and y is the sentence in another. The recipe is identical in all three: collect pairs, then train a model to map x to y. ImageNet, with about a million image and label pairs, made the first of these large enough for neural networks to shine.
deep: Image classification: $x$ is a pixel array, $y$ is a discrete class. Localization: $y\in\mathbb{R}^4$ (two corners define a box), so it is regression on four outputs, often combined with a class label. Translation: $x$ and $y$ are token sequences. ImageNet, assembled by Fei-Fei Li and collaborators at Stanford, had about one million labeled images, roughly 20 times more than the next largest dataset of its time. AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton) trained a neural network on it and started the current wave: vision first, then language, then large language models.
say: Image classification maps raw pixels to a label like flamingo. Object localization maps pixels to four numbers, the corners of a bounding box. Machine translation maps a sentence in one language to a sentence in another. All three are supervised learning: you collect pairs of x and y and train a model to map one to the other. ImageNet matters historically. It had about a million labeled images, around 20 times more than the next largest dataset then, and AlexNet trained on it showed neural networks working at scale, which kicked off the current era of AI.
must_mention: ImageNet and AlexNet started the era

followups.q: Why was ImageNet important?
followups.a: Its size, about 20 times the next dataset, let deep networks show large gains and started the modern wave.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: What is unsupervised learning, and why is its goal considered vague?
plain: In unsupervised learning you only have inputs, no labels, and you try to find interesting structure in them. Picture a scatter of points with no colors: your eye sees groups, and a clustering algorithm can find them too. The goal is vague because interesting structure depends on the method, so different algorithms report different structure in the same data. The lecture's examples are grouping people by gene expression patterns and grouping documents by the words they contain.
deep: Data $\{x^{(i)}\}$ only. Typical tasks are clustering (assign each point to a group), dimensionality reduction and topic discovery (latent semantic analysis, LSA, applied to a word by document count table, where reordering rows and columns exposes blocks such as space launch documents versus air pollution documents), representation learning, and generative modeling. With no ground truth $y$, evaluation is indirect: usefulness for a downstream task, held out likelihood, or inspection by a person. Because the objective is not given, choosing the method is choosing the notion of structure.
say: Unsupervised learning means I only have inputs and no labels, and I try to find structure in them. If I plot unlabeled points, I can often see groups by eye, and a clustering algorithm finds them automatically. The goal is vague because interesting structure depends on the method: different algorithms find different structure in the same data, and there is no ground truth to check against. Examples are clustering people by gene expression, or grouping documents by the words they use. Evaluation is indirect, usually by usefulness for a downstream task or by inspection.

followups.q: Name two uses from the lecture.
followups.a: Clustering individuals by gene expression and clustering documents by word counts (LSA).

traps: Saying there is one correct clustering of a dataset.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: What are word embeddings, and what does the country to capital direction show?
plain: A word embedding gives each word a list of numbers, a vector, sometimes thousands of entries long. Words with similar meanings get nearby vectors: Rome, Paris and Berlin sit close together. Directions in this space can also stand for relationships. Take the offset that goes from a country to its capital: start at Italy, move along that offset, and you land near Rome. The same offset takes France to Paris and Germany to Berlin. These vectors are learned from unlabeled text such as Wikipedia, as was done around 2014 and 2015.
deep: Each word maps to a vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$ learned from unlabeled text. Geometry carries meaning in two ways: similar words are close (high cosine similarity), and consistent offsets encode relations, for example $v_{\text{Paris}}-v_{\text{France}}\approx v_{\text{Rome}}-v_{\text{Italy}}$. The lecture does not name a training method here and promises to cover how embeddings are learned. It notes that Wikipedia, the corpus of that era, is a tiny fraction (around 1 percent or less) of what is used to train models today. Token embeddings are also the first layer of modern language models.
say: A word embedding maps each word to a vector, a list of numbers that can be thousands long. Similar words end up close together: Rome, Paris and Berlin are neighbors. Directions can encode relationships too. If I take the direction from a country to its capital, then starting at Italy and moving along it lands near Rome, and the same direction takes France to Paris. These vectors are learned from unlabeled text, with Wikipedia as the typical corpus around 2014 and 2015. Modern language models still begin by turning each token into such a vector.

followups.q: What is learned from, and with what labels?
followups.a: Unlabeled text only; the text itself provides the training signal.

traps: Thinking a word's vector is hand designed or comes from a dictionary.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: How do large language models and diffusion models fit the idea of learning without labels?
plain: Older unsupervised methods aimed at one or two jobs, such as finding similar words or clustering documents. A large language model is trained on a huge pile of unlabeled text and ends up as a general purpose model: you can ask it nearly anything. Diffusion models do the same for images. They train on many realistic images with no labels and then generate new realistic ones from noise or from an instruction. In both cases the data supplies its own training signal. The course covers the architecture, the pre training loss, prompting, and how post training makes models follow instructions.
deep: Both are generative models: they learn enough about the data distribution to sample from it. A language model learns the distribution of the next token given the context; a diffusion model learns to generate images from noise. The lecture contrasts these general purpose models with earlier methods built for one or two tasks. It also notes that the output of a language model depends on how the question is asked, and that labs now train models to follow instructions, which two years earlier models did less reliably. Pre training uses unlabeled data at massive scale. Post training makes the model respond to instructions.
say: Earlier unsupervised methods had narrow jobs, like finding similar words or clustering documents. A large language model trains on a huge amount of unlabeled text and becomes a general purpose model that I can ask nearly anything. Diffusion models do the same for images: they train on many realistic images without labels and then generate new ones from noise or from a prompt. In both cases the data provides its own training signal. A pre trained model then goes through post training, which teaches it to follow instructions, so the answer depends on how I ask.
must_mention: train on unlabeled data at scale
general purpose instead of one task

followups.q: What are the two stages the lecture distinguishes for language models?
followups.a: Pre training on unlabeled text, then post training so the model follows instructions.

traps: Saying these models need human labels for every training example.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: What defines reinforcement learning, and how does it differ from supervised learning?
plain: Reinforcement learning is about making a sequence of decisions where each action changes what happens next. A walking robot chooses how to move its legs, and one bad step can make it fall, so choices are linked over time. Unlike supervised learning, nobody hands the agent a fixed dataset of right answers. It tries a strategy, observes what happens, and uses that new data to improve in the next round. In the lecture's robot demo, early iterations fail and later ones walk. AlphaGo is the other classic example.
deep: The standard formalism, which this lecture only previews, is a Markov decision process: states, actions and rewards, with the goal of maximizing expected cumulative reward. Two properties come out of the lecture's examples. First, sequential dependence: actions affect future states, so a mistake can be unrecoverable. Second, interactive data collection: the algorithm alternates between collecting data (a trajectory is a sequence of actions and observations) and training on it. Supervised and unsupervised learning, traditionally, receive a fixed dataset and do not generate more of it.
say: Reinforcement learning is about sequential decisions: the agent takes an action, the world changes, and what it does now affects what is possible later. A robot learning to walk is the classic picture, because one bad step can make it fall. The difference from supervised learning is where the data comes from. There is no fixed set of correct answers. The agent tries something, observes the outcome, and trains on the data it just collected, then repeats. So it alternates between collecting data and learning. AlphaGo and robot control are the standard examples.

followups.q: What is a trajectory?
followups.a: A sequence of actions and observations collected during a trial.

followups.q: Why is a fixed dataset not enough?
followups.a: The data depends on the policy: a different strategy visits different situations, so the agent has to collect new data.

traps: Describing RL as supervised learning with a different loss.

topic: CS229 L1: Course overview and learning paradigms
q: Why is reinforcement learning used to train large language models, and what does the training loop look like?
plain: Generating text means sampling: at each step the model produces a probability distribution over tokens, picks one at random, and then conditions on that choice. Sampling is not a differentiable operation, so you cannot push error gradients back through the generated text. Reinforcement learning handles this. Treat each token choice as an action, score the whole generation with a reward, and update the model to make high reward text more likely. The reward can come from a person, a learned reward model, or another language model.
deep: Loop: a user query goes in, the model generates text by stochastic sampling, a reward module scores the text, and the reward is used to update the model so the next generation is better. The method is policy gradient, previewed here, and the lecture names RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) and training long chains of thought as applications. Each token is a decision and later tokens depend on earlier ones, so it is a sequential decision problem. A self reinforcing example is automatic theorem proving: the model proposes proofs, a checker keeps the correct ones, and training on them produces more correct proofs next round. The lecturer calls the classic RL view and the language model view two perspectives on the same idea.
say: Generating text involves sampling a token from a distribution at every step, and sampling is not differentiable, so I can't backpropagate through generated text. Reinforcement learning gets around that. I treat each token as a decision, score the finished output with a reward, and update the model to make high reward outputs more likely. The reward can come from a human, a reward model, or another language model. The method is policy gradient, and RLHF is the well known case. It can also form a loop, for instance generating proofs, keeping the verified ones, and training on them.

followups.q: Where can the reward come from?
followups.a: A human, a trained reward model, or another language model.

followups.q: What is the theorem proving loop?
followups.a: Generate candidate proofs, verify them, train on the correct ones, and repeat with a stronger model.

traps: Saying RL is used only because labeled data is scarce, when the real obstacle is that sampling blocks gradients.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: What is a hypothesis in supervised learning?
plain: A hypothesis is the function a learning algorithm produces: it takes an input and returns a prediction. Formally it maps a set X of possible inputs to a set Y of possible outputs. X could be all images and Y a fixed list of labels such as cat, dog and horse. X could be review text and Y positive or negative, or X could be house data and Y a price, which is a number rather than a label. It is supervised learning because we also collect a training set of example pairs of x and y to choose the hypothesis.
deep: A hypothesis is a function $h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$. The training set is $\{(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n}$, with the parenthesized superscript indexing examples. The definition is deliberately abstract: $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ are just sets, which is why one framework covers images, text and tabular data, and both classification and regression. The set of all functions from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathcal{Y}$ is enormous (uncountable when $\mathcal{Y}$ is continuous), so learning means restricting to a hypothesis class and choosing one member using the training data.
say: A hypothesis is the function the learning algorithm outputs. It maps an input from some set X to an output in some set Y. The sets are abstract on purpose. X might be images and Y a fixed set of labels like cat or dog. X might be review text and Y positive or negative. Or X could be house features and Y a price, which is a number. It's supervised learning because I have a training set of example pairs of x and y, and I use them to pick the hypothesis out of an enormous space of possible functions.
must_mention: X and Y are abstract sets
training set of x, y pairs

followups.q: Does Y have to be a set of labels?
followups.a: No. It can be a continuous number such as a price, which gives a regression problem.

followups.q: How do we cope with the huge space of possible functions?
followups.a: We restrict to a hypothesis class, such as lines, and pick one member using the data.

traps: Confusing the hypothesis (the learned function) with the training data.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: What makes a hypothesis good? Explain generalization.
plain: A good hypothesis is not the one that fits the training examples best but the one that works on inputs it has never seen. If a model labels a brand new cat photo as a cat, even though that photo was not in training, it has generalized. This works only if the training examples are representative of what the model will meet later. Fitting the training set and trusting that this carries over to the real world is the central bet of machine learning. For very simple hypothesis classes you can prove the bet pays off, and modern models use huge classes where the course explains why it can still work.
deep: The assumption is that the training set is a representative sample of the distribution the model will meet; fitting it should then give good performance in the real world. The lecturer calls this the cornerstone of statistical inference and admits it resembles believing in a miracle, promising examples where it failed, such as predicting economic indicators. Error on the training set is separated from error on a test set. For simple classes, generalization can be proved. Modern learning uses very large classes with enormous numbers of parameters, so the theory has to be extended, which later lectures take up.
say: A good hypothesis is one that generalizes, meaning it performs well on inputs outside the training set, not just on the examples it was fit to. The bet is that if the training set is representative of the real world, a model that fits it well will also do well on new data. For simple hypothesis classes I can actually prove that. For the huge models used today, it still tends to hold but the explanation is harder. The danger is that the training data might not represent reality, as with economic indicators, and then the fit is misleading.

followups.q: What can break the bet?
followups.a: A training set that does not represent the data the model meets later, as happened with economic indicators.

followups.q: How do we measure generalization?
followups.a: On a separate test set that was not used for fitting.

traps: Saying the best hypothesis is the one with the lowest training error.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: What is a linear hypothesis, and why is the class called parametric?
plain: With one input x, a linear hypothesis is a straight line: multiply x by a number theta one and add a number theta zero. Strictly this is an affine function because of the added shift, but everybody calls it linear. Out of all the possible functions from numbers to numbers, you now consider only lines, and each line is fully fixed by two numbers. That is what parametric means: a fixed small set of parameters, however many houses are in the data. Learning then means estimating those parameters, for example from lot size to sale price.
deep: $h_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1x$, where $\theta_0$ is the value at $x=0$ and $\theta_1$ is the slope. The class is parametric because it is indexed by finitely many parameters, independent of the sample size $n$. This is a drastic restriction from uncountably many functions to a two parameter family. Contrast with a method like nearest neighbors, which keeps the data and averages the neighbors of $x$. The lecturer stresses that linear models are the workhorse: the last step of many models used today is a linear model.
say: A linear hypothesis for one input is a line: theta one times x plus theta zero. Technically that's affine because of the intercept, but everyone says linear. The class is parametric because the whole model is pinned down by a fixed, small number of parameters, here two, no matter how many training houses I have. That's a huge simplification, from all possible functions to just lines. Learning means estimating those parameters from data. It's simple, but linear models are a real workhorse, and the final layer of many modern models is still a linear model.

followups.q: Give a non parametric contrast.
followups.a: Nearest neighbors, which stores the data and averages the neighbors of the query point.

traps: Thinking parametric means the model has few parameters in absolute terms. It means the number does not grow with the data.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: How do you write a linear model with many features, and what does the convention x0 equal to 1 do?
plain: With several inputs, such as lot size and number of bedrooms, each input gets its own weight, and you add the weighted inputs plus a base value. To avoid treating the base value as a special case, add a pretend input that is always 1 and give it a weight too. The prediction is then just a weighted sum of all inputs, and the same formula works for three inputs or three thousand. A model with more weights is richer, since setting some weights to zero gives back the smaller model.
deep: $h_\theta(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\theta_jx_j=\theta^\top x$ with $x_0=1$ and $\theta,x\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$. Here $n$ is the number of examples and $d$ the number of features, so vectors have $d+1$ entries. The class with more features is richer: it contains the smaller class as the case where the extra weights are zero, so it can fit the training data at least as well. Which features to use is a modeling decision. Classically you write code that turns raw data into numbers (for example rescaling the lot size), and deep learning later learns the features instead.
say: With many features, each one gets a weight and I sum the weighted features. To avoid a special case for the intercept, I add a constant feature x zero equal to one, so the model is just theta transpose x, a dot product. The same formula works with three features or three thousand. A model with more features is richer, because setting the extra weights to zero recovers the smaller model, so it can fit the training data at least as well. Choosing and scaling the features is a modeling decision that I make before fitting.
must_mention: more features give a richer class

followups.q: What are n and d?
followups.a: n is the number of training examples and d the number of features, so the vectors have d plus one entries.

traps: Forgetting that the intercept needs its own parameter.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: What is empirical risk minimization?
plain: Empirical risk minimization means choosing the hypothesis with the smallest average error on the training examples. For a house price model, you try different lines, measure how far each line's predicted price is from the real price on every training house, and keep the line with the smallest total error. Empirical means the error is measured on the data you actually have, not on future data. It is the recipe behind almost every supervised method: only the model and the way of measuring error change. Even the best line leaves some error, because prices depend on things the data does not contain.
deep: Choose $h\in\mathcal{H}$ to minimize $\hat R(h)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\big(h(x^{(i)}),y^{(i)}\big)$ for a loss $\ell$. The lecturer abbreviates this as ERM and notes that all the methods in the course follow one recipe: a hypothesis class, a way of measuring error, and a minimization. Residual error remains for two reasons given in the lecture: the model omits relevant features (is the house beautiful, is it close to places you care about), and even with every feature some noise is left. This is why training error is later contrasted with test error.
say: Empirical risk minimization means picking the hypothesis that has the lowest average error on the training set. I define a loss that measures how wrong a prediction is, compute it on each training example, average, and choose the model in my class that minimizes it. Empirical means measured on the data I have, as a stand in for the data I'll see later. Almost every supervised method follows this recipe, with a different model class and loss. The catch is that even the best fit leaves error, from missing features or noise, and training error is not test error.
must_mention: empirical means measured on the data we have
model class plus loss plus minimization
training error is not test error

followups.q: Why is there leftover error?
followups.a: The data lacks relevant features and there is irreducible noise.

traps: Treating training error as the quantity you actually care about.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Write the least squares cost function and explain each part.
plain: For each training house, take the model's predicted price minus the real price, square that difference, and add the results over all houses, with a one half in front. Squaring makes every error nonnegative, so overshoots and undershoots cannot cancel, and it punishes big mistakes much more than small ones. Least squares picks the parameters that make this total as small as possible. The notation arg min means the input that achieves the minimum, not the minimum value itself.
deep: $$J(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\big)^2,\qquad \hat\theta=\arg\min_\theta J(\theta).$$ The term $h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}$ is the prediction error for example $i$. With two features the model is a plane and the error is the vertical gap between a data point and that plane. Because the parameters range over the reals, this is a continuous optimization problem. Discrete parameter choices would need much harder methods such as integer programming.
say: The least squares cost adds up, over every training example, the squared difference between the prediction and the true value, with a factor of one half in front. Squaring keeps every term nonnegative so errors can't cancel, and it penalizes large errors much more than small ones. Training means finding the parameters that minimize this cost, and arg min means I want the minimizing parameters, not the minimum value. Because the parameters are real numbers this is a continuous optimization problem, which is what lets me use derivatives and gradient descent.
must_mention: sum of squared errors over examples

followups.q: What does arg min return?
followups.a: The parameter value that attains the minimum, not the minimum value of the function.

traps: Reading the cost as an average. The lecture's version is a sum.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Why does least squares use squared error and a factor of one half? Could you use something else?
plain: You can use other penalties, such as the absolute value of the error, and that is a legitimate method. Squared error is popular because its gradient is clean and its minimum can be found exactly with a formula, which mattered when Gauss did the arithmetic by hand. It also matches a statistical assumption that errors are roughly normally distributed, which the course derives later. The one half is only cosmetic: multiplying the objective by a positive constant does not change which parameters are best, and the half cancels the 2 that appears when you differentiate.
deep: Squared error makes $J$ a convex quadratic in $\theta$ with a gradient linear in $\theta$, so the normal equations give a closed form. Absolute error is a valid regression (least absolute deviations) but is not smooth and has no closed form. Under Gaussian noise, maximum likelihood gives least squares, which the lecture promises for later. Also $\arg\min_\theta cJ(\theta)=\arg\min_\theta J(\theta)$ for any $c>0$. The lecturer adds that with a large amount of data the exact form of the loss matters less than people expect, and that the classification loss (softmax) comes in the next lecture.
say: Squared error is a choice, not a law. Absolute error is also valid. I use squares because the gradient is a simple linear expression, so there's an exact closed form solution, and that's why Gauss used it. It also corresponds to assuming normally distributed errors, which gets derived later. The trade off is that squares punish large errors heavily, so outliers have a lot of influence. The factor of one half changes nothing about the best parameters, since scaling an objective doesn't move its minimizer. It just cancels the 2 you get when you differentiate.
must_mention: gradient is linear, closed form exists
absolute error is a valid alternative
constant factor does not change the minimizer

followups.q: What is the downside of squares?
followups.a: Large errors dominate, so outliers have a lot of influence on the fit.

traps: Saying squared error is the only correct loss.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Explain gradient descent. Why does stepping against the gradient reduce the loss?
plain: Gradient descent finds low points of a function by repeatedly walking downhill. At your current parameters, the gradient points in the direction that increases the loss fastest, so you step the opposite way. This works because near any point a smooth function looks like a straight line, its first order Taylor approximation, and a small step against that line's slope lowers the value. You repeat until the loss stops dropping. It only uses local slope information and does no search for the true minimum along the way.
deep:
Near $	heta_0$: $f(	heta)\approx f(	heta_0)+
abla f(	heta_0)^	op(	heta-	heta_0)$. The gradient is the direction of steepest increase, so moving along $-
abla f$ decreases this linear approximation fastest. Algorithm: choose an initial $	heta$ (random or zero), then repeat $	heta\leftarrow	heta-\alpha
abla J(	heta)$. This is a first order method with no line search. For convex, bowl shaped functions there are no spurious local minima, whereas non convex functions can trap the iterate. Initialization does not matter for least squares but matters for modern models.
say: Gradient descent minimizes a function by taking repeated small steps downhill. The gradient points in the direction the loss increases fastest, so I step in the opposite direction, scaled by a step size. It works because a smooth function looks linear locally, so a small step against the slope must lower the value. I repeat until the loss stops falling. It only uses local information, so on a non convex function it can get stuck in a local minimum, while on a convex bowl shaped function like least squares it heads to the global minimum.
must_mention: local minima on non convex functions

followups.q: Does the starting point matter?
followups.a: Not for least squares, because it is convex, but it does for non convex models such as neural networks.

traps: Claiming gradient descent always finds the global minimum.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Derive the gradient descent update rule for least squares.
plain: Differentiate the squared error for one example with respect to a weight: the 2 from the square cancels the one half, leaving the prediction error times the matching input. Summing over all examples gives the gradient for that weight. The update subtracts the step size times that sum. The shape error times input shows up again and again in later models, so it is worth memorizing. Intuitively, a weight on a feature that is large when you over predict gets pushed down.
deep: With $r_i=h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}=\theta^\top x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}$, the chain rule gives $\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\tfrac12 r_i^2=r_i\,x^{(i)}_j$. So $$\frac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\big)x^{(i)}_j,\qquad \theta_j:=\theta_j-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\big)x^{(i)}_j,$$ or in vector form $\theta:=\theta-\alpha X^\top(X\theta-y)$. This is batch gradient descent, which uses all $n$ examples per step. For a nonlinear $h$ an extra factor appears, the derivative of $h$ with respect to the parameters. I checked the gradient against finite differences on a small example.
say: For one example, the derivative of half the squared error with respect to weight j is the error, prediction minus label, times feature j. The two from the square cancels the half. Summing over examples gives the full gradient, and the update subtracts the step size times that sum. In vector form it's theta minus alpha times X transpose times X theta minus y. Each weight moves in proportion to how much its feature contributed to the errors. This error times input pattern shows up again in logistic regression and other models, with an extra factor for nonlinear predictions.

followups.q: What changes if the prediction is nonlinear in theta?
followups.a: There is an extra factor, the derivative of the prediction with respect to the parameters.

traps: Forgetting the sum over examples in batch gradient descent.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: What does the step size do in gradient descent, and what goes wrong if it is too small or too large?
plain: The step size, also called the learning rate, sets how far you move each time and reflects how much you trust the local slope. Too small and you creep toward the minimum and need very many steps. Too large and you overshoot, bouncing from one side of the bowl to the other, and the loss can grow instead of shrink. Example: fit a line to the points (1, 2), (2, 3) and (3, 5) using the summed squared error. The best line is one third plus 1.5 times x. Step size 0.1 converges to it, and step size 0.15 blows up.
deep: For $J=\tfrac12\|X\theta-y\|^2$ the Hessian is $X^\top X$, and gradient descent converges exactly when $0<\alpha<2/\lambda_{\max}(X^\top X)$. For the points above, $X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}3&6\\6&14\end{pmatrix}$ with $\lambda_{\max}\approx16.64$, so the threshold is about $0.12$. I ran it: $\alpha=0.1$ reaches $(0.333,1.500)$ and $\alpha=0.15$ diverges. With SGD the noise makes the iterate wander in a ball whose size scales with the step size. The best step size also depends on other quantities such as batch size and normalization, so in practice you tune it by watching the loss.
say: The step size controls how far each update moves. It reflects how much I trust the gradient as a guide. Too small and training crawls, needing huge numbers of steps. Too large and the updates overshoot the minimum and bounce back and forth, and the loss can even blow up. I checked a tiny example, fitting a line to three points. A step of 0.1 converged, while 0.15 diverged, because for least squares the step must stay below two over the largest eigenvalue of X transpose X. In practice I watch the loss curve and adjust the step.
must_mention: step size reflects trust in the gradient

followups.q: How do you see a too large step in practice?
followups.a: The loss oscillates or grows instead of falling smoothly.

traps: Assuming a larger step always speeds up training.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Why use minibatch SGD instead of full batch gradient descent, and what does the update look like?
plain: Full batch gradient descent reads every training example before it takes a single step. If the dataset is the whole internet, that is hopelessly slow. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a small random batch of examples and steps immediately. Each step is noisier but far cheaper, so you can take vastly more of them. This old, simple trick is a main reason models could scale to huge datasets, and the training loops in libraries like PyTorch are minibatch SGD under the hood.
deep: Minibatch update: $$\theta:=\theta-\alpha_B\sum_{i\in B}\big(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\big)x^{(i)},$$ where $B$ is a random subset with $|B|\ll n$. Cost per step drops from $O(nd)$ to $O(|B|d)$. The method goes back to Robbins and Monro in the 1950s and keeps being rediscovered. The step size $\alpha_B$ can differ from the full batch step, since it depends on other quantities such as how the loss is normalized by batch size. The lecturer calls it the real workhorse and says it will be the main tool for the rest of the course.
say: Full batch gradient descent needs a pass over the whole dataset for every single update, which is far too slow at large scale. Minibatch SGD computes the gradient on a small random batch and updates right away. The gradient is noisier, but each step is much cheaper, so I can take many more steps in the same time. That trade is why this very old algorithm scales to huge datasets. The update is the same error times feature rule, summed over just the batch, with its own step size. Modern training loops are essentially this.
must_mention: gradient from a small random batch
full batch needs a pass over all data

followups.q: What does the batch size change?
followups.a: Noise in the gradient estimate and the cost per step.

traps: Believing SGD is a different objective rather than a cheaper estimate of the same gradient.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Why must minibatches be a random sample of the data? What goes wrong otherwise?
plain: Suppose you showed the model all the cat photos first and all the dog photos afterwards. Early updates would teach it that everything is a cat, and later updates would swing it to the opposite extreme. A random batch is a miniature copy of the whole dataset, so its gradient points roughly the way the full gradient does. That is the second statistical assumption SGD relies on, after the assumption that the training set resembles the real world. For complicated tasks it gets harder to guarantee that a batch is representative.
deep: A uniformly random batch gives an unbiased estimate of the full gradient: $\mathbb{E}[\nabla J_B]=\nabla J$ up to scaling. A batch drawn in a systematic order (all cats, then all dogs) gives gradients that are biased and correlated from step to step. The lecture lists two assumptions: the training set represents the world, and the batches represent the training set. Practitioners sometimes build batches deliberately, for example mixing positive and negative examples that look alike, a theme returned to later in the course.
say: Random batches matter because each batch should be a small, fair copy of the whole training set, so its gradient points roughly the same way as the full gradient. If I fed all cats first and then all dogs, the model would first learn that everything is a cat, then swing to the opposite extreme. That's a biased, correlated sequence of updates. So SGD rests on two assumptions: the training set represents the real world, and each batch represents the training set. When tasks are complicated, that second assumption is harder to guarantee, and people sometimes design batches on purpose.
must_mention: batch is a fair sample of the dataset

followups.q: What are the two assumptions?
followups.a: The training set reflects the real world, and each batch reflects the training set.

traps: Feeding data in the order it was stored without shuffling.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Should minibatches be sampled with or without replacement, and what does the coupon collector problem warn about?
plain: Textbook SGD draws each example at random with replacement, so some examples repeat and others are missed for a while. In practice people shuffle the dataset once and sweep through it, which is sampling without replacement and is easier to implement. Theory and experiments suggest the difference is small, and shuffling often converges slightly better. The coupon collector problem explains the worry about random draws: with 10 coupons to collect, the first few arrive quickly but the last takes a long time, so rare examples can go unseen for long stretches.
deep: With replacement, the expected number of draws to see all $n$ items is about $n\ln n$ (coupon collector; for $n=10$ it is about $29$ draws), and the wait for the final item has high variance. Without replacement (random reshuffling), every example appears exactly once per pass. The lecturer says theory and experiments suggest the difference is small for large datasets, that shuffling tends to match better, and that there are counterexamples. A practical warning: a PyTorch data loader iterates in stored order unless shuffling is switched on. For language models, some data such as code is deliberately repeated, a topic called data mixing.
say: In theory SGD samples with replacement, but in practice most people shuffle the data once and sweep through it, which is sampling without replacement. Evidence suggests the difference is small, and shuffling often works a bit better. The coupon collector problem shows the risk of pure random draws: the last few distinct items take a long time to show up, so rare examples can be missed for a long stretch. Shuffling guarantees every example is seen once per pass. One practical warning: a data loader reads in stored order unless I turn shuffling on, which matters if the data is sorted.
must_mention: with replacement can miss or repeat examples
coupon collector: last item takes longest

followups.q: Is it ever right to repeat data on purpose?
followups.a: Yes, in language model training some data such as code is repeated deliberately, which is part of data mixing.

traps: Leaving the default data loader unshuffled on sorted data.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: How do you choose a batch size, and what is surprising about its effect on training?
plain: In practice the batch size is set by hardware: as large as fits in the GPU's fast memory while keeping the chip busy, because that gives the most training per dollar. The statistics are murkier. About 15 years ago the common belief was that small batches are better because you get many more updates, which is true when data is very redundant, like 90 photos of the same cat. Then results appeared where a batch size change made training loss and test performance disagree. Lower training loss did not mean better generalization, which the lecturer sums up as optimization being a leaky abstraction.
deep: Trade off: a bigger batch gives a lower variance gradient but costs more per step and gives fewer updates per pass, while small batches help when examples are redundant, since a full batch of near duplicates wastes computation. Hardware: the batch is chosen to fit in HBM, the memory on the chip, and to maximize model FLOPs utilization (MFU), which labs report. At multi gigawatt scale, keeping hardware loaded often matters more than fine statistical tuning. The lecture recounts being surprised by a result where worse training loss came with better generalization, since optimization quality was assumed to track test quality. Batches can also be designed, for example mixing similar looking positives and negatives.
say: In practice the batch size is mostly a hardware decision: I pick the largest batch that fits in GPU memory while keeping utilization high. The statistics are less clear. A common old belief was that small batches are better because they give more updates, which holds when data is redundant. Then results showed that changing the batch size could make training loss and test performance disagree, so a lower training loss didn't guarantee better generalization. The lesson I take is that optimization is a leaky abstraction, so I judge a setting by validation results, not training loss alone.
must_mention: largest batch that fits in GPU memory
small batches help with redundant data
training loss and generalization can disagree

followups.q: What is MFU?
followups.a: Model FLOPs utilization, the fraction of the hardware's peak compute that training actually uses.

followups.q: Why might a full batch waste compute?
followups.a: If the data has many near duplicates, the extra copies add little new information per step.

traps: Choosing the setting with the lowest training loss and ignoring held out performance.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: How does the goal of optimization in machine learning differ from classical statistics, and how do you know when to stop training?
plain: In statistics you often want to recover the true parameter values and prove you are close to them, with tests that say when the gradient is small enough. In machine learning the goal is good predictions, so many different parameter settings are fine as long as the predictions are close enough. That is why large models often train until the compute budget runs out and are then evaluated. For convex models you can measure how far you are from the optimum. For neural networks you cannot, so you watch the loss curves and decide partly based on resources.
deep: Statistics: parameter recovery guarantees, bounds on $\|\hat\theta-\theta^\star\|$, and stopping tests on the gradient norm. Machine learning: prediction quality, with no need to reach $\theta^\star$ (in the lecturer's words, when the compute is used up you stop). For convex objectives such as generalized linear models, which come in the next weeks, you can certify how far you are from the optimum. For neural networks the loss landscape is complicated, loss can plateau and then abilities can appear suddenly, so you cannot tell whether you are stuck or close. In practice you monitor the loss and metrics, and the stopping time is an engineering decision about GPU time.
say: Classical statistics often cares about recovering the true parameters, with guarantees and tests that tell you when the optimizer is close enough. In machine learning I care about predictions, so there can be many parameter settings that work equally well and I don't need to find a particular one. That's why big training runs often just stop when the compute budget is spent. For convex models I can bound how far I am from the optimum. For neural networks I can't, so I watch the loss and validation metrics and decide, partly on resources.
must_mention: neural networks have no principled stopping rule

followups.q: Why can't you tell if a neural network run is stuck?
followups.a: The loss can plateau and then drop as new abilities appear, so a flat curve does not prove convergence.

traps: Claiming there is always a gradient norm threshold that tells you when to stop.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: What practical tools exist for setting the step size beyond one fixed number?
plain: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam, AdamW and Adagrad adjust the step size for you, per parameter, based on what they have seen so far. Schedules change the step over time, and a cosine schedule that lowers it smoothly during training worked well for image models. Averaging the parameters along the SGD path reduces the bouncing, similar to using a bigger batch. In many research projects people simply keep the standard settings, because careful schedule tuning is mostly done in large production runs.
deep: Adagrad (developed by John Duchi and collaborators) adapts a step size per coordinate, and Adam and AdamW are the common choices for deep networks. Schedules include linear and exponential decay and cosine decay, and the lecture notes that several decay rules are closely related. Averaging the iterates reduces the noise of SGD and imitates a larger batch. The best step size depends on batch size and on normalization of the loss, and recipes do not transfer freely between image and text models because the architectures and the data distributions differ. A bandit based tuning method (Hyperband) is previewed for later.
say: Beyond one fixed step size, I can use adaptive optimizers like Adam, AdamW or Adagrad, which adjust the step per parameter from the gradients they've seen. I can also use a schedule, such as cosine decay, that shrinks the step over training. Averaging the iterates along the SGD path reduces the bouncing, a bit like a bigger batch. In practice, most people start with standard settings and tune the step size by watching the loss. Recipes also don't transfer automatically between image and text models, because architectures and data distributions differ.
must_mention: Adam, AdamW, Adagrad adapt step per parameter
recipes depend on batch size and normalization

followups.q: What does iterate averaging imitate?
followups.a: A larger batch, because averaging smooths the noise in the SGD trajectory.

traps: Copying an image model's learning rate recipe to a text model unchanged.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: Derive the normal equations for least squares.
plain: Stack all the training inputs as rows of a matrix X and all the prices into a vector y. The cost becomes half the squared length of X times theta minus y. Set its gradient to zero, because at the bottom of a bowl shaped function the slope is zero in every direction. That gives linear equations: X transpose X times theta equals X transpose y. If X transpose X can be inverted, theta equals its inverse times X transpose y, found in one shot with no iteration.
deep: Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(d+1)}$ have rows $x^{(i)\top}$ (the design matrix) and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Then $$J(\theta)=\tfrac12\|X\theta-y\|_2^2=\tfrac12\big(\theta^\top X^\top X\theta-2y^\top X\theta+y^\top y\big),\qquad \nabla_\theta J=X^\top X\theta-X^\top y.$$ Setting the gradient to zero gives $X^\top X\theta=X^\top y$, so $\hat\theta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$. A stationary point is a global minimum because the Hessian $X^\top X$ is positive semidefinite, so $J$ is convex. Check: for the points (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), $X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}3&6\\6&14\end{pmatrix}$ and $X^\top y=(10,23)^\top$, which gives $\hat\theta=(1/3,\,3/2)$.
say: I stack the inputs into a design matrix X and the labels into a vector y, so the cost is half the squared norm of X theta minus y. Expanding and differentiating gives the gradient X transpose X theta minus X transpose y. At the minimum the gradient is zero, so X transpose X theta equals X transpose y, and if X transpose X is invertible, theta is its inverse times X transpose y. Zero gradient is enough because the cost is convex. I checked it on three points and got intercept one third and slope one and a half.
must_mention: design matrix X and label vector y
gradient is X transpose X theta minus X transpose y
convexity makes it a global minimum

followups.q: Why is a zero gradient enough here?
followups.a: The cost is convex, since its Hessian X transpose X is positive semidefinite, so any stationary point is a global minimum.

traps: Forgetting that the closed form needs X transpose X to be invertible.

topic: CS229 L2: Linear regression and SGD
q: When does the normal equation break, and what does the solution set look like then?
plain: The formula needs X transpose X to be invertible. That fails when some feature is an exact combination of others, or when there are fewer examples than parameters. Then there is no single best parameter vector. If one solution exists, you can add any vector from the null space of X transpose X and the predictions on the training data do not change, so a whole subspace of answers is equally good. In the lecture's setting there are many more examples than parameters, so the inverse exists. X transpose X is always positive semidefinite, meaning it never has a negative eigenvalue.
deep: $X^\top X\succeq0$ always, and it is invertible if and only if $X$ has full column rank, which needs $n\ge d+1$ and no collinear features. Otherwise the solutions form $\hat\theta+\mathcal{N}(X^\top X)$, and $\mathcal{N}(X^\top X)=\mathcal{N}(X)$. Example: a single training example with three entries gives $\operatorname{rank}(X^\top X)=1$, so it is singular (checked). Standard remedies, not derived in this lecture: the pseudoinverse (minimum norm solution) and regularization. Gradient descent started at zero also converges to the minimum norm solution.
say: The normal equation needs X transpose X to be invertible, meaning X has full column rank. That breaks when there are fewer examples than parameters or when some features are exact linear combinations of others. Then the best parameters are not unique: I can add any vector from the null space and the training predictions stay the same, so there's a whole subspace of equally good solutions. X transpose X is always positive semidefinite, so it never has negative eigenvalues. The usual fixes are the pseudoinverse or regularization, and gradient descent from zero lands on the minimum norm solution.
must_mention: null space gives a subspace of solutions
X transpose X is positive semidefinite

followups.q: Name two remedies.
followups.a: The pseudoinverse, which picks the minimum norm solution, and regularization such as adding a ridge penalty.

traps: Inverting X transpose X numerically when features are collinear.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: What probabilistic model sits behind least squares?
plain: Assume each label was produced by a hidden true parameter vector plus random noise, so y equals theta transpose x plus epsilon. You never see the true theta or the noise, but the model says each observed label is a clean linear signal plus a small random error. The noise stands for measurement error, or for effects you know exist but choose not to model. Seen this way, fitting becomes a question about probability: which theta makes the observed labels most believable? That question has a clean answer, and it reproduces least squares.
deep: $y^{(i)}=\theta^\top x^{(i)}+\epsilon^{(i)}$, with the noise $\epsilon^{(i)}$ random, zero mean, iid, and (in this lecture) Gaussian with variance $\sigma^2$. Therefore $y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta^\top x^{(i)},\sigma^2)$: the mean shifts by $\theta^\top x^{(i)}$ and the variance is unchanged, because the linear part is deterministic given $x$. The lecturer frames modeling as an exercise in abstraction (all models are wrong, some are useful): the noise lumps together real measurement error and things you could model but do not. This probabilistic framing still lurks under many modern models.
say: The model says each label is a true linear signal, theta transpose x, plus random noise. I never see the true theta or the noise, but I assume the noise has zero mean, is independent across examples, and has the same variance, usually Gaussian. The noise covers measurement error and anything I choose not to model. That turns fitting into a probability question: which theta makes the labels I observed most likely? Under these assumptions, answering that question gives exactly the least squares solution, so least squares gets a statistical justification.
must_mention: label equals linear signal plus noise
noise is random with zero mean
iid Gaussian with variance sigma squared

followups.q: What is the distribution of y given x and theta?
followups.a: A Gaussian with mean theta transpose x and variance sigma squared.

traps: Treating the noise as something you can observe or subtract out.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: What do the zero mean and iid assumptions on the noise mean, and when do they fail?
plain: Zero mean means the errors have no systematic bias: on average they do not push labels up or down, so nothing hides a shift the regression cannot see. Independent and identically distributed, or iid, means each error is drawn separately from the same distribution, so one error tells you nothing about another. Both fail in realistic ways. If you merge data from a precise instrument and a noisy one, the errors do not share one variance, and a basic model ignores this. The iid assumption is also made partly because it makes the math tractable.
deep: Zero mean: $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{(i)}]=0$. Independence: $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{(i)}\epsilon^{(j)}]=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{(i)}]\,\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{(j)}]$ for $i\ne j$. Identical distribution: every error has the same variance $\sigma^2=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^2]$; the lecturer models only this first nontrivial moment. Failure modes: biased errors (a systematic shift), different variances per source, and dependent errors, such as repeated measurements from the same unit. Each can be modeled with a richer model. The lecturer calls iid a very strong assumption in general, adopted largely for computational reasons.
say: Zero mean says the noise isn't systematically biased: on average it doesn't push labels up or down. If it did, there'd be a hidden shift the regression couldn't see. Independent and identically distributed says each error is drawn separately from the same distribution, so errors don't inform each other and share one variance. Both can fail. If I pool data from a precise sensor and a sloppy one, the variances differ. If measurements come from the same person repeatedly, errors are dependent. Each failure can be modeled, but the simple model ignores them, mainly to keep the math tractable.

followups.q: Name a realistic violation of identical distribution.
followups.a: Pooling data from two sources whose errors have different variances.

traps: Believing iid is a fact about the data rather than a modeling choice.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Why is the Gaussian the default noise model, and when should you not use it?
plain: A Gaussian is described by just a center and a spread. Sums of many small independent effects tend to look Gaussian, because of the central limit theorem, so it is a good first approximation for noise. The question to ask is not whether the data is exactly Gaussian but whether the Gaussian model is good enough for what you need. If it approximates your data badly and you need the errors modeled more precisely, choose a different distribution. A single Gaussian is also symmetric with one peak, so it cannot capture skewed errors or several noise sources.
deep: The central limit theorem (and the law of large numbers) justifies the Gaussian as a good first model for aggregate noise. The Gaussian is also the maximum entropy distribution for a given mean and variance (a standard fact, not derived in the lecture), so it adds no assumption beyond the first two moments. A single Gaussian is symmetric and unimodal, so it cannot represent biased or skewed errors, or a mixture of noise sources such as two stations with different variances; mixtures of Gaussians come in a later lecture. The lecturer's test is usefulness: is the approximation good enough for the task, not is the data really Gaussian.
say: I use the Gaussian by default because it needs only a mean and a variance, and because sums of many small independent effects look roughly Gaussian by the central limit theorem. So it's a sensible first approximation for noise. The right question is whether it's good enough for my purpose, not whether the data is exactly Gaussian. It breaks down when the errors are skewed, have heavy tails, or come from several sources, since a single Gaussian is symmetric with one peak. Then I'd move to a richer model such as a mixture of Gaussians.
must_mention: described by mean and variance only

followups.q: What would you use for two noise sources?
followups.a: A mixture of Gaussians, one component per source, covered in a later lecture.

traps: Saying the Gaussian is chosen because real data is exactly Gaussian.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Write the Gaussian density and explain what each part does.
plain: The Gaussian density is a bell shaped curve centered at the mean. Its height at a point depends on the squared distance from the mean, divided by two times the variance, inside a negative exponential, so points far from the center get very little probability. The variance sets the width: a small variance gives a tall narrow bell and a large one gives a flat wide bell. A constant in front makes the total probability equal to one. About 99.7 percent of the probability lies within three standard deviations, and you never need to memorize the constant because it vanishes when you optimize.
deep: $$p(z;\mu,\sigma^2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{(z-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big),\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2).$$ The normalizing constant depends only on $\sigma$ and not on $\mu$, because shifting the curve does not change its area. The exponent carries the squared distance to the mean, which is where least squares will come from. The 2 in $2\sigma^2$ cancels when differentiating. Mass within $\pm3\sigma$ is about $99.7\%$. The density is symmetric about $\mu$ and never exactly zero.
say: The Gaussian density is a constant times the exponential of minus the squared distance from the mean, divided by two sigma squared. The exponent is the part that matters: points far from the mean get quickly smaller probability, and the variance sets the scale, so a small variance gives a tall narrow bell and a large one a flat wide bell. The constant in front only makes the area equal to one, and it depends on sigma but not on the mean. About 99.7 percent of the mass lies within three standard deviations. When I maximize likelihood, the constant drops out.
must_mention: exponent of squared distance over two sigma squared
normalizing constant depends on sigma only

followups.q: Why does the mean not appear in the normalizing constant?
followups.a: Shifting the curve does not change the area under it.

traps: Spending effort memorizing the normalizing constant.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: What is the likelihood, and what is the principle of maximum likelihood?
plain: A likelihood function tells you, for each candidate parameter value theta, how probable the data you actually observed would be if that theta were the truth. Maximum likelihood says to choose the theta that makes your observed data most probable. Think of it as picking, among all the distributions that could have generated your dataset, the one that explains it best. To compare two candidates you compute the probability of the whole dataset under each, and the bigger score wins. The data is fixed, and you search over parameters.
deep: $L(\theta)=p\big(y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(n)}\mid x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(n)};\theta\big)$, viewed as a function of $\theta$ with the data held fixed, and $\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=\arg\max_\theta L(\theta)$. In the notation $p(y\mid x;\theta)$, the bar marks what we condition on (the observed input $x$), and the semicolon marks $\theta$ as a parameter that indexes a family of distributions, not an event we condition on. The inputs $x^{(i)}$ are given, so the search is over $\theta$ only. The likelihood is not the probability that $\theta$ is true.
say: The likelihood of a parameter value is the probability the model assigns to the data I actually observed, if that parameter were the truth. Maximum likelihood picks the parameter that makes my observed data most probable. So among all the distributions in my family that could have generated the dataset, I choose the one that explains it best. The data is fixed and I search over parameters. One caution: a high likelihood is not the probability that the parameter is correct. It only ranks parameters by how well they explain the data.
must_mention: probability of the observed data given theta
not the probability that theta is true

followups.q: What does the semicolon in p of y given x semicolon theta mean?
followups.a: Theta is a parameter indexing the distribution, not a conditioning event.

traps: Reading the likelihood as the probability that the parameter is correct.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Why does the iid assumption let us write the likelihood as a product?
plain: The probability of the whole dataset is a joint probability over all the labels at once, a huge function of every label together. If the examples are independent, that joint probability factors into the product of one probability per example, which is what independence means. That turns one giant n dimensional object into n small pieces, and each piece is just the Gaussian formula for one data point. Identically distributed means every factor has the same form with the same parameter.
deep: $L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p\big(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta\big)$ follows from independence (the joint factorizes) and identical distribution (the same functional form and the same $\theta$ in every factor). We condition on the $x^{(i)}$ because they are observed. Without independence, for example with correlated errors, you would need the joint distribution (a covariance matrix) instead of $n$ separate terms. The lecturer cautions that this is a modeling assumption, and it may be wrong for your data.
say: The likelihood is the joint probability of all the labels given all the inputs, which in general is a huge function of every label at once. If the examples are independent, that joint probability factors into the product of one term per example. That's literally the definition of independence. It reduces an n dimensional object to n small, identical looking terms, each one just the model's probability for a single example. Identically distributed means every term has the same form and the same parameter. If errors were correlated, I'd need the full joint distribution instead.
