must_mention: identical form with the same theta

followups.q: What replaces the product if errors are correlated?
followups.a: The full joint distribution, for example a multivariate Gaussian with a covariance matrix.

traps: Applying the product formula to dependent data without noticing.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Why do we maximize the log likelihood instead of the likelihood itself?
plain: Taking the logarithm turns a product of n probabilities into a sum of n terms. A sum is easier to differentiate, and it is numerically stable, while a product of many numbers below one shrinks toward zero: 1000 probabilities of 0.1 multiply to 10 to the minus 1000, which a standard 64 bit float cannot represent. The logarithm always increases as its input increases, so the theta that maximizes the likelihood also maximizes the log likelihood. In the Gaussian case the log also removes the exponential. It does need every probability to be positive.
deep: $\ell(\theta)=\log L(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p\big(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta\big)$. The logarithm is a monotone transformation, so $\arg\max_\theta\ell=\arg\max_\theta L$. The additive form is what stochastic gradient methods need, since a minibatch of terms gives an unbiased estimate of the gradient. It requires $p>0$ because $\log 0$ is undefined: the Gaussian density is never exactly zero, and for discrete distributions you must check the support. Maximizing $\ell$ is the same as minimizing the negative log likelihood, the usual loss in practice.
say: Taking the log turns the product of n probabilities into a sum of n log probabilities. That's much easier to differentiate, and it's numerically stable: multiply a thousand probabilities of point one and you get ten to the minus a thousand, which underflows in floating point, while the sum of logs is a perfectly ordinary number. Since the log is monotone, the best parameter doesn't change. It also fits stochastic gradient methods, because a sum over examples can be estimated from a minibatch. The one condition is that probabilities must be positive, because the log of zero is undefined.
must_mention: log is monotone so the argmax is unchanged

followups.q: What loss do you minimize in practice?
followups.a: The negative log likelihood.

traps: Maximizing a long product of probabilities directly in floating point.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Show that maximum likelihood with Gaussian noise is the same as least squares.
plain: Plug the Gaussian density into the log likelihood. Each example contributes a constant plus minus the squared error divided by two sigma squared. The constants do not depend on theta, so they play no role in the search for the best theta. What remains is minus one over sigma squared times half the sum of squared errors, which is minus the least squares cost J. Maximizing the log likelihood is therefore the same as minimizing J, so least squares is maximum likelihood for linear regression with iid Gaussian noise of fixed variance.
deep: $$\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\log\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}-\frac{\big(y^{(i)}-\theta^\top x^{(i)}\big)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big]=n\log\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}J(\theta),$$ with $J(\theta)=\frac12\sum_i\big(y^{(i)}-\theta^\top x^{(i)}\big)^2$. So $\arg\max_\theta\ell=\arg\min_\theta J$, whatever fixed value $\sigma^2$ takes. I confirmed numerically that minimizing the Gaussian negative log likelihood reproduces the normal equation solution. The variance $\sigma^2$ can be assumed, set outside the model, or fitted as an extra parameter. If your conclusions change a lot with small changes to such a setting, be worried.
say: Take the log likelihood with Gaussian noise. Each example adds a constant minus its squared error divided by two sigma squared. The constants don't involve theta, so they can't affect which theta is best. What's left is a negative constant times the sum of squared errors, which is the least squares cost. So maximizing the log likelihood and minimizing the least squares cost pick the same theta, for any fixed sigma. That shows least squares is maximum likelihood for linear regression with iid Gaussian noise. It also explains why squared error is a natural loss under that assumption.
must_mention: plug the Gaussian into the log likelihood
constants do not depend on theta
remaining term is minus J over sigma squared
same minimizer for any fixed sigma

followups.q: Does the value of sigma squared change the fitted theta?
followups.a: No, for a fixed sigma it only rescales the objective, so the minimizer is the same.

followups.q: How can sigma squared be handled?
followups.a: Assume it, fit it outside the model, or fit it jointly as another parameter.

traps: Forgetting that this equivalence needs iid Gaussian noise with constant variance.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: What is the maximum likelihood recipe, and why is it so general?
plain: First, write down a probability model for how the data was generated, with unknown parameters. Second, take the log of the likelihood so it becomes a sum over examples. Third, optimize that sum with gradient methods, using minibatches when the dataset is large. Least squares fell out of this recipe with Gaussian noise, and logistic regression will fall out of it for yes or no labels. When you meet an unfamiliar kind of target, such as counts or categories, you pick a distribution that fits it and the same recipe applies.
deep: Recipe: (1) choose a model $p(y\mid x;\theta)$; (2) form the log likelihood, which is additive over examples; (3) maximize it with gradient ascent or stochastic gradient ascent, or equivalently minimize the negative log likelihood. The lecturer says many methods that look quite different in the older literature are instances of this one framework, and that it generalizes from continuous to discrete outputs up to modern AI models. It is the foundation of the next lecture on generalized linear models. Negative log likelihood is the standard training loss in classification and language modeling (cross entropy).
say: The recipe has three steps. First, I model the data with a probability distribution that has unknown parameters. Second, I take the log of the likelihood so it becomes a sum over examples. Third, I optimize that sum with gradient methods, using minibatches if the data is large. It's general because only the first step changes: Gaussian noise gives least squares, a Bernoulli model gives logistic regression, and other distributions cover counts or categories. Many methods that look different historically are just this recipe with different probability models.
must_mention: only the distribution changes between models

followups.q: Which models have we derived from it so far?
followups.a: Least squares from Gaussian noise and logistic regression from a Bernoulli label model.

traps: Thinking each new model needs a brand new training algorithm.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Why not just use least squares for binary classification?
plain: You can, and it often works better than you would expect, but it is a poor fit for the job. In classification only the boundary between classes matters, yet least squares tries to fit a straight surface through all the label values, so a few points far from the boundary pull the line and shift it. It also predicts values like 7 or negative 40 when only yes or no are valid answers, so you need extra code to round the outputs. A model built for the task should output a number between 0 and 1 that you can read as a probability.
deep: With labels in $\{0,1\}$, least squares fits a hyperplane to the target values, so points far from the boundary on the correct side still incur large squared error and tilt the fit: it is trying to match the labels' center of mass rather than locate a separating surface. Outputs are unbounded, so a thresholding wrapper is needed. The lecturer adds that least squares frequently works on real data anyway, since modeling is a matter of degree, and that high dimensional data behaves oddly (nearest and farthest points can be nearly equally far). The principled alternative is a probability model with a link function, which is logistic regression.
say: Least squares can work for classification, but it fits the wrong thing. For classification only the boundary matters, but least squares tries to fit a surface through the zero and one labels, so points far from the boundary still pull the fit and shift it. It also outputs numbers like seven or minus forty, which aren't valid answers for yes or no, so I'd need rounding code. It's better to use a model that outputs a probability between zero and one, which is what logistic regression does by passing the linear score through a sigmoid.

followups.q: Does least squares ever work for classification?
followups.a: Often yes in practice, since modeling is a matter of degree, but it is not designed for it.

traps: Saying least squares cannot be used at all for classification.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: What is the logistic regression hypothesis, and what does the sigmoid do?
plain: Logistic regression keeps the linear part, theta transpose x, and passes it through a smooth S shaped function g called the sigmoid, which squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. A very large score gives an output near 1, a very negative score gives an output near 0, and a score of 0 gives exactly one half. You read the output as the probability that the label is 1, and one minus the output as the probability that it is 0. The squashing function must be smooth and increasing, so a higher score never gives a lower probability. A hard threshold would not work for training because it cannot be differentiated.
deep: $h_\theta(x)=g(\theta^\top x)$ with $g(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$, $P(y=1\mid x;\theta)=h_\theta(x)$ and $P(y=0\mid x;\theta)=1-h_\theta(x)$. Example values: $g(0)=0.5$, $g(2)\approx0.881$, $g(-2)\approx0.119$, $g(4)\approx0.982$. The link function must be monotone and smooth, and the sigmoid is the popular choice among many options in the statistics literature. The lecturer notes logistic regression (and softmax for many classes) is the last layer of most chatbots. The score $\theta^\top x$ is sometimes called the logit. Non differentiable alternatives such as a step function are inconvenient for gradient based training.
say: Logistic regression computes the usual linear score, theta transpose x, and passes it through the sigmoid, which squeezes any real number into the interval from zero to one. A big positive score gives a probability near one, a big negative one gives near zero, and a score of zero gives one half. I read the output as the probability that the label is one. The sigmoid is smooth and always increasing, which is what I need for gradient training, unlike a hard threshold. The same idea, extended to many classes as softmax, is the final layer of most language models.
must_mention: linear score passed through a sigmoid

followups.q: What is the output when the score is zero?
followups.a: One half, so the model is undecided exactly on the decision boundary.

traps: Calling the sigmoid output a class label rather than a probability.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Write the likelihood and log likelihood of logistic regression.
plain: For one example, the probability of its label is h if the label is 1 and one minus h if the label is 0. A compact way to write both cases is h to the power y, times one minus h to the power one minus y, because the unused term has exponent zero and equals 1. Multiplying across independent examples gives the likelihood, and taking logs gives a sum: for each example, y times log h plus one minus y times log of one minus h. Maximizing it pushes h toward 1 on positive examples and toward 0 on negative ones.
deep: $p(y\mid x;\theta)=h_\theta(x)^{y}\big(1-h_\theta(x)\big)^{1-y}$, so $$L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}h_\theta(x^{(i)})^{y^{(i)}}\big(1-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)^{1-y^{(i)}},\qquad \ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y^{(i)}\log h_\theta(x^{(i)})+\big(1-y^{(i)}\big)\log\big(1-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)\Big].$$ The negative of this is the binary cross entropy (logistic) loss. Check: with $y=1$ the term reduces to $\log h$, and with $y=0$ to $\log(1-h)$, so each example is penalized by the log of the probability the model gave to the correct label.
say: For one example, the model gives the true label probability h if the label is one and one minus h if it's zero. I write both cases at once as h to the y times one minus h to the one minus y, since the inactive term has exponent zero and equals one. The likelihood is the product over examples, and the log likelihood is a sum where each example contributes y times log h plus one minus y times log of one minus h. Maximizing that pushes the predicted probability up on positives and down on negatives. Its negative is the cross entropy loss.
must_mention: h to the y times one minus h to the one minus y

followups.q: What happens to the term when y is 1?
followups.a: It reduces to log h, so the model is rewarded for giving the true label high probability.

traps: Forgetting the second term for negative examples.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: What is the gradient of the logistic regression log likelihood, and why does it look like the least squares update?
plain: Differentiating the log likelihood gives, for each weight, the sum over examples of the label minus the predicted probability, times that example's feature. This has the same shape as least squares: an error times an input, summed over the data. Because we are maximizing, we add the step rather than subtract it, which is gradient ascent. The only difference from linear regression is that the prediction passes through the sigmoid. The lecturer points out that this error times feature form recurs across a large family of models, which the next lecture explains.
deep: $$\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta_j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y^{(i)}-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)x^{(i)}_j,\qquad \theta_j:=\theta_j+\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y^{(i)}-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)x^{(i)}_j.$$ The minibatch version sums over a random batch, and the equivalent descent on the negative log likelihood is $\theta:=\theta-\alpha X^\top(h-y)$. The clean form comes from the identity $g'(z)=g(z)(1-g(z))$, which cancels the denominators from the logarithms. I verified the gradient against finite differences on synthetic data. This is not an accident: the same form holds for generalized linear models, covered next lecture.
say: The gradient of the log likelihood with respect to weight j is the sum, over examples, of the label minus the predicted probability, times feature j. That's the same error times input form as linear regression, just with the sigmoid inside the prediction. Because I'm maximizing, I add the step: gradient ascent, or equivalently descent on the negative log likelihood. The derivation is some algebra, using the fact that the sigmoid's derivative is g times one minus g, which cancels nicely. This pattern isn't a coincidence. It holds for a whole family of models called generalized linear models.
must_mention: gradient is label minus probability times feature

followups.q: How do you write the same update as descent?
followups.a: Minimize the negative log likelihood, so subtract the step times X transpose times (h minus y).

traps: Using a plus sign when minimizing the negative log likelihood.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Explain Newton's method for optimization and how it differs from gradient descent.
plain: Newton's method finds a zero of a function by approximating it with its tangent line, jumping to where that line crosses zero, and repeating. To maximize a log likelihood you apply it to the gradient, since the best point has zero gradient. In one dimension the update subtracts the function value divided by its slope, and in many dimensions the slope becomes the Hessian matrix of second derivatives, which you invert. It needs no step size, because the tangent line says how far to go. Example: solving theta squared minus 2 equals 0 from 1 gives 1.5, then 1.41667, then 1.41422, close to the square root of 2.
deep: Scalar root finding: $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-f(\theta_t)/f'(\theta_t)$, from setting the first order Taylor model $f(\theta_0)+f'(\theta_0)(\theta-\theta_0)$ to zero. To maximize $\ell$: $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-H^{-1}\nabla\ell(\theta_t)$ with $H=\nabla^2\ell$. If $H$ is singular, use the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. Near the answer, convergence is quadratic: for $\theta^2-2$ from $\theta_0=1$ the errors were $8.6\times10^{-2}$, $2.5\times10^{-3}$, $2.1\times10^{-6}$, $1.6\times10^{-12}$ (computed). On a 200 point synthetic logistic regression I found Newton reached a gradient norm near $4\times10^{-6}$ in 5 iterations, while gradient ascent with step $0.001$ needed 10,000 steps to reach the same parameters.
say: Newton's method finds where a function is zero by repeatedly replacing it with its tangent line and jumping to where that line crosses zero. To optimize a log likelihood I apply it to the gradient. In one dimension the update is theta minus f over f prime. In many dimensions it's theta minus the inverse Hessian times the gradient. There's no step size to tune, and near the solution the error roughly squares each step, so it converges in a handful of iterations. I tried it on a small logistic regression: Newton needed five steps where gradient ascent needed thousands.

followups.q: What if the Hessian is not invertible?
followups.a: Use the pseudoinverse, which returns a least squares or minimum norm step.

traps: Forgetting that Newton applied to optimization uses the gradient as the function whose zero is sought.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Compare the cost per step of SGD, full batch gradient descent and Newton's method. Why is minibatch SGD the workhorse?
plain: SGD costs about the number of features per step because it looks at one example, a minibatch costs batch size times that, and full gradient descent touches every example. Newton's method also builds and inverts a matrix of second derivatives. Newton takes the fewest steps, but each step is enormously expensive. With billions of examples and billions of parameters, even one such step is out of reach, while many cheap noisy steps are not. That trade is why minibatch SGD dominates large scale machine learning.
deep: Per step cost: SGD $O(d)$, minibatch $O(Bd)$, full gradient descent $O(nd)$, Newton $O(nd^2+d^3)$ (forming the Hessian and inverting it). Number of steps: Newton needs few, gradient descent more, SGD many but cheap and noisy. When $n$ and $d$ are both huge, for example training on all available text with $10^{10}$ to $10^{12}$ parameters, the $d^3$ term is infeasible. The lecturer's summary is that Newton wins when measured in steps, but SGD wins on cost, and so minibatch SGD is the workhorse of machine learning.
say: Per step, SGD costs on the order of the number of features d, a minibatch costs batch size times d, full batch gradient descent costs n times d, and Newton's method costs about n times d squared plus d cubed because it forms and inverts the Hessian. Newton needs the fewest steps, but each step is far more expensive. When n and d are in the billions, one Newton step is impossible, while many cheap noisy steps are fine. That's why minibatch SGD is the workhorse at scale, even though it needs more iterations and a tuned step size.
must_mention: full gradient order n times d
Newton n d squared plus d cubed
fewest steps but most expensive each

followups.q: Which term makes Newton infeasible for huge models?
followups.a: The d cubed cost of inverting the Hessian, along with storing a d by d matrix.

traps: Judging optimizers by the number of steps only.

topic: CS229 L3: Maximum likelihood and logistic regression
q: Where do second order methods still appear, and why did machine learning shift from caring about parameters to caring about predictions?
plain: Classical statistics still uses Newton's method and L BFGS, a memory saving variant, on models with a few hundred features or fewer, where you care about exact parameters and can afford the cost. Machine learning mostly uses cheap approximations of the same idea. Methods like Adagrad estimate curvature, often only its diagonal, to decide how far to trust each direction, and Adam can be seen as combining that with momentum. Practitioners also stopped worrying about getting the same parameter vector twice, and started caring about whether the predictions agree.
deep: L-BFGS is a limited memory quasi Newton method, used by classical statistical packages when $d$ is small, because parameter accuracy matters there. Hessian vector products avoid forming the full Hessian. Curvature information says how far a step can be trusted in each direction. Adagrad (Duchi, Hazan and Singer) and AdaDelta approximate it with cheap structure such as a diagonal, other options being diagonal plus low rank or sketching, and Adam combines this idea with momentum. Parameter space versus prediction space: different runs can return different $\theta$ with almost identical $h_\theta$, so machine learning judges stability by the predictions, while statistics usually wants the parameters.
say: Newton's method and L BFGS are still standard in classical statistics, where models have maybe tens or hundreds of features and I care about getting the parameters exactly right. In machine learning I mostly use cheap approximations of second order ideas. Adagrad estimates curvature, often just a diagonal, to decide how much to trust each direction, and Adam combines something similar with momentum. There was also a shift in attitude. Different training runs can give different parameters but nearly identical predictions, and machine learning decided that stability of the predictions is what matters, not the parameters themselves.
must_mention: Newton and L-BFGS for small models in statistics

followups.q: What does L-BFGS stand for conceptually?
followups.a: A limited memory quasi Newton method that approximates the Hessian from recent gradients instead of storing it.

traps: Claiming Newton's method is never used anywhere in machine learning.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Why study the exponential family? What do you get from it?
plain: Least squares and logistic regression looked like two separate methods, one for real valued labels and one for yes or no labels. The exponential family shows they are one method. A large class of distributions can be written in one common form, and for any of them you get a prediction rule, a maximum likelihood objective and an SGD update that look just like the ones you already know. So when you meet a new type of label, such as counts or categories, you pick the matching distribution and the same procedure applies.
deep: The exponential family is a cornerstone of statistics because one functional form covers regression, classification, counts and more, and brings three things with it: inference (the mean and variance follow by differentiating one function), training (maximum likelihood gives a concave problem), and an SGD update of the same error times feature shape. The lecture's message is to think in terms of errors: choose the error distribution that matches the type of $y$ and the rest of the model follows. Textbooks devote whole volumes to generalized linear models, and the course uses only the simplest case $T(y)=y$.
say: The exponential family says that many distributions share one mathematical form, and that form comes with everything I need. If my labels are binary, categorical, real valued, or counts, I pick the matching distribution, and I automatically get a prediction rule, a log likelihood to maximize, and an SGD update with the familiar error times feature shape. So least squares and logistic regression stop being two separate methods. They are two instances of one recipe, and I can extend it to new label types without inventing a new algorithm.
must_mention: inference and training come with it
least squares and logistic regression are instances
choose the distribution to match the label type

followups.q: What kinds of label types does it cover?
followups.a: Binary, multi class, real valued, counts, positive values and more.

traps: Treating least squares and logistic regression as unrelated algorithms.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: State the exponential family form and name each piece.
plain: A distribution is in the exponential family if you can write its probability as three factors. One is a base factor that depends only on the outcome y. Another is the exponential of a parameter vector eta dotted with a statistic of y, which carries the interaction between data and parameter. The third is the exponential of minus a function of eta alone, which makes the probabilities add up to one. For most distributions in this course the statistic is just y itself.
deep: $$p(y;\eta)=b(y)\exp\!\big(\eta^\top T(y)-a(\eta)\big).$$ $\eta$ is the natural parameter, with the same dimension as $T(y)$. $T(y)$ is the sufficient statistic (the course uses $T(y)=y$). $b(y)$ is the base measure and does not depend on $\eta$. $a(\eta)$ is the log partition function: it equals the log of the sum or integral over all $y$ of $b(y)e^{\eta^\top T(y)}$, so subtracting it normalizes the distribution to one. Most of the useful mathematics lives in $a$. The interaction between $\eta$ and $T(y)$ must be linear, though $b$ and $a$ can be nonlinear.
say: The exponential family form is p of y equals b of y times the exponential of eta transpose T of y minus a of eta. Eta is the natural parameter. T of y is the sufficient statistic, and in this course it's just y. B of y is the base measure, which doesn't depend on eta. And a of eta is the log partition function, which is the log of the sum or integral of everything else over all possible y, so it normalizes the distribution. The key structural fact is that eta and T of y interact linearly, and most of the useful math sits in a.

followups.q: What does a of eta do?
followups.a: It is the log of the normalizer, summing or integrating over all y, so that the probabilities add up to one.

traps: Letting the base measure b depend on the parameter eta.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Show that the Bernoulli distribution is in the exponential family and find its natural parameter.
plain: Start from the coin toss probability phi to the y times one minus phi to the one minus y. Take the logarithm and group the terms that multiply y: you get y times the log of phi over one minus phi, plus the log of one minus phi. The coefficient of y is the natural parameter eta, and it is the log odds. Solving for phi gives one over one plus e to the minus eta, which is the sigmoid from logistic regression. So the sigmoid appears automatically when the label is Bernoulli.
deep: $p(y;\phi)=\phi^{y}(1-\phi)^{1-y}=\exp\!\big(y\log\phi+(1-y)\log(1-\phi)\big)=\exp\!\Big(y\log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}+\log(1-\phi)\Big)$. Match with $b(y)\exp(\eta T(y)-a(\eta))$: $T(y)=y$, $b(y)=1$, $\eta=\log\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}$ (the log odds). Inverting, $\phi=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}$, so $1-\phi=\frac{1}{1+e^{\eta}}$ and $a(\eta)=-\log(1-\phi)=\log(1+e^{\eta})$. The logarithm step is valid for $\phi$ strictly between 0 and 1. The sanity check that a is a function of $\eta$ alone passes. Numerically, for $\phi=0.3$ the log odds is $-0.847$ and $a'(\eta)=0.3$, the mean.
say: I write the Bernoulli probability as phi to the y times one minus phi to the one minus y, take the log, and group the terms that multiply y. That gives y times the log of phi over one minus phi, plus the log of one minus phi. So T of y is y, the base measure is one, and the natural parameter eta is the log odds. Inverting that gives phi equals one over one plus e to the minus eta, which is exactly the sigmoid. The log partition function comes out as the log of one plus e to the eta. So logistic regression's sigmoid is built into the Bernoulli.
must_mention: take the log and group terms in y
phi is the sigmoid of eta

followups.q: Why does the sigmoid appear?
followups.a: Inverting the natural parameter, the log odds, gives the sigmoid, so logistic regression falls out of the Bernoulli model.

traps: Forgetting that this works only for phi strictly between 0 and 1.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Show that a Gaussian with fixed variance is in the exponential family.
plain: Write the Gaussian density with variance fixed at 1 and expand the square in the exponent. The expansion produces three kinds of terms: one with y squared, one with the mean times y, and one with the mean squared. The y squared term depends only on y, so it joins the base factor. The mean times y term is exactly the interaction between a parameter and the data, so the mean plays the role of the natural parameter. The mean squared term depends only on the parameter and becomes the log partition function.
deep: $p(y;\mu)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(y-\mu)^2/2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y^2/2}\exp\!\big(\mu y-\mu^2/2\big)$. Hence $b(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y^2/2}$, $T(y)=y$, $\eta=\mu$ and $a(\eta)=\eta^2/2$. The constant (here the variance) causes no trouble. This confirms that both error distributions seen so far, Bernoulli and Gaussian, fit one form. Differentiating gives $a'(\eta)=\eta=\mu$, the mean, and $a''(\eta)=1$, the variance, matching the general rule, and $a$ is convex.
say: I take the Gaussian with fixed variance, say one, and expand the square in the exponent. That produces a y squared term, a mu times y term, and a mu squared term. The y squared piece depends only on y, so it goes into the base measure. The mu times y piece is the linear interaction, so the natural parameter eta is the mean mu. The mu squared piece depends only on the parameter, so a of eta is eta squared over two. So the Gaussian fits the same form as the Bernoulli, and its log partition function is simply a parabola.

followups.q: What are the first and second derivatives of a here?
followups.a: The first is eta, the mean mu, and the second is 1, the variance.

traps: Putting the mean squared term into the base measure.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Why is the derivative of the log partition function the mean, and why does its convexity matter?
plain: The log partition function is the log of a sum over all possible outcomes. When you differentiate a log of a sum, you get a weighted average of the derivative of each term, and here that weighted average is the statistic T(y) weighted by its own probabilities, which is its expected value. The second derivative gives the variance. A variance is never negative, so the log partition function is convex. That makes the negative log likelihood convex, so gradient descent has no bad local minima and can recover the parameters.
deep: With $a(\eta)=\log\int b(y)e^{\eta^\top T(y)}dy$: $\nabla_\eta a=\dfrac{\int T(y)\,b(y)e^{\eta^\top T(y)}dy}{\int b(y)e^{\eta^\top T(y)}dy}=\mathbb{E}[T(y);\eta]$, and differentiating again, $\nabla^2_\eta a=\operatorname{Cov}(T(y);\eta)\succeq0$. Nothing here uses properties of any specific distribution, so inference (the mean and variance) comes free for the whole family. Since $a$ is convex, the negative log likelihood $\sum_i\big(a(\eta^{(i)})-\eta^{(i)\top}T(y^{(i)})\big)$ is convex in $\theta$ when $\eta=\theta^\top x$, so training has no spurious local minima and the parameters can be recovered. The lecture adds that the log partition function is a cumulant generating function: lower order cumulants and moments coincide, higher ones do not. Check: Bernoulli with $\phi=0.3$ gives $a'=0.3$ and $a''=0.21=\phi(1-\phi)$.
say: The log partition function is the log of a sum over all outcomes. Differentiating a log of a sum gives a weighted average of the derivative of each term, and here that works out to the expected value of the statistic T of y. The second derivative gives the variance or covariance. Nothing in that argument depends on a particular distribution, so the mean and variance come for free across the family. And since a variance is nonnegative, the log partition function is convex, so the negative log likelihood is convex too. That means gradient descent has no bad local minima for these models.
must_mention: derivative of the log of a sum is a weighted average
convex, so no bad local minima

followups.q: What is the second derivative of a for a Bernoulli?
followups.a: phi times one minus phi, the Bernoulli variance.

traps: Thinking the mean result is a coincidence of the Gaussian.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Which distributions belong to the exponential family, and which label type goes with each?
plain: Match the distribution to what the label is. A yes or no label uses the Bernoulli distribution, a choice among several classes uses the multinomial distribution, which leads to softmax, and a real valued label uses the Gaussian. A count, such as the number of customers arriving in an hour, uses the Poisson distribution. Positive quantities that decay, like waiting times, use the exponential or gamma distribution. You can even model a distribution over distributions with the Dirichlet. They all fit the same form.
deep: Bernoulli: binary labels, logistic regression. Multinomial: $K$ classes, softmax regression. Gaussian: real valued labels, least squares. Poisson: counts, Poisson regression. Gamma and exponential: positive values such as durations. Dirichlet: distributions over probability vectors. All have the form $b(y)\exp(\eta^\top T(y)-a(\eta))$, so each gets inference, a convex training objective and the same SGD update. The lecture's design advice is to think about the type of error you expect and let that choose the model. In this course the statistic is simply $T(y)=y$, while the GLM textbooks use more elaborate $T$.
say: I pick the distribution by looking at the label. Binary labels get a Bernoulli, which gives logistic regression. Several classes get a multinomial, which gives softmax regression. Real values get a Gaussian, which gives least squares. Counts get a Poisson. Positive, decaying quantities like waiting times get an exponential or gamma. There's even a Dirichlet for distributions over distributions. They all belong to the exponential family, so each one comes with the same machinery: a mean and variance from the log partition function, a convex objective, and the same SGD update.

followups.q: Which distribution would you use for the number of support tickets per day?
followups.a: A Poisson, since the label is a count.

traps: Using a Gaussian for counts without checking whether Poisson fits better.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: What is a generalized linear model? Which choices define it?
plain: A generalized linear model has three ingredients. First, you choose a distribution for the label given the input, matched to the type of label: Bernoulli for yes or no, multinomial for several classes. Second, you make the distribution's natural parameter a linear function of the input, eta equals theta transpose x. Third, you predict the average label under that distribution. Logistic regression and least squares are special cases, and so is softmax regression.
deep: Three design choices: (1) the distribution of $y\mid x;\theta$, an exponential family member chosen by the type of $y$; (2) linearity in the natural parameter, $\eta=\theta^\top x$ (the model parameters $\theta$ are learned, and $\theta^\top x$ mixes them with the data); (3) prediction $h_\theta(x)=\mathbb{E}[y\mid x;\theta]$. For the Bernoulli, $h_\theta(x)=1/(1+e^{-\theta^\top x})$; for the Gaussian, $h_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x$. Everything about the model, the loss and the update then follows from the exponential family, instead of being derived separately for each case.
say: A generalized linear model is built from three choices. First, I pick a distribution for the label given the input, matched to the label type, like Bernoulli for binary or multinomial for categories. Second, I make its natural parameter linear in the input, eta equals theta transpose x. Third, my prediction is the expected value of the label under that distribution. Linear regression, logistic regression and softmax regression are all special cases. Once I've made those choices, the training loss and the SGD update follow from the exponential family without a fresh derivation.
must_mention: natural parameter eta = theta transpose x
prediction is the expectation of y
linear and logistic regression are special cases

followups.q: What is h of x for the Bernoulli GLM?
followups.a: The sigmoid of theta transpose x, the probability that the label is 1.

traps: Thinking generalized linear means the prediction is linear in x. Only the natural parameter is.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: How do you train a GLM, and why does the SGD update always look like error times feature?
plain: Training is maximum likelihood: assuming independent examples, the log likelihood is a sum of the log probability of each label, and you climb it with gradient ascent. When you differentiate the log of an exponential family probability, the term from the statistic contributes the label, and the term from the log partition function contributes the model's predicted mean. So the gradient is the label minus the prediction, times the input. The same update then covers linear regression, logistic regression and every other member of the family.
deep: Log likelihood: $\ell(\theta)=\sum_i\big[\log b(y^{(i)})+\theta^\top x^{(i)}\,y^{(i)}-a(\theta^\top x^{(i)})\big]$ for $T(y)=y$. Using $\nabla a(\eta)=\mathbb{E}[y]=h_\theta(x)$, $$\nabla_\theta\ell=\sum_i\big(y^{(i)}-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)x^{(i)},\qquad \theta:=\theta+\alpha\big(y^{(i)}-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)x^{(i)}.$$ Since $\ell$ is concave in $\theta$ this ascent converges to the global optimum. The loss is determined by the choice of distribution through $\log p$, which is why the loss function changes when the label type changes. This form is not a coincidence: it is the shape for the whole family, and it can run as SGD over minibatches.
say: Training a GLM is maximum likelihood. With independent examples the log likelihood is a sum, and I do gradient ascent on it. When I differentiate the log probability, the statistic term contributes the label y and the log partition term contributes its derivative, which is the predicted mean. So the gradient is y minus the prediction, times the input, summed over examples. That same shape gives linear regression, logistic regression and every other GLM, and since the objective is concave, SGD reaches the global optimum. Only the distribution, and so the loss, changes between models.
must_mention: gradient is label minus prediction times input
derivative of a is the predicted mean

followups.q: What determines the loss function?
followups.a: The choice of distribution, through the log of its probability.

traps: Forgetting the sign flip when writing the update as ascent versus descent.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Distinguish the model parameters, the natural parameter and the canonical parameters of a GLM.
plain: There are three layers of parameters, and mixing them up is the most common confusion. The model parameters theta are the weights you actually learn. Multiplying them with an input gives the natural parameter eta for that example, a number the distribution's formula expects. A response function turns eta into the canonical parameters you would find on Wikipedia, such as the probability phi of a Bernoulli. Only theta is learned. The rest is how you model the noise.
deep: Chain: $x\;\to\;\eta=\theta^\top x\;\to\;$ canonical parameters (for example $\phi=1/(1+e^{-\eta})$ for the Bernoulli, or the mean $\mu=\eta$ for the Gaussian). The map from $\eta$ to the canonical parameters is the response (or inverse link) function, and its inverse is the link function. $\theta$ is the only quantity fit to data. The distribution's natural parameter varies per example because it depends on $x$. The lecturer admits this is the most confusing part of the lecture and the part that is hardest to remember by name, but that it clarifies things conceptually.
say: There are three kinds of parameters. The model parameters, theta, are the weights I actually learn from data. Multiplying theta with an input x gives the natural parameter eta, which the distribution's formula needs for that particular example. Then a response function, the inverse of the link, converts eta into the canonical parameters, like the probability phi in a Bernoulli or the mean in a Gaussian. Only theta is learned. Everything after that is the noise model. Mixing these up is the usual source of confusion, so I keep the chain in mind: x to eta to canonical parameters.

followups.q: What is the canonical parameter for a Bernoulli?
followups.a: The probability phi, obtained from eta by the sigmoid.

traps: Calling eta a learned parameter. It is computed from theta and x.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: How do you encode a multi class label and a multi class prediction?
plain: Encode each class as a one hot vector: with four classes cat, dog, car and bus, cat is 1, 0, 0, 0, dog is 0, 1, 0, 0, and so on. The label is one of these vectors. The model's prediction is a probability distribution over the classes, a list of nonnegative numbers adding up to one, like 0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.1. The label is just the extreme case of a distribution that puts all its mass on one class. This is why a language model's output at each step is a distribution over the whole vocabulary.
deep: Classes are one hot vectors $e_1,\dots,e_K$. A prediction lives on the probability simplex $\{p\in\mathbb{R}^K:p_k\ge0,\sum_kp_k=1\}$, which is a mixture of the one hot vectors, such as $0.5e_1+0.3e_2+0.1e_3+0.1e_4$. Because the entries sum to one, only $K-1$ are free. For $K=2$ this is the single number used in logistic regression. The same structure is what a language model produces for each generated token: a distribution over the whole vocabulary from which one token is chosen.
say: I encode each class as a one hot vector, a vector of zeros with a single one. With cat, dog, car and bus, cat is one zero zero zero, and so on. The label is one of those vectors. The model's prediction is a probability distribution over the classes, nonnegative numbers that add up to one, such as point five, point three, point one, point one. A one hot label is just a distribution with all its mass on one class. Since the entries sum to one, only K minus one are free, and with two classes that's the single number logistic regression predicts.
must_mention: prediction is a distribution on the simplex
entries nonnegative and sum to one

followups.q: Why does a language model's prediction look like this?
followups.a: At each step it outputs a distribution over every token in the vocabulary.

traps: Encoding classes as the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and treating them as ordered.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Write the softmax function and work through an example with scores 2, 1 and 0.1.
plain: Give each class its own weight vector, compute a raw score for each class as the dot product with the input, exponentiate every score, and divide each by the total. The exponentials make everything positive, and dividing by the sum makes the probabilities add to one. With scores 2, 1 and 0.1, the exponentials are about 7.39, 2.72 and 1.11, which sum to 11.21, so the probabilities are about 0.659, 0.242 and 0.099. The largest score gets the largest probability, but the others keep some.
deep: $$p(y=k\mid x;\theta)=\frac{\exp(\theta_k^\top x)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\theta_j^\top x)},$$ where each $\theta_k$ has the same dimension as $x$ (so $\theta_k^\top x$ is a scalar score, sometimes called a logit). Example computed: scores $(2,1,0.1)$ give $(0.659,\,0.242,\,0.099)$. Library implementations subtract the maximum score before exponentiating for numerical stability: scores $(1000,999,998)$ would overflow naively but give $(0.665,0.245,0.090)$ with the shift. The result is a point on the simplex, and for one hot targets it connects to cross entropy.
say: Softmax gives every class its own weight vector, computes a score for each class as a dot product with the input, exponentiates the scores, and divides by their total. Exponentiating makes everything positive and dividing makes the probabilities add up to one. For scores two, one and point one, the exponentials are about seven point four, two point seven and one point one, summing to about eleven point two, so the probabilities come out near point six six, point two four and point one. The top score wins most of the mass, but the others keep a share. In code I subtract the max score first for numerical stability.

followups.q: Why subtract the max score in implementations?
followups.a: To prevent overflow in the exponentials; the result is unchanged because it cancels in the ratio.

traps: Applying softmax to the probabilities instead of the raw scores.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: What is the geometry of softmax classification, and why can linear scores work in high dimensions?
plain: Each class has its own direction in input space, and its score grows as you move along that direction. The line where a class's score is zero is a hyperplane, and the class's weight vector points away from it, toward more cat like points. Where the regions of different classes conflict, the model compares the scores and the largest wins. In two dimensions many datasets cannot be split like this, but in hundreds of dimensions, such as the 768 of GPT 2 in the lecturer's example, classes become much easier to separate with flat surfaces.
deep: For each class $k$, the set $\{x:\theta_k^\top x=0\}$ is a hyperplane with normal vector $\theta_k$, and $\theta_k^\top x$ grows along $\theta_k$. Where per class regions conflict, the comparison of scores decides, so the decision boundaries between classes $j$ and $k$ are the hyperplanes $(\theta_j-\theta_k)^\top x=0$. In low dimensions most datasets are not linearly separable, but in high dimensions things behave differently: the volume of a ball concentrates near its boundary and nearest and farthest neighbors are similar in distance, so linear separation becomes much more plausible. Kernels, covered later, extend this to infinite dimensional feature spaces. Classes here are mutually exclusive: an image with both a cat and a dog needs a different error model such as multi label detection.
say: In softmax classification each class has a weight vector, and its score increases as I move in that direction. The set where the score is zero is a hyperplane, and where regions overlap the class with the highest score wins, so the boundary between two classes is a hyperplane too. In two dimensions that would be a weak model, since most datasets can't be split with lines. But in hundreds of dimensions, like the 768 of an early GPT model's embeddings, flat boundaries are much more capable. One limit: the classes are mutually exclusive, so a picture with a cat and a dog needs a different model.
must_mention: weight vector is the normal direction
high dimensions make linear separation plausible

followups.q: What if an image has a cat and a dog?
followups.a: The classes are not mutually exclusive, so use a multi label or detection model instead of a single softmax.

traps: Judging linear classifiers by two dimensional pictures alone.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Show that softmax with two classes reduces to logistic regression.
plain: With two classes, divide the numerator and denominator of softmax by the exponential of the first class's score. The first class's probability becomes one over one plus the exponential of minus the difference of the two scores. That is a sigmoid of the dot product of the input with the difference of the two weight vectors. So a two class softmax is exactly logistic regression, with the difference of the weight vectors playing the role of theta. More generally, K classes need only K minus 1 free weight vectors, because the probabilities must sum to one.
deep: $$\frac{e^{\theta_1^\top x}}{e^{\theta_1^\top x}+e^{\theta_2^\top x}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(\theta_1-\theta_2)^\top x}}=g\big((\theta_1-\theta_2)^\top x\big).$$ So set $\theta=\theta_1-\theta_2$ to recover logistic regression. For $K$ classes the probabilities sum to one, so one parameter vector can be fixed (for example $\theta_K=0$) without loss of generality, leaving $K-1$ free vectors. Check: scores $(1.3,-0.4)$ give $0.8455$ both ways. Softmax is therefore the generalization of logistic regression, with each class weighed against all alternatives.
say: With two classes, I divide the top and bottom of the softmax by e to the theta one transpose x. The probability of class one becomes one over one plus e to the minus of theta one minus theta two, transpose x. That's a sigmoid applied to a single linear score whose weight vector is the difference of the two class vectors. So two class softmax is exactly logistic regression. In general, because probabilities sum to one, K classes only need K minus one free weight vectors. Softmax regression is the natural generalization of logistic regression to many classes.
must_mention: sigmoid of the difference of weight vectors

followups.q: How many free weight vectors does K class softmax have?
followups.a: K minus 1, since the probabilities sum to one.

traps: Thinking two class softmax is a different model from logistic regression.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: What is the cross entropy loss, how does it come from maximum likelihood, and what is its gradient?
plain: Training a softmax classifier by maximum likelihood means raising the probability the model gives to the correct class. Take the negative log of that probability and you have the cross entropy loss. With a one hot label, all the terms for wrong classes are multiplied by zero, so only the correct class contributes. If the model says a cat picture is 70 percent cat, the loss is minus the log of 0.7. The gradient with respect to the scores is neat: the predicted probabilities minus the label.
deep: $$\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat p_k\log p_k,\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z_k}=p_k-\hat p_k,$$ where $z_k=\theta_k^\top x$ are the scores, $p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)$ and $\hat p$ is the target distribution. With a one hot target this equals $-\log p_y$, the negative log likelihood of the true class, which is what PyTorch's cross entropy loss computes. The gradient has the same prediction minus target shape as before. Check: scores $(2,1,0.1)$ with true class 1 give loss $0.417$ and gradient $(-0.341,\,0.242,\,0.099)$. Intuitively: increase the correct class's score and decrease the rest, in proportion to the probability mass they hold.
say: Cross entropy is the negative log of the probability the model assigns to the right class. It comes straight from maximum likelihood: maximizing the log probability of the correct label is the same as minimizing this loss. With a one hot label only the correct class term survives, so if the model gives the right class seventy percent, the loss is minus log point seven. The gradient with respect to the scores is just the predicted probabilities minus the target. So wrong classes with high probability get pushed down, and the correct class gets pushed up. It's the standard loss for classification and language models.
must_mention: negative log probability of the true class
one hot kills the other terms

followups.q: What is the gradient with respect to the logits?
followups.a: The softmax probabilities minus the one hot target.

traps: Applying cross entropy to softmax outputs and then applying softmax again.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: What is label smoothing and why does it help?
plain: Label smoothing replaces the hard one hot target with a softer one that puts most of the probability on the true class and a small amount on the others. For three classes, the target might be 0.8 for the true class and 0.1 for each of the others instead of 1, 0, 0. It helps for three reasons: some labels in real data are wrong, a model trained forever on a single answer becomes overconfident, and the extra noise acts as a regularizer. With predictions of 0.659, 0.242 and 0.099, the loss on the first class rises from 0.417 with a hard label to 0.707 with the smoothed target.
deep: Instead of the one hot $\hat p=e_y$, use a smoothed target such as $(1-2\varepsilon,\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ for three classes (in general mass $1-\alpha$ on the true class and the rest spread over the others) in the cross entropy $-\sum_k\hat p_k\log p_k$. Reasons given: labels may be wrong, so the model should be honest about its confidence; training on one example for long would push the model to an extreme; and it regularizes, like penalizing large weights, with a similar effect. If you know which confusions are plausible (cat or dog but not car), that knowledge can be put into the target distribution. Computed: with $p=(0.659,0.242,0.099)$ and target $(0.8,0.1,0.1)$ the loss is $0.707$ against $0.417$ with the hard label.
say: Label smoothing replaces the hard one hot target with a softer distribution, for example point eight on the true class and point one on each of two others. I do it for three reasons. Real labels are sometimes wrong, so I shouldn't push the model to be certain. Training long on a single hard answer drives the model toward extreme confidence. And the added noise acts as a regularizer, much like penalizing large weights. If I know which confusions are plausible, say cat versus dog but not car, I can build that into the target distribution too.
must_mention: soft target instead of one hot

followups.q: Can the smoothed target be informed rather than uniform?
followups.a: Yes, it can put mass on plausible confusions, such as cat and dog, and none on implausible ones.

traps: Using label smoothing with a metric that needs calibrated probabilities without checking calibration.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Why softmax and not some other function for turning scores into probabilities?
plain: Softmax is a convenient choice rather than the only valid one. It makes every output positive, makes them sum to one, and interpolates smoothly between zero and one, behaving like the sigmoid in the two class case. It is numerically well behaved and fast to compute. A hard argmax would throw away information about the other classes and would not pass gradient to them. The exponential also pushes far away classes toward zero, so clear cases get clean probabilities. You would need a good reason to use something else.
deep: Properties: positivity and normalization, smooth interpolation (gradient flows to all classes, whereas an argmax gives no useful derivative), a clean gradient $p-\hat p$ with cross entropy, numerical stability and speed with the max subtraction trick, and consistency with logistic regression for $K=2$. A maximum entropy argument motivates exponential family distributions for discrete data (the lecturer notes statisticians used this to justify them, and says he disagrees somewhat philosophically). The lecturer's own view is pragmatic: there is no unique special choice, softmax is simply convenient, and you would have to argue for an alternative. Other functions exist and are used in special cases.
say: Softmax isn't uniquely correct, it's just very convenient. It makes outputs positive and sum to one, it interpolates smoothly like the sigmoid, and with cross entropy it gives a clean gradient, predicted probabilities minus targets. A hard argmax would throw away information about the other classes and give no useful gradient. The exponential also suppresses classes that are far from the winner. There's a maximum entropy argument for it too, though I treat that as a bonus. In practice it's numerically stable and fast, so the burden is on any alternative to show it's better.

followups.q: Why not just take the argmax?
followups.a: It discards information about the other classes and has no useful gradient for training.

traps: Claiming softmax is the only function that can produce probabilities.

topic: CS229 L4: Exponential family, GLMs and softmax
q: Why does the full output distribution matter for generation, and not only the most likely class?
plain: A classifier trained for accuracy only needs its top class. A language model generates text by sampling from the full distribution at each step, so the whole distribution matters. If you ask the same model the same question twice, you usually get different answers, unless it is very confident. That variety is useful: sampling many answers and keeping a good one can solve problems that a single answer misses. The lecturer's student paper on this idea is titled Large Language Monkeys.
deep: For inference in this course, the output is the vector of probabilities over all classes. For generation, you can take the maximum (MAP output) or sample from the distribution, and in practice the model samples, so repeated runs differ unless the distribution is very peaked. This makes the calibration and shape of the distribution important: hidden statistical structure lets the model produce a non obvious answer. Repeated sampling from a model, the idea behind the Large Language Monkeys paper from the lecturer's group, can improve the chance that at least one sample is right. The lecture does not give numbers for this, so treat it as the idea only.
say: For a plain classifier I can just take the top class. But a language model generates by sampling from the whole predicted distribution at every step, so the shape of that distribution matters, not just which class is on top. That's why asking the same question twice gives different answers unless the model is very confident. The variety is useful. If I sample many answers and can check them, I can find a correct one that a single most likely answer would have missed. That's the idea behind the Large Language Monkeys paper from the lecturer's group.
must_mention: many samples can raise the chance of a right answer

followups.q: What is the alternative to sampling?
followups.a: Taking the most likely token at every step, which is deterministic.

traps: Assuming a language model always returns the argmax token.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: What is the difference between a generative and a discriminative model?
plain: A discriminative model learns how the label depends on the input: it models p of y given x, as linear and logistic regression do. A generative model learns how the data itself is produced: it models p of x given y, plus how common each class is, and then classifies by Bayes' rule. Think of cats versus elephants described by height and weight. A discriminative model only learns the boundary between them, while a generative model learns what a typical cat looks like and what a typical elephant looks like. Generative models are the G in GPT.
deep: Discriminative: model $p(y\mid x;\theta)$ directly (linear regression with Gaussian error, logistic regression with Bernoulli, GLMs), and the model only has to be good near the boundary. Generative: model the joint through $p(x\mid y)\,p(y)$, then recover the posterior with Bayes' rule, $p(y\mid x)=p(x\mid y)p(y)/p(x)$. A generative model therefore carries more information, because it models the data distribution, which is why it can also be used to generate data. The lecturer notes that people were not very interested in generative models when he first taught the course because they seemed to underperform, but they are now behind much of the growth in AI.
say: A discriminative model learns the conditional distribution of the label given the input, so logistic regression, linear regression and other GLMs are discriminative. A generative model learns how the inputs are produced for each class, the distribution of x given y, plus the class prior, and then classifies with Bayes' rule. With cats and elephants described by weight, a discriminative model learns the boundary between them, while a generative model learns what each class typically looks like. The generative one carries more information and can generate new data, which is the G in GPT.
must_mention: generative models p(x given y) and p(y)

followups.q: Is logistic regression generative or discriminative?
followups.a: Discriminative, since it models the label given the input directly.

traps: Saying generative models only classify worse. They also model the data itself.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: What are the mean vector and covariance matrix of a multivariate Gaussian, and what does positive definite mean?
plain: A multivariate Gaussian has a mean vector, the center of the cloud, and a covariance matrix, which describes how the cloud is stretched and tilted. The covariance matrix is symmetric, and its diagonal entries are the variances of each coordinate. Positive definite means that for any nonzero direction, the variance of the data along that direction is positive, so the cloud has real thickness in every direction. This guarantees the matrix can be inverted and its determinant is positive, which the Gaussian formula needs.
deep: $x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)$ with $\mu\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ symmetric positive definite: $z^\top\Sigma z>0$ for all $z\ne0$, equivalently all eigenvalues are positive (a symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues). Density: $$p(x;\mu,\Sigma)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\Big).$$ The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues, so it is positive and the square root exists; $\Sigma^{-1}$ exists; the quadratic form is a distance weighted by the inverse eigenvalues. Zero variance in some direction would break all three. Positive eigenvalues do not mean positive entries: off diagonal entries can be negative.
say: A multivariate Gaussian is described by a mean vector, which is the center, and a covariance matrix, which sets how the cloud is stretched and rotated. The covariance is symmetric with the variances on its diagonal. Positive definite means that along every nonzero direction the variance is strictly positive, equivalently that all its eigenvalues are positive. That matters because the density needs the inverse and the determinant of the covariance, and a zero eigenvalue would make the inverse undefined. Positive eigenvalues don't mean positive entries, since off diagonal entries can be negative.

followups.q: Can a covariance matrix have negative entries?
followups.a: Yes, off diagonal entries can be negative; positive definite refers to eigenvalues.

traps: Reading positive definite as all entries positive.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: How does the covariance matrix control the shape of a Gaussian's contours?
plain: Draw the contour lines of a two dimensional Gaussian: points of equal probability. If the covariance is the identity, they are circles and the two coordinates are independent. If it is diagonal, such as variances 1 and 5, each axis is stretched by its own amount and you get ellipses aligned with the axes. If the covariance has nonzero off diagonal entries, the ellipses are tilted, and the sign of those entries says whether the two features rise together or move oppositely. Changing the mean only slides the whole picture without changing its shape.
deep: Contours are level sets of $(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)=c$. With $\Sigma=I$: circles (spherical). With $\Sigma$ diagonal with entries $\sigma_j^2$: axis aligned ellipses with semi axes proportional to $\sigma_j$. With a general positive definite $\Sigma=U\Lambda U^\top$: ellipses with axes along the eigenvectors $U$ and lengths proportional to $\sqrt{\lambda_j}$, which is a rotation plus a scaling. Off diagonal entries are covariances (positive or negative correlation). The mean $\mu$ sets the center. So $\Sigma$ controls the shape, size and orientation, while $\mu$ controls the location.
say: The contours of a two dimensional Gaussian are the sets of points with equal probability. With an identity covariance they're circles and the coordinates are independent. With a diagonal covariance, each axis is stretched by its own variance, giving ellipses aligned with the axes. With off diagonal entries the ellipses tilt, and the sign tells me whether the features are positively or negatively correlated. In general the axes of the ellipse are the covariance's eigenvectors, with lengths set by the eigenvalues. The mean just moves the center without changing the shape.
must_mention: off diagonal tilts and encodes correlation

followups.q: What gives the axes of the contour ellipses?
followups.a: The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, with lengths set by the square roots of the eigenvalues.

traps: Expecting the mean to change the shape of the contours.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: What does a zero in the inverse covariance matrix of a Gaussian mean?
plain: If the entry linking variables i and j in the inverse covariance matrix is zero, those two variables are conditionally independent given all the others. That is not visible from the covariance matrix itself, because two variables can be correlated through a third even when they are directly unrelated. So the inverse covariance, also called the precision matrix, is the one to inspect for a map of direct dependencies. This is the basis of Gaussian graphical models, which the lecturer mentions as an aside and says you do not need to know.
deep: For $x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)$ with precision matrix $\Lambda=\Sigma^{-1}$: $\Lambda_{ij}=0$ if and only if $x_i\perp x_j\mid x_{\text{rest}}$. A zero in $\Sigma$ itself means marginal independence, but a nonzero $\Sigma_{ij}$ can arise from indirect paths. This underlies Gaussian graphical models, connected to the Hammersley and Clifford theorem on Markov random fields. The lecturer presents it as an aside that gives a useful test of whether data sources are approximately independent, and explicitly not as required material.
say: In a multivariate Gaussian, a zero in the inverse covariance matrix, the precision matrix, means the two variables are conditionally independent given all the others. The covariance itself doesn't show that, because two variables can be correlated through an intermediate variable even when they're not directly linked. So to read off direct dependencies I look at the precision matrix. That's the foundation of Gaussian graphical models. The lecturer gave it as an interesting aside that gives a useful independence test, not as something required for the course.

followups.q: What does a zero in the covariance matrix mean?
followups.a: The two variables are uncorrelated, which for a Gaussian means marginally independent.

traps: Reading zeros in the covariance as direct independence of all pairwise relationships.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: Describe the Gaussian discriminant analysis (GDA) model.
plain: GDA tells a story of how data is made. First, flip a biased coin with probability phi to decide the class: cat or elephant. Then draw the features from a Gaussian bell whose center depends on the class, mu zero for cats and mu one for elephants. Both classes use the same covariance matrix, so their bells have the same shape and only the centers differ. Training means estimating phi, the two centers and the shared covariance from the data; prediction then uses Bayes' rule to ask which class more likely produced a new point.
deep: $y\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\phi)$, $x\mid y=0\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\Sigma)$, $x\mid y=1\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\Sigma)$. The parameters are $\phi,\mu_0,\mu_1,\Sigma$. The shared covariance is a modeling assumption: it keeps the number of parameters down and, as shown later, makes the decision boundary linear. The lecturer notes assumptions are not true or false but more or less bad, and that two non trivial things distinguish the classes here: different means and different class frequencies. Despite the name, GDA is a generative algorithm.
say: GDA is a generative story. First I choose the class with a Bernoulli coin, probability phi. Then I draw the features from a Gaussian whose mean depends on the class, mu zero or mu one, and both classes share the same covariance matrix, so their bells have the same shape and differ only in location. Learning means estimating phi, the two means and the shared covariance from data. To classify a new point, I use Bayes' rule to see which class was more likely to have produced it. Despite the name, it's a generative, not a discriminative, algorithm.
must_mention: Gaussian features with class specific mean
four parameter groups: phi, mu0, mu1, Sigma

followups.q: Why share one covariance?
followups.a: It cuts the number of parameters and makes the decision boundary linear.

traps: Assuming the name implies GDA is a discriminative model.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: Why share one covariance matrix across the classes in GDA? What does a covariance cost?
plain: A full covariance matrix for d features has about d squared over 2 free numbers, because it is symmetric. With 10,000 features that is roughly 50 million parameters, for a single class. Fitting a separate covariance for every class multiplies that cost, and needs more data to estimate well. Sharing one covariance is a pragmatic modeling choice: it may look unrealistic, since elephants vary more in weight than cats, but it keeps the model cheap, and you can drop it later at the price of a few extra lines in the estimator.
deep: A symmetric $d\times d$ covariance has $d(d+1)/2$ free parameters; for $d=10{,}000$ that is $50{,}005{,}000$ (computed). A model with one covariance per class multiplies this by the number of classes and each needs enough data to be estimated. The lecturer's point is that the assumption (same shape in both classes) is a modeling choice that is not true or false but more or less costly, and that the case of different covariances is a small extension of the estimation procedure, giving a quadratic boundary (QDA). The first thing to ask of any such choice is what the model assumes and what capacity it is using and why.
say: A full covariance matrix has about d squared over two free parameters, because it's symmetric. With ten thousand features that's roughly fifty million numbers per covariance, and a separate one for each class would multiply that and demand much more data to estimate. Sharing one covariance across classes is a modeling choice. It may be unrealistic, since elephants vary more in weight than cats, but it's cheap and it makes the decision boundary linear. If I need different shapes I can fit one covariance per class, which only costs a few more lines but more parameters.
must_mention: covariance has about d squared over 2 parameters
tens of millions of parameters at d = 10,000

followups.q: How many free parameters does a d by d symmetric covariance have?
followups.a: d times d plus 1, divided by 2.

traps: Counting d squared parameters and forgetting symmetry.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: How does the class prior affect a generative classifier? Use the million cats and one elephant example.
plain: The prior says how common each class is before you look at the features. Suppose your data has a million cats and one elephant. A new animal whose weight falls between the typical cat and the typical elephant is almost certainly a cat, simply because cats are so common. Bayes' rule combines two pieces of evidence: how well the features fit each class, and how common each class is. More common classes need less feature evidence, and rarer classes need more. The catch is that this only works if test time class proportions match the training proportions.
deep: The posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior, $p(y\mid x)\propto p(x\mid y)p(y)$, so a skewed $\phi$ shifts the decision boundary toward the rarer class. Computed in one dimension with $\mu_0=0$, $\mu_1=2$, $\sigma^2=1$: with equal priors the boundary is at $x=1$, and with $\phi=0.01$ it moves to $x\approx3.30$ (the formula is $1+\tfrac12\log\frac{1-\phi}{\phi}$). The lecturer flags the implicit assumption: if the model is trained on a skewed set and tested on a population where the classes are balanced, it will make systematic mistakes, calling small elephants cats. Estimates must also be based on enough data to be reliable.
say: The class prior says how common each class is before I see any features. If my training data has a million cats and one elephant, a new animal with a weight between the two typical sizes is almost surely a cat. Bayes' rule combines how well the features fit each class with how common that class is, so the decision boundary moves toward the rarer class. In a one dimensional example I computed, the boundary moved from one to about three point three when the prior dropped to one percent. The risk is that if the test population is balanced, those skewed priors produce systematic errors.

followups.q: What breaks if test proportions differ from training?
followups.a: The prior baked into the model is wrong, so the model systematically favors the common class.

traps: Ignoring the prior and comparing likelihoods only.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: Write the likelihood of the GDA model and explain how it differs from the discriminative likelihood.
plain: Because the examples are independent, the likelihood is a product over examples. For each example the factor is the probability of its features given its class, times the probability of its class. Taking logs turns that into a sum of two pieces: a Gaussian term and a Bernoulli term. The difference from logistic regression is what is being modeled: here the model explains the features and the labels jointly, not just the labels given the features. The lecturer calls this modeling the world.
deep: $$\ell(\phi,\mu_0,\mu_1,\Sigma)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p\big(x^{(i)}\mid y^{(i)};\mu_0,\mu_1,\Sigma\big)+\log p\big(y^{(i)};\phi\big).$$ The product over examples comes from the iid assumption, and the factorization of the joint into $p(x\mid y)p(y)$ is the chain rule (Bayes' rule), which assumes nothing. Logs turn the product into a sum and are valid because Gaussian densities are never zero. A discriminative likelihood would maximize $\sum_i\log p(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta)$, conditioning on $x$. Maximizing the joint models $p(x,y)$, so the model explains where the data lies, which is why the lecturer calls it world modeling. Energy based and diffusion models also model the data distribution directly.
say: Because examples are independent, the likelihood is a product over examples, and each factor is the probability of the features given the class times the probability of the class. Taking logs gives a sum of a Gaussian term and a Bernoulli term. The difference from logistic regression is what gets modeled. A discriminative likelihood only explains the labels given the features. This one explains the features and the labels together, so it's a model of how the data is generated, which the lecturer calls modeling the world. Diffusion and energy based models also model the data distribution directly.
must_mention: factor is p(x given y) times p(y)
log gives Gaussian plus Bernoulli terms
models the joint, not just the conditional

followups.q: What does the discriminative likelihood condition on?
followups.a: The inputs: it maximizes the probability of the labels given the features.

traps: Writing the GDA likelihood as a product of p(y given x) terms.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: What are the maximum likelihood estimates for GDA?
plain: They are just counting and averaging. The class prior is the fraction of training examples in class 1. Each class mean is the average of the feature vectors in that class. The shared covariance is the average, over all examples, of the outer product of how far each point is from its own class's mean. No gradient descent is needed: setting the derivatives of the log likelihood to zero gives these formulas directly. On a synthetic test I ran with 300 and 100 points, nudging any parameter away from these values lowered the likelihood.
deep: $$\hat\phi=\frac1n\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{y^{(i)}=1\},\quad \hat\mu_k=\frac{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{y^{(i)}=k\}x^{(i)}}{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{y^{(i)}=k\}},\quad \hat\Sigma=\frac1n\sum_{i}\big(x^{(i)}-\hat\mu_{y^{(i)}}\big)\big(x^{(i)}-\hat\mu_{y^{(i)}}\big)^\top.$$ Derivation sketch: the prior term involves only $\phi$ (a Bernoulli log likelihood), so it vanishes when differentiating with respect to the means. The mean terms are a quadratic form; differentiating and using that $\Sigma^{-1}$ is invertible gives $\sum_{i:y=k}(x^{(i)}-\mu_k)=0$. I checked these on synthetic data: perturbing $\phi$, $\mu_0$, $\mu_1$ or scaling $\Sigma$ all decreased the log likelihood. The lecturer notes a Laplace style adjustment (add one) can be used for the prior.
say: The maximum likelihood estimates are just counts and averages. The prior phi is the fraction of examples in class one. Each class mean is the average of the feature vectors in that class. The shared covariance is the average, over all examples, of the outer product of each point's deviation from its own class mean. I get them by setting the derivatives of the log likelihood to zero, so there's no iteration at all. I also checked on synthetic data that nudging any of them away from these values lowers the likelihood.
must_mention: covariance pools deviations from own class mean

followups.q: Why does the prior vanish in the mean's derivative?
followups.a: The prior term does not depend on the means, so its derivative with respect to them is zero.

traps: Subtracting the overall mean instead of each point's own class mean when estimating Sigma.

topic: CS229 L5: GDA and naive Bayes
q: If GDA has a closed form solution, is it still learning? Why not use gradient descent?
plain: Yes, it is still learning, because the parameters are estimated from data and then used to predict new cases. Solving the equations in one step instead of climbing step by step is simply a more efficient way to reach the same maximum. You could use gradient descent on the GDA likelihood and get the same answer, only more slowly. The lecturer's point is that learning is not defined by gradient descent: other procedures, even Hebbian style updates, are also forms of learning. For richer models, no closed form exists and you fall back on gradient descent.
deep: The maximum likelihood derivation shows the optimum can be found in one step, which does not deny that this is learning: parameters are inferred from data to make future predictions. Gradient descent on the same objective converges to the same estimates, only less efficiently. Closed forms exist because the GDA objective is a simple quadratic in the means and has a tractable structure, so such generative models are very cheap to fit and are often used when you need something fast, such as naive Bayes later in the lecture. For more complex generative models the likelihood has no closed form maximizer and you use gradient methods.
