must_mention: surrogate touches the likelihood at the current guess
E step builds, M step maximizes

followups.q: Why does initialization matter?
followups.a: The likelihood can have many hills, and EM climbs whichever one the start is on.

traps: Describing EM as gradient descent on the likelihood.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: Derive the lower bound used by EM, using the Q(z) trick and Jensen's inequality.
plain: The log likelihood of one data point has a sum over the hidden variable inside the log, which is awkward. Multiply and divide each term by Q of z, where Q is any probability distribution over z. Now the sum is an expectation over z drawn from Q of the ratio of the joint probability to Q. Jensen's inequality says the log of an expectation is at least the expectation of the log, because the log is concave. Swapping them gives a lower bound that no longer has a log of a sum. It is valid for every choice of Q.
deep: $$\log p(x;\theta)=\log\sum_zp(x,z;\theta)=\log\sum_zQ(z)\frac{p(x,z;\theta)}{Q(z)}=\log\mathbb{E}_{z\sim Q}\!\Big[\frac{p(x,z;\theta)}{Q(z)}\Big]\ \ge\ \mathbb{E}_{z\sim Q}\!\Big[\log\frac{p(x,z;\theta)}{Q(z)}\Big]=\sum_zQ(z)\log\frac{p(x,z;\theta)}{Q(z)}.$$ $Q(z)$ must be a distribution ($\ge0$, summing to one, and positive wherever $p(x,z;\theta)>0$). The step "multiply and divide by $Q$" changes nothing, but it lets us treat the sum as an expectation and apply Jensen to the concave $\log$, so the inequality points the right way. Each data point may have its own $Q_i$. The motive is operational: it makes available the one tool for expectations we have. By iid, the full bound is the sum over data points.
say: For one data point, the log likelihood is the log of a sum over the hidden variable z. I multiply and divide each term by Q of z, where Q is any distribution over z. That turns the sum into an expectation over z drawn from Q, of the joint probability divided by Q. Because the log is concave, Jensen's inequality says the log of the expectation is at least the expectation of the log. So I get a lower bound with the log moved inside, which is easy to work with. It holds for any valid Q, and each data point can have its own Q.
must_mention: sum becomes an expectation under Q
log is concave so Jensen gives a lower bound
each point has its own Q

followups.q: Why introduce Q at all?
followups.a: Only to turn the sum over z into an expectation, so Jensen's inequality can be applied.

traps: Applying Jensen with the wrong direction for the concave log.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: Which Q makes the EM lower bound tight, and why?
plain: Jensen's inequality becomes an equality when the quantity inside the expectation is constant: no matter which value z takes, the ratio of the joint probability to Q has the same value. That happens when Q of z equals the probability of z given the observed point at the current parameters. By Bayes' rule, the joint probability then divides by that posterior to give just the probability of the point itself, which does not depend on z. So the surrogate touches the true likelihood exactly at the current parameters. That choice of Q is the E step.
deep: If $p(x,z;\theta_t)/Q(z)=c$ for all $z$, then $\log\mathbb{E}[c]=\log c=\mathbb{E}[\log c]$ so Jensen holds with equality. Choose $Q(z)=p(z\mid x;\theta_t)=p(x,z;\theta_t)/p(x;\theta_t)$. Then $p(x,z;\theta_t)/Q(z)=p(x;\theta_t)$ for every $z$, a constant, giving tightness $L_t(\theta_t)=L(\theta_t)$. The choice depends on $x$ and $\theta_t$ but not on $z$ in the ratio. Together with the inequality for all $\theta$, this gives the two defining properties of the surrogate (tight at $\theta_t$ and below $L$ elsewhere), and the bound is the evidence lower bound (ELBO).
say: Jensen's inequality is an equality when the quantity inside the expectation is constant, so I want the ratio of the joint probability to Q to be the same for every value of z. If I choose Q of z to be the posterior, the probability of z given the data point at the current parameters, then by Bayes' rule that ratio equals just the probability of the point itself, which doesn't depend on z. So the bound is tight at the current parameters. That choice of Q is exactly the E step, and in a mixture model it's the soft assignment.
must_mention: equality when the ratio is constant in z
Q equals the posterior p(z given x)
ratio becomes p(x), independent of z

followups.q: What is Q in a Gaussian mixture?
followups.a: The soft assignment w_ij, the posterior probability that point i came from source j.

traps: Choosing Q uniformly and expecting the bound to be tight.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: What is the ELBO, and how does the choice of Q change it? Show a numeric example.
plain: Add the per point lower bounds over all data points and you get the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. It is at most the true log likelihood for every parameter value, and equal to it when Q is the posterior. Take one point at 2 under a two source mixture with means 0 and 3, unit widths and weights 0.7 and 0.3. The true log likelihood of the point is minus 2.204. With Q equal to the posterior, 0.342 and 0.658, the bound equals minus 2.204. With a flat Q of 0.5 and 0.5 it is minus 2.256, and with a poor Q of 0.9 and 0.1 it is minus 2.885.
deep: $$L(\theta)=\sum_i\log p(x^{(i)};\theta)\ \ge\ \sum_i\sum_zQ_i(z)\log\frac{p(x^{(i)},z;\theta)}{Q_i(z)}=L_t(\theta).$$ The bound is an evidence lower bound (the marginal likelihood is the evidence), used again and again in latent variable models; diffusion models use it underneath too. Computed: $x=2$, $\mu=(0,3)$, $\sigma=1$, $\phi=(0.7,0.3)$ gives $\log p(x)=-2.2038$, the posterior $(0.3424,0.6576)$, and bounds $-2.2038$ (posterior), $-2.2561$ ($Q=(0.5,0.5)$) and $-2.8853$ ($Q=(0.9,0.1)$). So the bound is always below $\log p(x)$ and the posterior closes the gap exactly. The curvature of $L$ is a property of the problem, not of the algorithm.
say: The evidence lower bound, the ELBO, is the sum over data points of the per point lower bounds. It's never above the true log likelihood and equals it when Q is the posterior. I checked a single point at x equals two under a two source mixture. The true log likelihood is minus two point two oh four. With Q set to the posterior, the bound matches it exactly. A flat Q gives minus two point two five six, and a poor Q, ninety percent on the wrong source, gives minus two point eight eight five. Latent variable models and diffusion models both rely on this bound.
must_mention: sum of per point lower bounds
equals it when Q is the posterior
used in latent variable and diffusion models

followups.q: How far below is a poor Q?
followups.a: In the example, a Q of 0.9 and 0.1 gave minus 2.885 against a true value of minus 2.204.

traps: Thinking the ELBO can exceed the log likelihood.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: How does EM derive the Gaussian mixture M step, and why does phi need a Lagrange multiplier?
plain: The M step maximizes the surrogate over the parameters. For a mean, differentiate the surrogate with respect to that mean and set it to zero. Only the term involving that source matters, and the result is a weighted average of the data points, with the soft assignments as weights. The covariance works the same way, giving a weighted average of outer products. The mixing weights phi are different because they must be nonnegative and add up to one. Maximizing with a constraint needs a Lagrange multiplier. Skip it and the answers are wrong, because you would have an extra degree of freedom.
deep: The surrogate's $\theta$ dependent part is $\sum_i\sum_jw_{ij}\big[\log\phi_j+\log\mathcal{N}(x^{(i)};\mu_j,\Sigma_j)\big]$ (the $Q\log Q$ term has no $\theta$). Setting $\partial/\partial\mu_j=0$ gives $\Sigma_j^{-1}\sum_iw_{ij}(x^{(i)}-\mu_j)=0$; since $\Sigma_j$ has full rank, $\sum_iw_{ij}(x^{(i)}-\mu_j)=0$, so $\mu_j=\sum_iw_{ij}x^{(i)}/\sum_iw_{ij}$ (if $\Sigma_j$ were singular, the mean would be determined only up to its null space). Similarly $\Sigma_j=\sum_iw_{ij}(x^{(i)}-\mu_j)(x^{(i)}-\mu_j)^\top/\sum_iw_{ij}$. For $\phi$, maximize $\sum_i\sum_jw_{ij}\log\phi_j$ subject to $\sum_j\phi_j=1$ with a Lagrange multiplier, giving $\phi_j=\frac1n\sum_iw_{ij}$. The result recovers the ad hoc updates from the previous lecture.
say: In the M step I maximize the surrogate over the parameters. For a mean, I differentiate and set the derivative to zero. The covariance is invertible, so I can cancel it, and what's left says the weighted sum of deviations is zero, giving a weighted average of the points with the soft assignments as weights. The covariance update comes out the same way, a weighted average of outer products. The mixing weights are different because they must be nonnegative and sum to one, so I need a Lagrange multiplier. Without it I'd get wrong answers, with an extra degree of freedom. The result is the same as the earlier ad hoc updates.
must_mention: differentiate the surrogate and set to zero
full rank covariance lets you cancel it
Lagrange multiplier for phi summing to one

followups.q: What does the Lagrange multiplier enforce?
followups.a: That the mixing weights sum to one.

traps: Maximizing phi without the sum to one constraint.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: What assumptions does EM make, and why not just run gradient descent on the mixture likelihood?
plain: EM assumes you know the structure of the hidden variable and the form of the joint distribution of the data and that hidden variable. For the mixture, that means knowing there are a number of point sources and that each is shaped like a Gaussian. That is a strong, specific assumption, but many latent variable models fit it, and how much you are willing to assume about the hidden structure determines whether the method applies. You could use gradient descent on the marginal likelihood, but you would have to marginalize over the hidden variable inside every gradient. EM uses the structure to split the problem into two easy alternating steps.
deep: EM needs $p(x,z;\theta)$ in a known form, so that the posterior $p(z\mid x;\theta)$ can be computed (E step) and the surrogate maximized (M step). This is a relatively strong assumption since it requires fully characterizing $z$ (number of sources, shapes), but a large class of latent variable models factor this way, and the modeling choice of how much you assume about $z$ decides the fidelity and applicability. Alternatives exist: gradient descent on $\sum_i\log\sum_zp(x^{(i)},z;\theta)$ requires summing (or integrating) over all $z$ in each step, which can be huge. The lecturer's analogy: you could also run gradient descent on the K-means objective, but the alternating structure gives extra, useful structure. The hidden $Q_i$ exists only while the algorithm runs: it is the algorithm's current belief, not a statement about the world.
say: EM assumes I know the structure of the hidden variable and the form of the joint distribution of the data and that variable. For a mixture, that means knowing there are K sources and that each is Gaussian. That's a strong, specific assumption, but many latent variable models fit it, and how much I'm willing to assume decides whether EM applies. I could run gradient descent on the marginal likelihood instead, but each gradient would need a sum over all hidden values. EM uses the structure to split the problem into two easy steps. And the soft assignments are the algorithm's current belief, not a fact about the world.
must_mention: needs a known form for the joint of x and z
gradient descent needs marginalization over z
soft assignments are beliefs, not facts

followups.q: What happens to the hidden variable during the algorithm?
followups.a: It is never observed, but its distribution Q is estimated at each E step.

traps: Using EM when you cannot compute the posterior of the hidden variable.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: What is PCA, and what does the first principal component represent?
plain: Principal component analysis finds the directions along which your data varies most. Take cars with city and highway fuel economy as two numbers each. The points form a long cloud, since cars that do well in the city also do well on the highway. The first principal component is the line along the long axis of that cloud, roughly overall fuel efficiency. The second component is the direction perpendicular to it with the next most variation, here roughly the difference between highway and city performance. PCA is a workhorse for visualization, compression, and building features.
deep: PCA seeks orthonormal unit vectors $u_1,u_2,\dots$ with $u_1$ the direction of maximum variance of the (centered) data, $u_2$ the direction of maximum remaining variance orthogonal to $u_1$, and so on. Each point can be written as $x=\sum_j\alpha_ju_j$ in this orthonormal basis, and keeping the first few gives a lower dimensional description. In a simulated cars dataset (200 cars, city and highway mpg driven by a shared efficiency factor) the first component was $(0.64,0.77)$ and carried 97.8 percent of the variance. It is non probabilistic (unlike EM), is used for visualization, data analysis and feature creation, and can be computed cheaply even for large data (thin PCA).
say: PCA finds the directions along which the data varies most. With cars described by city and highway fuel economy, the points form a long cloud, since cars that do well in the city tend to do well on the highway. The first principal component is the direction along that long axis, roughly overall fuel efficiency. The second is perpendicular to it, with the next most variation, here something like highway versus city performance. I use PCA for visualization, for compression, and sometimes for building features, and it's cheap to compute even for large datasets.
must_mention: orthonormal components in order of variance
each point expressed in the component basis

followups.q: What does the second component capture?
followups.a: The most variance left after removing the first, in a direction orthogonal to it.

traps: Confusing the first principal component with the first original feature.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: Why must you center and scale data before PCA? What goes wrong otherwise?
plain: PCA looks for directions of maximum variance, so the data must be centered first by subtracting the mean. If you skip that, the biggest spread seen from the origin is the distance to the data cloud, so the top direction simply points at the mean. Scaling matters too: if one feature is measured in huge units, such as feet instead of miles, its numbers are enormous and it dominates the variance. Standardizing each feature to unit variance fixes this. In a test I ran with unequal units, the top direction was almost entirely the large feature, 0.99 against 0.15, and after standardizing it was an even 0.71 and 0.71.
deep: Step 1: center, $x^{(i)}\leftarrow x^{(i)}-\bar x$, so $\frac1n\sum_ix^{(i)}x^{(i)\top}$ is the covariance matrix. Step 2: scale each coordinate by its standard deviation so units do not matter. Without centering, the top eigenvector aligns with the mean: in my simulation the uncentered top direction was $(0.614,0.789)$ against the normalized mean direction $(0.613,0.791)$. With features in different units, one feature with huge numbers dominates the variance: with highway economy rescaled to much larger numbers, the top direction became $(0.15,0.99)$, whereas standardizing gave $(0.71,0.71)$. The lecturer notes that none of this is strictly required, and that other preprocessing can help, but these are the basics that people forget. Missing data is not handled by PCA and requires imputation or dropping rows.
say: PCA looks for directions of maximum variance, so I center the data first by subtracting the mean. If I don't, the largest spread measured from the origin is the distance to the cloud, so the top direction just points at the mean. I also scale each feature to unit variance. Otherwise a feature in huge units, like feet instead of miles, dominates the variance. In a test I ran, the top direction was almost entirely the big feature, but after standardizing it was an even mix. Centering and scaling are the two preprocessing steps people most often forget.
must_mention: uncentered top direction points at the mean

followups.q: What about missing values?
followups.a: PCA does not handle them; impute or drop the rows first.

traps: Running PCA on raw features measured in different units.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: How do you project a point onto a line or subspace, and why is maximizing projected variance the same as minimizing residuals?
plain: To find the closest point to x along a line in the direction of a unit vector u, write the point as alpha times u and minimize the distance. Setting the derivative to zero gives alpha equal to the dot product of u and x, so the closest point is the orthogonal projection. With several orthonormal directions, the closest point in their span is the sum of the projections onto each. The leftover, x minus its projection, is the residual. By the Pythagorean theorem, the squared length of x splits into the projected part plus the residual part, so making the projected part large is the same as making the residual small.
deep: Minimize $\|x-\alpha u\|^2=\|x\|^2+\alpha^2\|u\|^2-2\alpha u^\top x$ over $\alpha$ with $\|u\|=1$: setting the derivative to zero gives $\alpha=u^\top x$, so $\operatorname{proj}_u(x)=(u^\top x)u$. For orthonormal $u_1,\dots,u_k$ the closest point in their span is $\sum_j(u_j^\top x)u_j$; orthogonality is what makes the decomposition work. The residual is $x-\operatorname{proj}(x)$, orthogonal to the projection, so $\|x\|^2=\|\operatorname{proj}(x)\|^2+\|x-\operatorname{proj}(x)\|^2$. Since $\sum_i\|x^{(i)}\|^2$ is fixed, maximizing $\sum_i\|\operatorname{proj}(x^{(i)})\|^2$ (projected variance) minimizes $\sum_i\|\text{residual}\|^2$. I verified the identity numerically: the mean squared residual equaled the second eigenvalue.
say: To find the closest point to x on a line through the origin in the direction of a unit vector u, I write the point as alpha times u and minimize the squared distance. Differentiating gives alpha equals u transpose x, so the closest point is the orthogonal projection. With several orthonormal directions, I sum the projections onto each. The leftover is the residual, and it's perpendicular to the projection, so the squared length of x splits into the projected part plus the residual part. That means maximizing the projected variance is exactly the same as minimizing the squared residuals.
must_mention: orthogonality makes the subspace sum work

followups.q: Why does orthonormality matter for subspace projection?
followups.a: It lets the projection decompose into independent projections onto each direction.

traps: Using non orthogonal basis vectors in the sum of projections.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: Show that the first principal component is the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix.
plain: PCA wants the unit direction u that maximizes the sum of squared projections of the centered data, which equals n times u transpose times the covariance matrix times u. The covariance matrix is symmetric, so it has an eigendecomposition with orthonormal eigenvectors. Write u in that eigenbasis with coefficients alpha, which must square and add to one. Then the quantity to maximize is the sum of each eigenvalue times its squared coefficient. With the eigenvalues sorted, you maximize it by putting all the weight on the largest eigenvalue. So the answer is the top eigenvector, and the maximum is the top eigenvalue.
deep: With centered data, $\sum_i(u^\top x^{(i)})^2=u^\top\big(\sum_ix^{(i)}x^{(i)\top}\big)u=n\,u^\top\hat\Sigma u$, where $\hat\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix. Since $\hat\Sigma$ is symmetric, $\hat\Sigma=U\Lambda U^\top$ with orthonormal $U$ and $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$. Write $u=\sum_j\alpha_ju_j$ with $\sum_j\alpha_j^2=1$. Then $$u^\top\hat\Sigma u=\sum_j\lambda_j\alpha_j^2\le\lambda_1,$$ with equality when all mass is on $\alpha_1$, so $u=u_1$. For $k$ directions the maximum of the total projected variance is $\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_k$, attained by the top $k$ eigenvectors (the same argument with matrices). I checked a brute force search over angles: the maximum variance, $76.42$, matched $\lambda_1$ and the direction matched $u_1$.
say: PCA wants the unit direction u that maximizes the sum of squared projections of the centered data. That sum is n times u transpose times the covariance matrix times u. The covariance matrix is symmetric, so I can write it as U lambda U transpose with orthonormal eigenvectors. Writing u in that basis with coefficients alpha, the quantity becomes the sum of lambda j times alpha j squared, with the alphas squaring to one. That's maximized by putting all the weight on the largest eigenvalue. So the first principal component is the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix, and the variance it captures is the top eigenvalue.
must_mention: quadratic form is a weighted sum of eigenvalues

followups.q: What do the top k components maximize?
followups.a: The total projected variance, which equals the sum of the top k eigenvalues.

traps: Forgetting that the data must be centered for the matrix to be a covariance matrix.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: Why is PCA unstable when eigenvalues are equal or close, and what should you do about it?
plain: If the top two eigenvalues are exactly equal, every direction in the plane spanned by their eigenvectors is equally good, so there is no single first principal component. If they are only close, tiny changes in the data swing the answer: a fresh sample can give you a very different direction. That is a problem when you use PCA coordinates as features for a model, since you could train on one set of coordinates and then receive new data whose coordinates mean something else. In a test I ran with variances 1.0 and 0.999, the top direction of five resamples came out at 40, 144, 122, 156 and 163 degrees. So only trust components whose eigenvalues are clearly separated from the rest.
deep: If $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$, any unit $u\in\operatorname{span}(u_1,u_2)$ maximizes $u^\top\hat\Sigma u$ (all of the weight can sit on the tied coordinates), so the principal component is a whole subspace. When eigenvalues are close, the eigenvectors are ill conditioned: sampling noise in $\hat\Sigma$ rotates them within the near degenerate subspace. Experiment: with true covariance $\operatorname{diag}(1,0.999)$ and 100 samples, the angle of the top eigenvector across five resamples was $40^\circ,144^\circ,122^\circ,156^\circ,163^\circ$. The practical risk is training a model on PCA coordinates and then recomputing PCA on new data, getting different coordinates so the model breaks. The lecturer therefore says PCA for dimensionality reduction only makes sense when the kept eigenvalues are distinct and separated from the rest, and that he is not a big fan of using it blindly for that purpose.
say: If the top two eigenvalues are exactly equal, every direction in their plane is equally good, so there's no single first principal component. If they're just close, small changes in the data rotate the answer a lot. I tried variances of one and point nine nine nine, and the top direction on five resamples came out at wildly different angles. That's a real risk if I train a model on PCA coordinates and then recompute PCA on new data, because the coordinates may no longer mean the same thing. So I only trust components whose eigenvalues are clearly separated from the rest.
must_mention: equal eigenvalues give a whole subspace

followups.q: Why is this dangerous for a downstream model?
followups.a: A model trained on one set of PCA coordinates can break when PCA on new data returns different directions.

traps: Using PCA scores as stable features when the eigenvalue spectrum is flat.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: What is explained variance, and how do you choose how many components to keep?
plain: The total variance of the centered data is the trace of its covariance matrix, which is the sum of the eigenvalues. The variance captured by the top k components is the sum of the top k eigenvalues, so the explained variance fraction is that sum divided by the total. Plot it against k: usually a few components explain most of the variance and the extra gain from each further component keeps shrinking. In my cars example the first component alone explained 97.8 percent. Choose k where adding components stops adding much, and where the eigenvalues are well separated.
deep: $$\text{total variance}=\operatorname{tr}(\hat\Sigma)=\sum_j\lambda_j,\qquad \text{explained}(k)=\frac{\sum_{j\le k}\lambda_j}{\operatorname{tr}(\hat\Sigma)}.$$ The trace is cheap (the sum of the diagonal), and the top $k$ directions give $\lambda_i$ via $\hat\Sigma u_i=\lambda_iu_i$ without forming all $n$ pairwise terms. In my simulated cars data, $\lambda=(76.42,1.69)$ and the trace was $78.11$, so the first component explained $97.8\%$, and the residual variance after one component equalled $\lambda_2=1.69$. The amount of variance added by each further component shrinks, so a handful of components often explain most of a dataset, which is a kind of data compression that also teaches you about the structure of the problem.
say: The total variance of centered data is the trace of its covariance matrix, which equals the sum of the eigenvalues. The variance captured by the top k components is the sum of the top k eigenvalues, so the explained variance fraction is that over the total. I plot it against k. Usually a few components explain most of the variance and each extra one adds less. In my simulated cars data, the first component alone explained about ninety eight percent. I pick k where the gains flatten and the kept eigenvalues are clearly separated from the rest.
must_mention: top k variance is the sum of top k eigenvalues

followups.q: What is the variance left after keeping the top k components?
followups.a: The sum of the remaining eigenvalues.

traps: Keeping components just because they have nonzero variance.

topic: CS229 L10: EM derivation and PCA
q: Why reduce dimensionality with PCA, and when does it make sense or not?
plain: Data with many measurements often really lives near a much smaller subspace. A few underlying pseudo features may explain nearly everything, and finding that subspace lets you draw stronger conclusions, visualize the data, and compress it. PCA assumes the structure is a subspace with clearly dominant directions, so it makes sense when the top eigenvalues are distinct and well separated from the rest. It does not handle missing data, which you must impute or drop. And PCA is a modeling choice with assumptions, just as EM assumed hidden Gaussian sources, so justify it rather than applying it blindly.
deep: When data in $\mathbb{R}^d$ lives near a $k$ dimensional subspace, finding it allows stronger conclusions and compression, and gives a denoised view. PCA's assumption is subspace structure with well separated leading eigenvalues; otherwise the selected subspace is arbitrary and unstable (previous card). It does nothing about missing data (impute, or drop). Beyond preprocessing (centering, scaling), the lecturer emphasizes that every method here carries assumptions: EM assumed hidden probabilistic sources, PCA assumes a subspace, and these assumptions are central. The extra variance captured falls as components are added, so a handful often suffice. He says PCA is a workhorse and often overused, simply because it is used so often, and he is not a big fan of blind dimensionality reduction with it.
say: Data with many measurements often lives near a much smaller subspace, so a few underlying directions explain most of it. Finding them gives me compression, a way to visualize the data, and stronger conclusions. PCA assumes that structure is a subspace with clearly dominant directions, so it's reliable when the top eigenvalues are distinct and well separated from the rest. It doesn't handle missing data, so I impute or drop first. And it's a modeling assumption, like the Gaussian sources in EM, so I should justify it for my data instead of applying it by habit.
must_mention: data lives near a low dimensional subspace
an assumption to justify, not a default

followups.q: How does PCA's assumption compare with EM's?
followups.a: PCA assumes subspace structure, while EM assumed hidden probabilistic sources such as Gaussians.

traps: Applying PCA to reduce dimensions without checking the eigenvalue spectrum.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: What problem do diffusion models solve, and how do they generate an image?
plain: You have many samples from an unknown distribution, such as natural images, and want a model that produces new samples from the same distribution. A diffusion model generates by starting from pure noise, an image whose pixel values are completely random, and applying a learned step many times. Each step removes a little noise, so the picture goes from a blur, to faint outlines, to a sharp image. To learn the steps, you do the opposite during training: take real images and add noise gradually, and teach a network to undo each small noising step. The same recipe works for video, robot actions and text.
deep: Given empirical samples $x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, learn a model that generates from the distribution (similar but not identical to training data). Generation: sample $x_T$ from white noise and apply $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ repeatedly to reach $x_0$, a Markov chain with $\theta$ the parameters of a neural network. Training uses a fixed noising process $q$ from clean to noisy images and learns its reversal. Diffusion models are used for images, video and robotics (many vision language action models use them to generate actions) and for text.
say: A diffusion model learns to generate samples from a data distribution, like natural images. To generate, it starts from pure random noise and applies a learned denoising step many times, so the image goes from noise to blur to faint outlines to a sharp picture. To train it, I do the opposite on real data: I gradually add Gaussian noise to clean images with a fixed process, and I train a neural network to reverse each small step. The same recipe is used for video, for generating robot actions, and even for text.
must_mention: start from noise, denoise step by step
train by reversing a fixed noising process
samples are new but from the same distribution

followups.q: What is the model's output at each step?
followups.a: A distribution over the slightly less noisy sample, parameterized by a neural network.

traps: Thinking the model memorizes and retrieves training images.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: How do diffusion models compare with GANs, VAEs and autoregressive language models?
plain: GANs and variational autoencoders were the standard image generators before diffusion, but diffusion has become the main approach, so the course no longer teaches the older ones. A key difference from a variational autoencoder is that diffusion fixes its noising process by design and learns only the reverse, while a variational autoencoder learns both directions. Compared with autoregressive language models, which produce one token at a time, diffusion can generate in parallel, so it can be faster for text. One of the lecturer's colleagues has a startup using diffusion to speed up language models.
deep: The lecturer says diffusion is now the main approach for image generation and is much better than GANs and VAEs, hence those are no longer taught. Differences: (1) in a VAE, both the forward (encoder) and reverse (decoder) maps are neural networks that are learned, whereas in diffusion the forward noising process is designed and only the reverse process is trained; (2) autoregressive models generate token by token, while diffusion can refine all positions in parallel, which can reduce generation time for language models; (3) the training of a diffusion model is itself a latent variable ELBO objective, like EM. These are claims made in the lecture, not benchmarks.
say: GANs and variational autoencoders used to be the standard for image generation, and diffusion has largely replaced them. Compared with a variational autoencoder, diffusion fixes the noising direction by design and only learns the reverse, while the VAE learns both. Compared with autoregressive language models, which emit one token at a time, diffusion can generate in parallel, so it can be faster for text, and there's active work on diffusion language models. Under the hood it's trained with an ELBO, the same lower bound idea as in EM.
must_mention: diffusion replaced GANs and VAEs for images
forward process fixed, only reverse learned

followups.q: What does a VAE learn that diffusion does not?
followups.a: The forward, noising or encoding, direction, which diffusion fixes by design.

traps: Saying diffusion uses a learned encoder like a VAE.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: Write the forward noising step of a diffusion model.
plain: Each noising step shrinks the current image a little and adds a small amount of fresh Gaussian noise. The new image equals the square root of one minus beta times the old image, plus the square root of beta times a standard Gaussian noise vector. Beta is a small number, such as 0.01, that sets how much noise is added in that step. After one step the image looks almost the same, only slightly blurry, but repeating this many times buries the image in noise. The noise vectors at different steps are independent.
deep: $$x_t=\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\epsilon_t,\qquad\epsilon_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\ \text{independent for each }t,$$ with $\beta_t\in(0,1)$ small (order $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-4}$; the lecturer leaves the schedule to the lecture notes). Shrinking the signal by $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$ and adding noise with standard deviation $\sqrt{\beta_t}$ means $\beta_t$ is the variance of the added noise, and the product of $\sqrt{\cdot}$ factors is the field's convention (the lecturer fixed a missing square root on the board). In notation, $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\beta_tI\big)$. This direction is fixed, with no learned parameters.
say: Each forward step shrinks the current image slightly and adds a little fresh Gaussian noise. The new image is the square root of one minus beta times the old image, plus the square root of beta times a standard Gaussian noise vector, where beta is a small number like point oh one. After one step the image only looks slightly blurry, since most of the signal survives, but repeating it many times buries the image in noise. The noise at every step is independent, and this whole process is fixed by design, so there's nothing to learn in the forward direction.
must_mention: shrink by square root of 1 minus beta

followups.q: How small is beta?
followups.a: Typically between about 10 to the minus 4 and 10 to the minus 2 per step.

traps: Adding noise without shrinking the signal, which makes the variance grow without bound.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: Why does the forward process shrink the signal by the square root of one minus beta?
plain: Because it keeps the overall scale of the data constant. Suppose your data is normalized so that its spread is one in every direction. After one step the signal part has variance 1 minus beta and the new noise has variance beta, and these add up to exactly one. So the spread stays at one at every step, instead of growing as noise piles up. The image gradually changes from mostly signal to mostly noise without ever exploding or collapsing in scale. If the data's spread is not exactly one, the spread still moves smoothly toward one rather than jumping.
deep: Since $\epsilon_t$ is independent of $x_{t-1}$, covariances add: $$\operatorname{Cov}(x_t)=(1-\beta_t)\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t-1})+\beta_tI.$$ If $\operatorname{Cov}(x_0)=I$ (normalized data), then $\operatorname{Cov}(x_t)=I$ for all $t$: the process mixes noise in without changing the scale. For a general $\operatorname{Cov}(x_0)$ the covariance moves along the straight line between $\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t-1})$ and $I$, converging to $I$, so the scale stays in the same order, and any scalar such as the trace never changes drastically. I confirmed numerically that starting from unit variance data the variance of $x_T$ stayed at $0.9996$ after 1000 steps.
say: The shrink keeps the overall scale constant. If my data is normalized to have unit covariance, then after a step the signal part has variance one minus beta and the fresh noise has variance beta, and those add to exactly one. So the covariance of every x t stays the identity, instead of growing as noise accumulates. For data that isn't exactly normalized, the covariance just slides linearly toward the identity. That's why the image smoothly goes from mostly signal to mostly noise with no explosion or collapse. I checked it in simulation: variance stayed at essentially one over a thousand steps.

followups.q: What if the data covariance is not the identity?
followups.a: It moves linearly toward the identity and converges to it.

traps: Forgetting the shrink factor and watching the variance grow each step.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: What is the closed form of the forward process, and what happens as t gets large? Give numbers.
plain: Instead of adding noise one step at a time, you can jump straight to any step. Let alpha be one minus beta for each step and alpha bar be the product of alphas up to step t. Then x t equals the square root of alpha bar times the clean image plus the square root of one minus alpha bar times a single standard Gaussian. Because each alpha is just below one, alpha bar shrinks toward zero as t grows, so the clean image's contribution vanishes and x t becomes pure Gaussian noise. With beta equal to 0.01 for 1000 steps, alpha bar ends near 0.00004, so the image weight is about 0.007.
deep: Unrolling $x_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\epsilon_t$ gives $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+$ (a linear combination of independent Gaussians, itself Gaussian), so $$x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat\epsilon_t,\quad\hat\epsilon_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),\quad\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s\le t}\alpha_s.$$ The noise scale is forced by variance preservation: if $\operatorname{Cov}(x_0)=I$ then $1=\bar\alpha_t+\kappa^2$, so $\kappa^2=1-\bar\alpha_t$. The $\hat\epsilon_t$ for different $t$ are each standard normal but correlated with each other. As $t\to\infty$, $\bar\alpha_t\to0$ (a product of numbers below one), so $x_T\approx\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ whatever $x_0$ is. Computed: constant $\beta=0.01$ and $T=1000$ gives $\bar\alpha_T=4.3\times10^{-5}$ (signal weight $0.0066$); a linear schedule from $10^{-4}$ to $0.02$ gives $4.0\times10^{-5}$. Simulation of the chain from $x_0=3$ matched the formula: at $t=100$ mean $2.842$ and variance $0.103$ against $2.841$ and $0.103$.
say: I can jump straight to any noise level. With alpha equal to one minus beta at each step, and alpha bar the running product of the alphas, x t equals the square root of alpha bar times the clean image plus the square root of one minus alpha bar times a single standard Gaussian. Since every alpha is just under one, alpha bar shrinks toward zero, so eventually the clean image's weight vanishes and x t is basically pure noise. For example, with beta point oh one and a thousand steps, alpha bar ends around four times ten to the minus five, so the image weight is under one percent.
must_mention: x_t = sqrt(alpha bar) x_0 + sqrt(1 minus alpha bar) epsilon
alpha bar is the product of alphas

followups.q: Why does the noise coefficient equal square root of 1 minus alpha bar?
followups.a: Variance preservation: for unit variance data, alpha bar plus the noise variance must equal 1.

traps: Assuming the epsilons at different steps are independent after merging.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: Is the forward process learned? How does this differ from a variational autoencoder?
plain: No. In a diffusion model the noising process is designed by hand: you choose the betas, so you know exactly how any clean image becomes a noisy one, and there is no uncertainty and nothing to train. Only the reverse process, the denoiser, is learned. In a variational autoencoder, by contrast, the process that maps data to hidden variables is also a neural network that has to be learned, in addition to the one that maps back. That makes diffusion training simpler, because half of the pipeline is known in closed form.
deep: The forward process $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}x_{t-1},\beta_tI)$ is fixed: $\beta$ is chosen, so $q$ is known exactly, and $x_t$ can be sampled from $x_0$ in one shot via the closed form. The reverse process $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ is unknown and is the thing approximated by $p_\theta$. In a VAE both directions (the posterior $q_\phi$ and the model $p_\theta$) are parameterized and learned. In the ELBO for diffusion this means the variational distribution $Q$ has no parameters, which is what makes the per step posteriors tractable (a later card). It is one of the main differences between diffusion and VAEs.
say: No, the forward process isn't learned. I choose the betas by design, so I know exactly how a clean image becomes a noisy one, and I can sample any noise level in closed form. Only the reverse process, the denoiser, is trained. That's a key difference from a variational autoencoder, where the encoder that maps data to latents is also a neural network that has to be learned along with the decoder. In diffusion, the variational distribution in the ELBO has no parameters at all, which keeps training simple and makes the per step targets computable exactly.
must_mention: noising process is designed, betas chosen
the ELBO's Q has no parameters

followups.q: What do you gain from a fixed forward process?
followups.a: Exact, closed form noisy samples and tractable per step targets for the reverse model.

traps: Training a network to add the noise.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: How is the reverse process parameterized in a diffusion model?
plain: The reverse process takes a noisy image x t, together with the step number t, and outputs a distribution over the slightly cleaner image x t minus one. That distribution is chosen to be a Gaussian. The center of the Gaussian is the output of a neural network that takes x t and t as inputs, and the spread is a fixed number sigma t that the designer picks rather than learns. Because the network predicts a whole image, its output is a vector of the same size as the image. Training means choosing the network's parameters theta.
deep: $$p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)=\mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\theta(x_t,t),\,\sigma_t^2I\big).$$ $\mu_\theta:\mathbb{R}^d\times\{1,\dots,T\}\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is a neural network (the lecturer mentions a structure such as an MLP in the simplest case), with the time $t$ as input so that one network handles every noise level. $\sigma_t$ is chosen, not learned here, though it can be studied in other treatments. The model $p_\theta$ is itself a Markov chain: starting from $x_T$, it gives a joint distribution $p_\theta(x_0,\dots,x_T)$ and hence a marginal over $x_0$, which is what is maximized. Diagonal covariance is used, as in the lecturer's own work.
say: The reverse process takes a noisy image x t and the step number t, and outputs a distribution over the slightly cleaner x t minus one. I choose that distribution to be Gaussian. Its mean is the output of a neural network that takes both x t and t as input, so one network can handle all noise levels, and its variance sigma t squared is a number I set in advance rather than learn. The network outputs a full image sized vector. So training just means finding the network parameters theta, and generation is sampling from this Gaussian repeatedly, starting from pure noise.
must_mention: mean from a neural network of x_t and t

followups.q: Why is t an input to the network?
followups.a: So a single network can denoise at every noise level, since the right correction depends on how noisy the input is.

traps: Training a separate network for every step without sharing.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: Why denoise in many small steps instead of jumping from noise to an image in one step?
plain: You could in principle map pure noise directly to an image, but that mapping would be extremely hard to learn, because the network would have to invent all the structure at once. Adding noise gradually means the reverse can also be gradual, and each small denoising step only has to fix a little: undo a tiny amount of noise from an image that is already mostly formed. Learning many easy steps is easier than learning one impossible step. The first diffusion papers used about a thousand steps, and later work found ways to generate in far fewer, even about four, steps.
deep: A one shot noising (multiply $x_0$ by zero and add noise) would discard all the information, so reversing it would be very hard. A halfway option, a deep network (say 5 to 10 layers) that adds noise and removes information, resembles a variational autoencoder, but diffusion instead uses a coarse, fixed process with a small amount of noise per step and large $T$ (about 1000 or a few thousand in the first paper). The intuition the lecturer endorses: gradual noising allows gradual denoising, each step is easier to reproduce, and one can read that as an easier ELBO minimization or a more accurate approximation of the ELBO. Practitioners later found ways to do the reverse in about four steps, but one learns with many steps first and then tries to speed up sampling.
say: Jumping from pure noise straight to an image would be extremely hard to learn, since the network would have to invent all the structure at once. If I add noise gradually, the reverse can be gradual too, and each denoising step only has to remove a little noise from an image that's already mostly formed. Many easy steps are easier to learn than one impossible step. The original models used around a thousand steps, which makes sampling slow, and later work found ways to get good samples in far fewer steps, but you still learn with many small steps first.
must_mention: one shot reverse is too hard
small steps are easy to learn

followups.q: What is the cost of many steps?
followups.a: Slow generation, since each step is a network evaluation, which motivated faster samplers.

traps: Assuming more noise per step is always better.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: Why is the reverse step Gaussian, and why does it still add noise if the forward process added noise?
plain: Given a noisy image, you cannot know exactly which slightly less noisy image it came from, because many different paths of noise could lead to the same point. So the reverse step cannot be a single point; it has to be a distribution, and some randomness stays in each reverse step. The distribution is Gaussian because the forward steps are tiny: many tiny random changes add up to a Gaussian, so over a small step the true reverse is also well approximated by one. Even if it were not exactly Gaussian, you can train a Gaussian approximation.
deep: In one dimension the forward process is a random walk; knowing $x_t$ does not pin down $x_{t-1}$ because different trajectories reach the same $x_t$, so $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ is a genuine distribution and noise remains. Gaussianity: (1) a pragmatic justification is to approximate whatever the true reverse is with a Gaussian; (2) in the continuous limit of infinitesimal steps the true reverse process is Gaussian (a result for stochastic processes, going back to the 1980s). More generally, in continuous time almost every steady process with many small increments becomes Gaussian by a law of large numbers effect, though there are counterexamples. The lecturer calls this a pretty deep theorem and skips the proof, which uses Bayes' rule with factorized distributions and is in the lecture notes.
say: Given a noisy image, I can't know exactly which slightly cleaner image it came from, because many noise paths lead to the same point. So the reverse step has to be a distribution, and some randomness stays, even though it's removing noise. It's Gaussian because the forward steps are tiny, and many tiny random changes add up to a Gaussian. In the continuous limit of infinitesimal steps, the true reverse process is Gaussian, and even if it weren't, I could train a Gaussian approximation. So the reverse step is a Gaussian with a learned mean and a chosen variance.
must_mention: many paths lead to the same noisy image

followups.q: Does noise in the reverse process contradict denoising?
followups.a: No, it reflects genuine uncertainty about the previous step, and sampling that uncertainty gives diverse images.

traps: Expecting the reverse step to return a deterministic image.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: What is the continuous time view of diffusion, and what does the reverse process look like?
plain: Imagine the noise steps becoming infinitely small. The forward process then turns into a continuous equation: a small deterministic drift pulling the data toward zero, plus random Brownian motion. A classical result says that if you run this process backward in time, you get another equation of the same kind, with Brownian noise again, but its drift now also depends on the probability density of the data at that noise level. That is why the reverse step needs to be learned: the correction depends on which images are likely. This view is why Gaussians are the right building block.
deep: Forward: $dx_t=f(x_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t$, with $g(t)=\sqrt{\beta(t)}$ and, for the discrete scheme above, drift $f=-\tfrac12\beta(t)x_t$ (since $\sqrt{1-\beta}\approx1-\beta/2$); $W_t$ is Brownian motion. Anderson's result on time reversal: with $y_\tau=x_{T-\tau}$, the reversed process is again an SDE with Brownian noise, and its drift involves the density of $x_t$; the standard form (not written out in this lecture) is $dx=\big[f-g^2\nabla_x\log p_t(x)\big]dt+g\,d\bar W$ with time running backward. Intuition from the lecture: if $x_t$ is very high, it was more likely reached from below, so the mean of the previous point is shifted down; if $x_t$ is in the middle, it is roughly symmetric. The lecturer gives this to justify Gaussian reverse steps and skips the proof, which is in the lecture notes.
say: If I let the noise steps become infinitesimal, the forward process becomes a stochastic differential equation: a small deterministic drift plus Brownian motion. A classical result by Anderson says that running it backward in time gives another equation of the same type, with Brownian noise again, but the drift now also depends on the probability density at that noise level. The intuition is that if a value is unusually high, it was probably reached from below, so the previous point is more likely lower. This is why the reverse step needs to be learned, and why Gaussian reverse steps are justified.
must_mention: reverse drift depends on the density

followups.q: Why can't you just reverse the drift?
followups.a: The reverse drift depends on the density of the data at that noise level, which is unknown and must be learned.

traps: Assuming the reversed process just has the sign of the drift flipped.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: How is a diffusion model trained as a latent variable model with the ELBO?
plain: The goal is to maximize the probability the model assigns to real images, but the noisy images in between are hidden variables, so the likelihood cannot be computed directly. This is exactly the situation from the EM lecture, so we use the same lower bound. Treat the clean image as the observed variable and the whole chain of noisy images as the latent variable. For the distribution over latents we use the forward noising process, which has no parameters. The bound is the expected reconstruction term minus a KL divergence between that forward process and the model's chain. Maximizing the bound trains the network.
deep: Maximize $\log p_\theta(x_0)$, where $p_\theta$ defines a joint over $x_0,\dots,x_T$ and hence a marginal over $x_0$. Map this onto the ELBO: observed $X=x_0$, latent $Z=x_{1:T}$, and variational distribution $Q=q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ (the forward process; the lecture writes $q_Z$ without conditioning because $x$ was fixed in the earlier lecture). Then $$\log p_\theta(x_0)\ge\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_{1:T})\big]-\operatorname{KL}\big(q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\,\|\,p_\theta(x_{1:T})\big).$$ The KL term acts as regularization: without it the posterior could copy $x$ and get perfect reconstruction. The inequality holds for any $P$ and $Q$; here only $P=p_\theta$ is parameterized. The lecturer says he has not seen others derive it this way and hopes this shortens the proof.
say: I want to maximize the probability the model gives to real images, but the noisy images in between are hidden variables, so I can't compute that directly. It's the same situation as in EM, so I use the evidence lower bound. I treat the clean image as observed and the chain of noisy images as latent, and I use the forward noising process as the distribution over latents, which has no parameters. The bound is the expected reconstruction term minus a KL divergence between the forward chain and the model's chain. The KL term acts as a regularizer, and maximizing the bound trains the network.
must_mention: x_0 observed, x_1 to x_T latent
Q is the forward process, parameter free

followups.q: Why do we need the KL term?
followups.a: Without it, the posterior could copy x and get perfect reconstruction, which gives no useful regularization.

traps: Treating the forward process as a learned encoder in the ELBO.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: State the chain rule for KL divergence and say how it simplifies the diffusion objective.
plain: The KL divergence between two joint distributions splits into two pieces: the KL between their marginals for one variable, plus the average, over that variable, of the KL between the conditional distributions of the other. For Markov chains you can apply this repeatedly. The diffusion objective compares two chains over the whole noisy trajectory, so the chain rule turns one hard KL between joint distributions into a sum of simple KLs, each involving a single step. Each of those compares the model's reverse step with the true reverse step.
deep: $$\operatorname{KL}(P_{XY}\,\|\,Q_{XY})=\operatorname{KL}(P_Y\,\|\,Q_Y)+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P}\big[\operatorname{KL}(P_{X\mid y}\,\|\,Q_{X\mid y})\big],$$ which can be verified by expanding the definition. For sequences $X_1,\dots,X_T$ that are Markov chains under both $P$ and $Q$, apply it recursively, peeling off one variable at a time: $\operatorname{KL}\big(P_{X_{1:T}}\|Q_{X_{1:T}}\big)=\sum_{t}\mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{KL}\big(P_{X_{t-1}\mid X_t}\|Q_{X_{t-1}\mid X_t}\big)\big]+\operatorname{KL}(P_{X_T}\|Q_{X_T})$. In diffusion (all conditioned on $x_0$) the left side is the KL between the forward chain $q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ and $p_\theta(x_{1:T})$. Each resulting term involves only one step, and the model's step is compared with $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$.
say: The chain rule for KL says the KL between two joint distributions equals the KL between their marginals for one variable, plus the average over that variable of the KL between the conditionals of the other. For Markov chains I can apply that repeatedly, peeling off one variable at a time. That turns the KL between two whole noisy trajectories into a sum of per step KLs, each comparing the model's reverse step with the true reverse step given x zero. Instead of one big hard divergence, I get many small, tractable Gaussian comparisons.
must_mention: KL of joints equals marginal KL plus expected conditional KL
compare model step with true reverse step

followups.q: Why does it need the Markov property?
followups.a: So each conditional depends only on the next variable, giving single step terms.

traps: Forgetting to take the expectation over the conditioning variable.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: What is the true reverse step given x_0, and why can it be computed exactly?
plain: Given the clean image x zero, the forward process is completely known. By Bayes' rule you can compute the distribution of the previous noisy image given the current noisy image and the clean image, using only Gaussians you can write down. The result is itself a Gaussian. Its mean is a fixed linear mix of the clean image and the current noisy image, and its variance depends only on the noise schedule. This is the target the model's reverse step should match. Without the clean image the reverse step is very hard, but with it, it is easy to compute.
deep: $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\propto q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)$, a product of Gaussians, where the Markov property removes $x_0$ from the first factor and the closed form $x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\epsilon$ gives the second. The result is Gaussian, $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)=\mathcal{N}(\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0),\tilde\beta_tI)$ with $$\tilde\mu_t=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t,\qquad\tilde\beta_t=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\beta_t.$$ The lecturer says the mean is a linear combination of $x_0$ and $x_t$ and does not recall the coefficients; the ones above are the standard ones, and I checked them against a Monte Carlo conditional at $t=500$ (empirical mean $0.5285$ and variance $0.0102$ against the formula's $0.5287$ and $0.0100$).
say: Given the clean image x zero, the forward process is completely known, so I can apply Bayes' rule to get the distribution of the previous noisy image given the current one and x zero. It's a product of Gaussians, so the result is a Gaussian. Its mean is a fixed linear mix of x zero and x t, and its variance depends only on the noise schedule. That's the target the model's reverse step should match. Without x zero this reverse step would be very hard, but with it, it's exact. I checked the formula for the mean and variance against a Monte Carlo simulation.
must_mention: mean is a linear mix of x_0 and x_t
variance depends only on the schedule

followups.q: Why does conditioning on x_0 make it easy?
followups.a: Given x_0 every forward distribution is a known Gaussian, so the posterior has a closed form.

traps: Assuming the reverse step without x_0 has a simple closed form.

topic: CS229 L11: Diffusion models
q: What is the per step training loss of a diffusion model?
plain: Each step's loss is the KL divergence between two Gaussians: the model's reverse step and the true reverse step given the clean image. If you choose the model's variance to equal the true variance, the two Gaussians have the same covariance and differ only in their means. Then their KL is just the squared distance between the means, divided by twice the variance. So the loss for one step is a squared error between the network's predicted mean and the known target mean, which is the simplest kind of regression loss. You minimize it over the network's parameters, averaged over images and steps.
deep: For Gaussians with equal covariance, $\operatorname{KL}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2I)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(\tilde\mu,\sigma^2I)\big)=\dfrac{\|\mu-\tilde\mu\|^2}{2\sigma^2}$ (check: means $0.3$ and $0.5$ with $\sigma^2=0.04$ in one dimension give $0.5$, and the general quadratic form is $(\mu-\tilde\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-\tilde\mu)/2$). Setting $\sigma_t^2=\tilde\beta_t$, the term for step $t$ is $$L_{t-1}=\mathbb{E}\Big[\tfrac{1}{2\tilde\beta_t}\big\|\mu_\theta(x_t,t)-\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)\big\|^2\Big].$$ Minimizing the sum of these losses (with the other terms in the ELBO) maximizes the lower bound, since the KL enters with a minus sign. The lecturer ran out of time and defers a further simplification to the next lecture.
say: Each step's loss is the KL divergence between the model's reverse step and the true reverse step given the clean image. Both are Gaussians, and if I set the model's variance equal to the true variance, they share the same covariance and differ only in their means. The KL then reduces to the squared distance between the means divided by twice the variance. So each step's loss is just a squared error between the network's predicted mean and the known target mean. I minimize it over the network parameters, averaged over images and over steps. The next lecture simplifies it further.
must_mention: same covariance, so only the means differ
squared difference of means over 2 sigma squared
regression loss to a known target

followups.q: Why minimize rather than maximize?
followups.a: The KL enters the ELBO with a minus sign, so maximizing the bound means minimizing the KL.

traps: Using different variances for the model and the target and assuming the loss stays a plain squared error.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: In the diffusion ELBO, why does the term comparing x_T with the prior vanish, and what about the first step's reconstruction term?
plain: The lower bound has three kinds of terms. The big group compares the model's and true reverse steps at each noise level. A second term compares the forward noised image at the last step with the prior, a standard Gaussian. Once enough noise is added, the noised image is itself a standard Gaussian whatever the starting image, so this comparison is a KL between identical distributions and equals zero. The third term, reconstructing the clean image from the first noisy one, looks different but turns out to have the same form as the others once you define the first target mean to be the clean image itself.
deep: The bound is $\mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)]-\operatorname{KL}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\|p(x_T))-\sum_{t\ge2}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{KL}(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\|p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t))$. For large $T$, $q(x_T\mid x_0)\to\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ (the noise washes out the signal) and the prior is $p(x_T)=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$, so the second term is $0$ (strictly, it converges to $0$ as $T\to\infty$). For the first term, choose $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)=\mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(x_1,1),\sigma_1^2I)$; its log density is $-\frac{1}{2\sigma_1^2}\|x_0-\mu_\theta\|^2+\text{const}$, and defining $\tilde\mu_1(x_1,x_0):=x_0$ gives the same formula as the other terms. It also agrees with the general expression, since $x_0=(x_1-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_1}\hat\epsilon_1)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_1}$. So one formula covers every step $t=1,\dots,T$, which the lecturer calls either a clear organization or a happy coincidence.
say: The diffusion lower bound has a term comparing the fully noised image at step T with the prior, which is a standard Gaussian. Once enough noise has been added, the noised image is a standard Gaussian whatever the starting image, so that KL compares two identical distributions and is zero in the limit. The reconstruction term, producing the clean image from the first noisy one, looks different, but if I give it a Gaussian form and define the target mean at the first step to be the clean image itself, it has exactly the same squared difference form as every other step. So a single formula covers all steps.
must_mention: x_T is standard Gaussian, prior is standard Gaussian
that KL is zero in the limit
reconstruction term is also a Gaussian log likelihood

followups.q: Why does the noise wash out the signal?
followups.a: Because alpha bar goes to zero as t grows, so the clean image's weight vanishes.

traps: Treating the prior matching term as something to optimize. It is a constant zero.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: Derive the noise prediction loss for a diffusion model.
plain: The mean matching loss compares the network's predicted mean with the true reverse mean. Since x t equals a scaled clean image plus a scaled noise vector, you can solve for the clean image and rewrite the true mean using only x t and the noise that was added. Then build the network so that the part that depends only on x t is written in by hand, and the network only has to estimate the noise. When you subtract the two means, everything cancels except a constant times the difference between the true noise and the network's noise estimate. So the loss becomes: guess the noise that was added. Practitioners drop the constant.
deep: From $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\hat\epsilon_t$, eliminate $x_0$ in $\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)$: $$\tilde\mu_t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\hat\epsilon_t\Big)$$ (I verified numerically that this matches the two coefficient form in $x_0$ and $x_t$). Parameterize $\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\big(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\big)$, hard coding the known part, so $\mu_\theta-\tilde\mu_t=-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\big(\epsilon_\theta-\hat\epsilon_t\big)$. Then $L_{t-1}=\frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}\,\mathbb{E}\|\hat\epsilon_t-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2$, a scalar (about $5.5\times10^{-3}$ at $t=500$ for a linear schedule) times a noise prediction error. In practice the scalar is dropped, so the loss is just $\mathbb{E}\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2$. Dropping the weights changes the relative weighting of noise levels.
say: The mean matching loss compares the network's predicted mean with the true reverse mean. Since x t is a scaled clean image plus scaled noise, I can solve for the clean image and rewrite the true mean using only x t and the noise that was added. Then I parameterize the network the same way, hard coding the part that depends only on x t, so the network only has to estimate the noise. Subtracting the two means, everything cancels except a constant times the difference between the true noise and the predicted noise. So the loss becomes guess the noise, and in practice the constant is dropped.
must_mention: eliminate x_0 using the closed form
mean written in terms of x_t and epsilon
network predicts the noise, known part hard coded
loss is a constant times the noise error, constant dropped

followups.q: What does dropping the coefficients change?
followups.a: The relative weighting of different noise levels in the loss.

traps: Predicting the clean image and the noise with the same loss weights and assuming it makes no difference.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: Write the training algorithm for a diffusion model.
plain: Training repeats the following steps. Pick a clean image from the dataset, pick a random noise level (a step t between 1 and T), and draw a fresh random noise vector the same size as the image. Mix the image and the noise using the closed form to get the noisy image x t. Then run the network on x t and t, and compare its output with the noise you actually added. The loss is the squared error between the two, and you take a gradient step on the network's parameters. Because the loss is a sum over steps, picking one random t per example gives an unbiased estimate.
deep: Repeat: (1) sample $x_0$ from the training set; (2) sample $t\sim\text{Unif}\{1,\dots,T\}$ (the loss is a sum of $T$ terms and one term is chosen at random); (3) sample $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$; (4) form $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$; (5) compute $\mathcal{L}=\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2$ and take a gradient step (SGD, Adam). $$\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_0,t,\epsilon}\Big[\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,\,t\big)\big\|^2\Big].$$ In most references the subscripts on $\epsilon$ are dropped, since it is just a standard Gaussian random variable. Gradients come from backpropagation and any optimizer can be used; the forward noising needs no learning.
say: Each training step goes like this. I sample a clean image from the dataset, a random time step t uniformly from one to capital T, and a fresh standard Gaussian noise vector the size of the image. I build the noisy image x t from the closed form, a scaled copy of the image plus scaled noise. Then I run the network on x t and t, compare its output to the noise I added using squared error, and take a gradient step. Picking one random t per example is an unbiased way to sample from the sum over time steps in the loss.
must_mention: build x_t with the closed form
squared error between epsilon and the network output
one random t gives an unbiased estimate

followups.q: Why sample t uniformly?
followups.a: The objective is a sum of per step terms, and sampling one uniformly estimates it without bias.

traps: Running the whole noising chain step by step during training instead of jumping with the closed form.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: Write the sampling algorithm for a trained diffusion model.
plain: Start from pure noise: draw x T from a standard Gaussian. Then go backward from step T down to step 1. At each step, run the network to estimate the noise in the current image, use that estimate to compute the mean of the previous, slightly cleaner image, and add a small amount of fresh Gaussian noise to get x t minus one. The fresh noise is there because the reverse step is a distribution, not a single point. After the last step you have a clean image. Generating one image therefore needs about T network evaluations, which is why speeding sampling up matters.
deep: Draw $x_T\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. For $t=T,\dots,1$: compute $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$, then $$\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\Big),\qquad x_{t-1}=\mu_\theta(x_t,t)+\sigma_tz,\ \ z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),$$ with $\sigma_t=\sqrt{\tilde\beta_t}$ (the choice made when training the mean). The injected noise reflects that even the reverse process has uncertainty about $x_{t-1}$. Output $x_0$. Cost: $T$ sequential network evaluations (about a thousand in the original setup), which motivates faster samplers.
say: To sample, I start with x T drawn from a standard Gaussian, pure noise. Then I loop from step T down to one. At each step I run the network to estimate the noise in the current image, use that estimate to compute the mean of the slightly cleaner previous image, and add a little fresh Gaussian noise with standard deviation sigma t to get x t minus one. The fresh noise is there because the reverse step is a distribution. After the last step I have a clean image. It takes about T network calls per image, which is why faster samplers matter.
must_mention: start from a standard Gaussian x_T

followups.q: Why add noise at each reverse step?
followups.a: The reverse step is a Gaussian distribution, and sampling from it, not just taking its mean, matches the model.

traps: Using only the mean at every step and expecting diverse, sharp samples.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: What is a foundation model, and what are pretraining and adaptation?
plain: A foundation model is one big model trained once on a huge amount of data and then reused for many tasks. The first phase, pretraining, uses enormous amounts of unlabeled, general purpose data scraped from the internet, often orders of magnitude more than earlier models, with data quality mattering less at first. The second phase, adaptation, tailors the model to specific tasks, and the number of possible tasks is effectively unlimited, unlike older models built for one task such as image classification. The term was popularized by a Stanford report around 2021, after GPT-3, which described it as an emerging new paradigm.
deep: Two phases: (1) pretraining on massive, diverse, mostly unlabeled data, general purpose, with the labels ignored (documents of all formats are used, including HTML and Word documents), and quality initially a lesser concern but improved over time through cleaning; (2) adaptation to a wide range of tasks. Earlier practice was to train one model per task, or multitask over a few (image classification, object detection, bounding boxes); now there are so many tasks that the notion of a task is blurry (GPT's paper graded about 100 tasks and later models many more). The term was coined in a Stanford review report (Percy Liang and colleagues) around 2021, a response to the excitement over GPT-3 in the summer of 2020; the lecturer says it should no longer be called merely emerging. The lecture will cover pretraining and adaptation techniques from around 2019 to 2022, then the post 2022 dominant approach, and post training later.
say: A foundation model is one big model trained once and then reused for many tasks. In the first phase, pretraining, it learns from huge amounts of mostly unlabeled, general purpose data, often scraped from the internet, orders of magnitude more than earlier models, and at first nobody worried much about data quality. In the second phase, adaptation, I tailor it to specific tasks, and the number of possible tasks is effectively unlimited, unlike older models built for just one task. The term was popularized by a Stanford report around 2021, after GPT three showed this new paradigm.

followups.q: How does this differ from older practice?
followups.a: Older models were trained for one task or a handful; a foundation model is pretrained once and adapted to a very large number of tasks.

traps: Describing pretraining as supervised training on labeled task data.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: What are zero shot and few shot adaptation?
plain: In few shot adaptation you have a small labeled dataset for the new task, perhaps 5 to 10 examples, and you use it to adapt the model. In zero shot you have none: you simply describe the task to the model and ask it to solve it, with no new data and no parameter update. Few shot, or even larger labeled sets for a task, dominated around 2019 to 2022. A breakthrough of GPT-3 was that zero shot often works, and today almost nobody collects new labels to adapt a model. For example, for sentiment classification you could describe the task in words, or collect a small sentiment dataset and tune the model on it.
deep: Given an application dataset $\{(x^{(i)}_{\text{task}},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^n$: with $n$ small (say 5 to 10) it is few shot; with $n=0$ it is zero shot (the task is described and no new data is collected). In 2019 to 2022 few shot or more labeled adaptation was the dominant approach (for example collecting a small sentiment classification dataset and retraining on it); GPT-3's key advance was that few shot, and even zero shot, can work without retraining, and now zero shot is the mode people mostly think about. Separate question: does adaptation update the parameters? The lecture first covers methods that do (linear probing, fine tuning, LoRA), and later ones that need no update, which is what zero shot prompting amounts to.
say: Few shot adaptation means I have a handful of labeled examples for the new task, maybe five to ten, and I use them to adapt the model. Zero shot means I have none: I just describe the task to the model and ask it to solve it, with no new data and no parameter updates. Around 2019 to 2022 few shot or bigger labeled sets were the norm, and GPT three showed that zero shot can work. Today, almost nobody collects new labels to adapt a model for a task. A related question is whether adaptation updates parameters at all, and zero shot prompting doesn't.
must_mention: few shot: about 5 to 10 labeled examples
zero shot: just describe the task
GPT-3 showed zero shot can work

followups.q: Does zero shot update the model?
followups.a: No. The task is specified in the input, and the parameters stay unchanged.

traps: Equating zero shot with training on no data at all. The model was still pretrained.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: What is representation learning, and what is an embedding?
plain: Representation learning trains a model that turns each input into a list of numbers, a vector of fixed length, that captures what matters about it. That vector is called a representation, a feature vector or an embedding. You do not build a chatbot here; you build a general purpose encoder. Once trained, you can feed any new input through the encoder and get a vector that is useful for many downstream tasks. Similar inputs end up with similar vectors, so a simple model on top of the vectors can already do well.
deep: Train $f_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^m$ by minimizing a pretraining loss $\frac1n\sum_i\ell(\theta;x^{(i)})$ (no task labels; the loss is chosen in the next lecture), giving $\hat\theta$, which defines the representation function $f_{\hat\theta}$. The output vector is called a representation, feature or embedding. The architecture is fixed in advance (the structure of the neural network) and the numbers in $\hat\theta$ are what training produces. The lecturer notes representation learning is a special kind of pretraining that is still relevant for many applications, and that the loss will be designed so that the representations are suitable for linear use. Multimodal models try to produce one model that covers images, text, speech and video.
say: Representation learning trains a model that maps each input to a fixed length vector that captures what matters about it, called a representation, feature vector or embedding. I'm not building a chatbot here, I'm building a general purpose encoder. After pretraining, I can pass any new input through it and use the resulting vector for many downstream tasks, and similar inputs get similar vectors. The loss is designed so those vectors are suitable for simple models such as a linear classifier. Modern models increasingly produce embeddings for images, text and speech in one unified model.
must_mention: maps data to an m dimensional vector

followups.q: Are the representations tied to a task?
followups.a: No. They are learned by pretraining without task labels and reused across tasks.

traps: Treating an embedding as hand designed features.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: What is linear probing, and why does it work?
plain: Linear probing freezes the pretrained encoder and trains only a simple linear model on top of its output vectors. You compute the vector for each labeled example, take its dot product with a weight vector w, and fit w to the labels, using a regression loss for numbers or softmax for classes. Because the encoder is fixed, the only unknown is w, so it is a very simple, cheap problem. It works much better than fitting a linear model on raw inputs because the pretrained features capture meaning: the label is nearly linear in the features, though not in the raw input. It is also used to test what a model has learned.
deep: With $f_{\hat\theta}$ fixed, learn $$\hat w=\arg\min_{w\in\mathbb{R}^m}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}L\big(w^\top f_{\hat\theta}(x^{(i)}),\,y^{(i)}\big),$$ where $L$ is a regression loss (or a softmax cross entropy for classification, applied after the dot product). Only $w$ (the linear head) is trained.
