The representation is better than manual features or a linear model on raw $x$ because it captures semantic information, making $y$ nearly linear in $f_{\hat\theta}(x)$; pretraining losses are designed to make the representation linearly useful (next lecture). Typical use: a small labeled dataset per task, for example medical imaging tasks, each with a small linear head on one shared representation. Linear probes are also used for mechanistic interpretability of language models.
say: Linear probing freezes the pretrained encoder and trains only a linear head on its output vectors. For each labeled example I compute the embedding, take the dot product with a weight vector w, and fit w to the labels, with a regression loss for numbers or softmax for classes. Since the encoder is fixed, it's a simple, cheap problem. It works much better than a linear model on raw inputs because the pretrained features capture meaning, so the label is close to linear in the features. It's also used to test what a model has learned, in interpretability work.
must_mention: train only the linear head w
features make the label nearly linear

followups.q: Why is linear probing cheap?
followups.a: Only the head's weights are trained, on top of fixed features that can be computed once.

traps: Updating the encoder and still calling it linear probing.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: How does fine tuning differ from linear probing, and why does a pretrained initialization help even though the loss is the same?
plain: Fine tuning trains both the linear head and the encoder's own parameters, starting the encoder from the pretrained values. The loss is the same one you would use to train from scratch. Yet starting from the pretrained encoder gives much better test results than starting from random numbers. That means the loss has many different solutions that all fit the training data almost perfectly, but they generalize very differently, and where you start decides which one you land in. So initialization carries information about what a good solution looks like, not just a head start.
deep: Fine tuning: $\min_{w,\theta}\frac1n\sum_iL\big(w^\top f_\theta(x^{(i)}),y^{(i)}\big)$ with $\theta$ initialized at $\hat\theta$ and $w$ at a random value (there is still disagreement on how to initialize it). The final objective has nothing to do with pretraining; the same objective from random $\theta$ would be training from scratch. That a pretrained initialization gives far better test performance shows that the loss has many global minima with essentially zero training loss (the dataset is small), some much better on test data than others, and the initialization determines which one the optimizer finds. This is an implicit bias effect, tied to the double descent discussion. Linear probing, by contrast, optimizes only $w$, and its problem is convex (linear in $w$), while fine tuning is not.
say: Fine tuning trains both the linear head and the encoder's own parameters, with the encoder starting at the pretrained values. The objective is exactly the one I'd use to train from scratch, yet starting from the pretrained encoder gives much better test results than a random start. That tells me the loss has many solutions that all fit the small training set almost perfectly but generalize very differently, and the initialization picks which one the optimizer finds. So the pretrained weights carry information about good solutions, not just a head start. Linear probing only trains the head, which is a much simpler, convex problem.
must_mention: same loss as training from scratch
many global minima with near zero training loss

followups.q: What does this say about the loss landscape?
followups.a: It has many global minima with similar training loss but very different generalization.

traps: Concluding the pretrained model helps because the objective is different.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: What is LP FT, and why can it beat plain fine tuning?
plain: LP FT stands for linear probing then fine tuning. First, freeze the pretrained encoder and train only the linear head until it fits well. Second, unfreeze everything and fine tune the head and the encoder together, starting from the probed head and the pretrained encoder. It tends to beat plain fine tuning, where the head starts random. The reason is not fully understood, but a random head gives bad gradients early in training and can distort the good pretrained features before the head is even sensible. Starting from a sensible head makes the encoder change less.
deep: Step 1 (LP): minimize $L(w,\hat\theta)$ over $w$ only, giving $w_0$ with $\theta=\hat\theta$ unchanged. Step 2 (FT): minimize over both $(w,\theta)$ starting at $(w_0,\hat\theta)$. The lecturer calls this probably the dominant approach for fine tuning with labels today. Why it helps is hard to explain and not fully known; the rough account is that with a random head, the gradients flowing into the encoder early on can ruin the pretrained representation, whereas after LP the encoder's change during fine tuning is smaller than with a random head. There is some theory on this. There are many other options, and the recipe addresses only part of what matters.
say: LP FT means linear probe first, then fine tune. I first freeze the pretrained encoder and train only the linear head until it fits. Then I unfreeze everything and fine tune the head and encoder together, starting from the probed head. It tends to beat plain fine tuning with a random head. Why isn't fully understood, but the rough story is that a random head sends bad gradients into the encoder early on and can distort the good pretrained features, whereas a sensible head means the encoder changes less. It's become a common recipe for fine tuning with labels.
must_mention: first linear probe, then fine tune
start fine tuning from the probed head
random head can distort the representation

followups.q: What changes less in LP FT than in plain fine tuning?
followups.a: The encoder's representation, since the head is already sensible when the encoder starts to update.

traps: Claiming a theorem explains exactly why LP FT works.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: What is LoRA, and how many parameters does it train?
plain: LoRA, low rank adaptation, changes how a weight matrix is updated during fine tuning. Instead of changing every entry of the pretrained matrix W zero, it freezes it and learns a correction made of two thin matrices, A and B, multiplied together. For a d by d matrix, the full update has d squared free numbers, but the product of a d by r matrix and an r by d matrix has only 2 d r, with r small. With d equal to 1000 and r equal to 10, that is 20,000 numbers instead of 1,000,000, about 2 percent. A starts at zero so the model begins identical to the pretrained one.
deep: Reparameterize $W=W_0+AB$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}$, $B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}$ and $r\ll d$, so the update has rank at most $r$ and $2dr$ free parameters instead of $d^2$ (for $d=1000$, $r=10$: $20{,}000$ against $1{,}000{,}000$, or $2\%$). During adaptation $W_0$ is frozen and only $A,B$ are optimized: $\min_{A,B}L(W_0+AB)$. Initialize $A=0$ and $B$ randomly so that $W_0+AB=W_0$ at the start (checked numerically: the outputs agree exactly). The motivation: the base model is huge, the new data small, and the pretrained model is already powerful, so a small change should suffice, and limiting degrees of freedom reduces the risk of overfitting. It is a prior that the useful update is low rank, and it applies whatever the adaptation loss is.
say: LoRA stands for low rank adaptation. Instead of updating every entry of a pretrained weight matrix W zero, I freeze it and learn a correction that's the product of two thin matrices, A and B. For a d by d matrix, a full update has d squared numbers, but A is d by r and B is r by d, so the correction has only two d r numbers, with r small. With d a thousand and r ten, that's twenty thousand instead of a million, about two percent. I set A to zero at the start so the model begins identical to the pretrained one.
must_mention: freeze W_0, learn A times B
A is d by r, B is r by d

followups.q: Why initialize A to zero and B randomly?
followups.a: The product is then zero, so the adapted model starts exactly at the pretrained one, while B being random lets gradients flow.

traps: Initializing both A and B to zero, which gives zero gradients for both.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: What does LoRA actually save in compute and memory?
plain: Less than people expect in compute. The forward pass still has to multiply by the frozen big matrix, and the backward pass still has to multiply the incoming gradient by its transpose, so the cost is nearly unchanged. Only the weight gradient is smaller. The real savings are in memory: you no longer store gradients or optimizer state, such as Adam's momentum, for the frozen weights. The weights themselves stay in memory, and when training is sharded across GPUs, gradients and optimizer states are already split up, which shrinks the benefit. It matters when memory is tight, for example fitting on one GPU rather than two.
deep: Compute: the forward pass still computes $W_0x$ in every layer (the bottleneck) and the backward pass still multiplies by $W_0^\top$ for the activation derivatives; only the weight gradient is smaller (fewer parameters), so there is no big saving. Memory: training must hold parameters, gradients, and optimizer state such as Adam's momentum, and the latter two can far exceed the parameter memory (for fp32 Adam, gradient plus two moments is about three times the weights; the lecturer is unsure of his own factor of 6 to 12). With LoRA, gradients and optimizer states exist only for $A,B$, but the frozen $W_0$ must still be stored. Under sharded data parallelism (FSDP), gradients and optimizer states are already distributed across GPUs, so they are not always a bottleneck. The savings are most decisive when memory is scarce, for example one GPU instead of two. Both arguments hold for training; for inference the frozen weights dominate.
say: LoRA saves less compute than people think. The forward pass still multiplies by the big frozen matrix, and the backward pass still multiplies by its transpose, so the cost barely changes, except that the weight gradient is smaller. The main saving is memory: I don't need gradients or optimizer state like Adam's momentum for the frozen weights. But the weights themselves stay in memory, and with sharded training the gradients and optimizer states are already split across GPUs, so the benefit shrinks. It matters most when memory is tight, say when it lets a job fit on one GPU instead of two.
must_mention: forward and backward still use the frozen matrix
no gradients or optimizer state for frozen weights

followups.q: Which part of optimizer memory does LoRA remove?
followups.a: The gradients and momentum states for the frozen weights; only A and B need them.

traps: Claiming LoRA makes each training step much faster.

topic: CS229 L12: Diffusion training, foundation models, LoRA
q: Why is LoRA the main way fine tuning services are offered, and how does it help serve many users?
plain: A provider can keep one copy of the big base model in GPU memory and give each customer their own tiny low rank adapter. When a request comes in, the system applies that customer's adapter on top of the shared weights. A small adapter is a tiny fraction of the full model, so thousands of customers' adapters fit in the space of one extra copy of the model. Swapping between users just means loading a different small matrix pair, which is fast even from CPU memory. Without this, serving every customer's separately fine tuned full model would need far too much memory.
deep: With LoRA, users share a common $W_0$ and each has their own $(A_k,B_k)$. If each user's adapter costs on the order of tens or hundreds of millions of parameters against a base of billions or more, many users' adapters fit alongside one copy of the base model, and the system can preload most adapters to the GPU and switch between them quickly, loading the others from the CPU (a low rank matrix pair loads much faster than a full matrix). The lecturer says this serving advantage is probably the main reason why fine tuning services offered by large providers (he mentions GPT and Gemini) are offered only through LoRA, saying that every user gets their own low rank update, while memory for full weights per user would be prohibitive. The other important advantage is fitting training into limited memory.
say: The key point is serving. A provider keeps one copy of the big base model in GPU memory, and each customer gets only their own small low rank adapter. When a request arrives, the system applies that customer's adapter on top of the shared weights. Adapters are tiny compared with the base model, so many customers' adapters fit in the memory of what would otherwise be one extra model copy, and switching users means loading a different small matrix pair, which is fast even from CPU memory. Giving each customer a full fine tuned copy would need far more memory, which is why services offer LoRA style tuning.
must_mention: adapters are small and fast to swap
full copies per user would be too large

followups.q: What do you load when a different user arrives?
followups.a: Only that user's small A and B matrices, which is much faster than loading a full model.

traps: Thinking each fine tuned user needs a separate copy of the full model.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: What is an embedding model, and what do you use embeddings for today?
plain: An embedding model turns any input, such as an image, a sentence or an audio clip, into a vector of numbers, so each item becomes a point in space. Training aims to put similar items close together and different items far apart. Two photos of cats should have nearby vectors, while a cat and an airplane should be far apart. This enables similarity search: to find images like a given cat photo, find the stored images whose vectors are nearest. Embeddings used to be fed to a linear classifier, but today similarity search is their most important use.
deep: A model $\varphi_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^m$ maps images, text, audio or video to a vector (the terms embedding, representation and feature are used interchangeably; embedding is the most common word now). The aim is that similar inputs map to nearby points in Euclidean space and different inputs to distant ones, so that similarity in meaning is reflected as geometric closeness, unlike raw pixel space where two images of the same cat can be very far apart. Uses: similarity search; as input to linear classification (linear probing), which is useful but less used now since end to end models skip the two step approach. The lecturer says similarity search is the most important application of representation learning today.
say: An embedding model maps an image, sentence or audio clip to a vector, so each item becomes a point in space. Training makes similar items land close together and different items far apart, so two photos of cats get nearby vectors and a cat and an airplane get distant ones. That gives me similarity search: to find images like a given one, I look for stored vectors that are nearest. Raw pixels don't have this property, since two pictures of the same cat can be far apart pixel by pixel. Similarity search is now the main use of embeddings.
must_mention: maps an input to a vector
similar items close, different items far
raw pixels do not have this property
similarity search is the main use

followups.q: Why not compare raw pixels?
followups.a: Two images of the same cat can differ a lot pixel by pixel, so pixel distance does not reflect semantic similarity.

traps: Assuming embeddings are fixed hand designed features.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: How can a supervised classifier be used to learn an embedding, and what are its limits?
plain: Train a large neural network to classify images into many labeled classes, such as the thousand ImageNet categories, then take the vector from the second to last layer as the embedding and throw away the final classification layer. The network had to find features that separate the classes, so those features usually describe images well. The catch is labels. If the task only has two classes, or ten digits, the network can succeed with very simple features that do not transfer. Many diverse labels fix that, but labels are expensive, and scaling up means paying many annotators.
deep: Supervised pretraining: a deep classifier whose penultimate layer is a vector $f_\theta(x)$, followed by a matrix $W$ producing logits and a softmax; after training, keep $f_\theta$ as the representation (discard what comes after) and use it for linear probing or similarity. It requires a large, diverse labeled set: with binary labels (even black and white versus color) or 0 to 9 digit labels, the features learned would be narrow and useless elsewhere, while 1000 ImageNet classes give generally good features. The limitation is cost, since scaling requires more labels, more data and many annotators, which motivates label free contrastive learning. The lecturer notes there is no true representation: a representation is judged by whether it has useful properties.
say: I can train a big classifier on many labeled classes, like the thousand ImageNet categories, then take the vector from the second to last layer as the embedding and discard the final layer. The network had to find features that separate the classes, so they usually describe images well. The limit is labels. With only two classes, or ten digits, the network can succeed with very simple features that don't transfer. Many diverse labels fix that, but labels are expensive to collect, which is why people moved to methods that need no labels, like contrastive learning.

followups.q: Why would a binary label give poor features?
followups.a: The network can solve it with simple features, so it never needs rich ones that transfer to other tasks.

traps: Training a two class classifier and expecting a general purpose embedding.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: How does contrastive learning work without labels, and why does it need negatives?
plain: Take one image and make two random versions of it, for example two different crops, with different blur or color changes. Feed both through the network and train it so that their embeddings are close. No labels are needed. But if closeness were the only goal, the network would map every image to the same point and everything would trivially be close. So there is a second force: embeddings of versions of different images must be far apart. The push toward closeness for the same image and the push apart for different images balance each other and give useful embeddings.
deep: Augmentations $\hat x,\tilde x$ of the same image (random crop, rotation, blur, noise, color changes; the exact kinds matter less than being diverse) should have embeddings $\varphi(\hat x)\approx\varphi(\tilde x)$, a loss expressed as a distance. With only this term, the trivial solution maps every input to one point (collapse). The counterweight is a repulsion term: augmentations of different images should be far apart. The lecturer stresses that this means similar things must be close and different things far apart, which requires a well organized space (planes near planes and far from cats), not random placement. No labels are used, and diverse unlabeled images are easy to download. It is one of the unsupervised approaches to representation learning.
say: In contrastive learning I take one image and make two random augmentations, like different crops or blurs. I pass both through the network and train it so their embeddings are close, with no labels needed. But if closeness were the only goal, the network would map everything to a single point and trivially win. So I add a second force: embeddings of augmentations of different images should be far apart. The pull toward the partner and the push away from everything else balance, and the result is a space where similar images cluster and different ones separate.
must_mention: two augmentations of one image should be close
closeness alone collapses to one point

followups.q: What are examples of augmentations?
followups.a: Random crops, rotations, blur, added noise and color changes.

traps: Using only the attraction term and expecting useful embeddings.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: What goes wrong when two different images in a contrastive batch are actually similar, and why is it acceptable?
plain: The loss treats any two different images as something to push apart. If they are actually two cats, the loss pushes similar things apart, which works against the goal. This is collateral damage. It is acceptable because if you pick two random images from a big varied dataset, they are almost always genuinely different, like a plane and a chair. The occasional wrongly pushed pair is outweighed by the benefit of keeping everything else spread out, and other terms in the loss pull real cats back together through their own partners.
deep: Treating all non partner pairs as negatives is noisy: two cat images, or two similar planes, would be pushed apart though they should be close, which the loss does reward against. The justification: for two random draws from a diverse dataset, the probability that they are semantically similar is small, so the net effect of pushing random pairs apart outweighs the harm, and the damage never fully succeeds because the positive pairs and other negatives keep pulling in other directions. The lecturer notes that diversity is easy to get because unlabeled images can be downloaded, and that the loss does not achieve its goal 100 percent, which would be too easy. He also says the primary effect is to keep very close things, such as cats of the same breed, together, while a hierarchy across breeds is a secondary effect.
say: The loss treats any two different images as a pair to push apart, so if they are both cats, it pushes similar things apart, which is counterproductive. It's collateral damage, but acceptable. If I pick two random images from a large, varied dataset, they're almost always genuinely different, so the benefit of spreading things out outweighs the occasional wrong push. And that wrong push doesn't fully win, because each cat is also pulled toward its own augmentation and pushed away from many unrelated images. The more diverse the data, the smaller the harm.
must_mention: non partner pairs are treated as negatives
random pairs are mostly truly different

followups.q: What makes the damage smaller?
followups.a: A larger, more diverse dataset, where random pairs are rarely similar.

traps: Assuming negatives are always truly dissimilar.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: How is a batch set up in SimCLR style contrastive learning, and what does the similarity matrix look like?
plain: Take a batch of B random images and make two augmentations of each, so you have two versions of every image. Embed all of them. Then fill a B by B grid where row i, column j holds the similarity, a dot product of normalized embeddings, between the first version of image i and the second version of image j. The diagonal compares two versions of the same image and should be large. Every other entry compares different images and should be small. Normalizing the embeddings makes the dot product the cosine similarity.
deep: Batch of $B$ images, two augmentations each: $\hat x_i,\tilde x_i$ for $i=1,\dots,B$ ($2B$ examples). Embeddings are usually normalized, so similarity is the cosine, $S_{ij}=\varphi(\hat x_i)^\top\varphi(\tilde x_j)$. Diagonal entries $S_{ii}$ (positive pairs: augmentations of the same image) should be large; off diagonal entries (negative pairs) should be small. How large is large is set by the loss on the next card. Writing the objective via a matrix is a matter of efficiency: it is not the simplest expression of the idea, but one batch gives $B$ positives and $B^2-B$ negatives at once. $B$ is a minibatch (for example 128 to 4000) taken from the dataset, not the whole dataset.
say: I take a batch of B random images and make two augmentations of each. I embed all two B of them and normalize the embeddings. Then I fill a B by B matrix where entry i, j is the dot product, the cosine similarity, between the first augmentation of image i and the second augmentation of image j. The diagonal entries compare two views of the same image and should be large. Every off diagonal entry compares different images and should be small. One batch gives me B positive pairs and many negative pairs at once.
must_mention: diagonal is positive pairs, should be large
off diagonal is negative pairs, should be small

followups.q: Why normalize the embeddings?
followups.a: The dot product then equals the cosine similarity, so only direction matters.

traps: Including the same image's two views as negatives for each other.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: Write the SimCLR style contrastive loss and explain why it is a classification problem. What is its value if the embeddings collapse?
plain: For each row of the similarity matrix, take the exponential of the diagonal entry, divide by the sum of the exponentials of all entries in that row, and take minus the log. That is exactly the softmax cross entropy loss for a classification problem with B classes where the correct class is the true partner. So the model is being asked: given this image, which of the B candidates is its other augmentation? Sum the loss over all rows. If every embedding collapses to the same point, all entries are equal and the loss per row is log B, the loss of random guessing.
deep: $$\ell_i=-\log\frac{\exp(S_{ii})}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp(S_{ij})},\qquad\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\ell_i$$ (summing over columns too is a symmetric variant). With $a=\exp(S_{ii})$ and $b=\sum_{j\ne i}\exp(S_{ij})$, $\ell_i=-\log\frac{a}{a+b}$ is decreasing in $a$ (raise the diagonal similarity) and increasing in $b$ (shrink the off diagonal ones), and is minimized when $S_{ii}$ is much larger than the others in the exponential sense. It is the softmax cross entropy of a $B$ way classification, with similarities as logits. Example computed: $B=3$ with rows $(0.9,0.1,0.0)$, $(0.2,0.8,0.1)$, $(0.0,0.3,0.7)$ gives row losses $0.618,0.716,0.773$; with the partners wrong the losses are about $1.42$ to $1.47$; for collapsed embeddings the loss is $\log 3=1.099$ per row. (An implementation detail beyond the lecture: with unit norm embeddings and no temperature, the loss cannot go below $\log(1+(B-1)e^{-2})$, so a temperature is usually added.)
say: For each row of the similarity matrix, I take the exponential of the diagonal entry, divide by the sum of the exponentials of the entire row, and take minus the log. That's softmax cross entropy for a classification problem with B classes where the right answer is the true partner. So the model must pick out, among all candidates, the other augmentation of this image. The loss falls when the diagonal similarity rises and when the off diagonal ones fall. If all the embeddings collapsed to one point, every entry would be equal and the loss would be log B, the same as random guessing, so collapse is penalized.
must_mention: minus log of exp(diagonal) over sum of exp(row)
softmax cross entropy over B candidates
decreases with larger diagonal, smaller off diagonal

followups.q: What does the model have to identify?
followups.a: Which of the B candidates is the other augmentation of the same image.

traps: Forgetting that the denominator includes the diagonal entry as well.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: What are positive and negative pairs, and how can positives be built without augmentations, such as for text or images with captions?
plain: A positive pair is two items that should have similar embeddings, and a negative pair is two items that should be far apart. In image contrastive learning, positives are two augmentations of one image and all other pairs are negatives. But positives can come from anywhere you have two matched views. Pair an image with its text description and you train a shared embedding space for images and text. For documents, pair a title and sections with the raw text of the same document, and treat a title from one document with the raw text of another as a negative.
deep: Positive pairs sit on the diagonal of the similarity matrix and negative pairs everywhere else; some negatives may actually be similar, but they are treated as negative. The loss only needs a matched pair with index $i$: it can be an image $\hat x_i$ with its caption $\tilde x_i$, which builds a joint text and image representation (the idea behind image text embedding models), or, for language where augmentations are rarely used, a document's title and sections paired with its raw text. A title of one document with the raw text of another document is unlikely to match, so it is a negative pair. There are many more negative pairs than positive ones, but each negative carries a weaker signal, so this imbalance is natural.
say: A positive pair is two items that should have similar embeddings, and a negative pair is two that should be far apart. For images, positives are two augmentations of the same image. But the positives can come from any matched views. If I pair an image with its text description, I train a shared embedding space for images and text. For documents, I can pair a title and sections with the raw text of the same document as a positive, and a title with another document's text as a negative. There are many more negatives than positives, but each negative carries a weaker signal.
must_mention: title and sections paired with raw text
other pairs in the batch are negatives

followups.q: Why is a shared text and image space useful?
followups.a: It lets you search images with text and text with images, since both live in one space.

traps: Pairing items that merely look similar and calling them positives without any link.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: What are hard negatives, and how does batch composition make the contrastive loss more demanding?
plain: If the negatives in a batch are random, many are obviously different, such as a plane next to a chair, and the loss is easy to push down without learning fine distinctions. Hard negatives are pairs that look similar but are not actually a match, such as a photo of a child playing soccer and a caption about the World Cup. Including them forces the model to learn finer differences. A simple way to get them is to build each batch from one source, for example code from one programming language or one repository. The limit is that if negatives become too similar, they should really be positives.
deep: With random negatives the loss is easy to minimize because most pairs are trivially distinguishable; stronger negatives make it more demanding and yield a better representation, a technique called negative mining or hard negatives. Example: an image of a child playing soccer and text about FIFA are related but not the same, which is confusing and demanding. In practice the $B$ examples in a batch are drawn from the same source (for instance images from one website, text from one programming language, or one repository) so that they are harder to tell apart; the lecturer has used this in an industry project on code. Trade off: as you keep filtering for harder negatives you eventually cannot tell them from true positives, so you have to stop before that point. Cost note: the $B^2$ similarity computations are cheap, and the bottleneck is the $2B$ forward passes through a huge network.
say: If the negatives in a batch are random, most are obviously different, like a plane next to a chair, so the loss is easy to push down without learning fine distinctions. Hard negatives are pairs that look similar but aren't a match, like a photo of a child playing soccer and a caption about the World Cup. Including them forces finer discrimination. A simple way to get them is to build each batch from one source, say code from a single programming language or repository. The limit is that if negatives get too similar, they're effectively positives, so I stop before that.
must_mention: hard negatives look similar but are not a match
too similar means they should be positives

followups.q: How do you build harder batches cheaply?
followups.a: Draw each batch from a single source, such as one programming language or repository.

traps: Mining negatives so aggressively that true positives become negatives.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: How does semantic search work with embeddings?
plain: You prepare by running every document, image or passage through the embedding model once and storing the resulting vectors. When a query arrives, you embed it with the same model, then look for the stored vectors with the largest dot product with the query vector. The documents attached to those vectors are the most relevant results, and you can take the top one or the top ten. You do not rerun the big network on the documents at query time. For a small collection you just compute all the dot products, and for a large one you use a vector database or a nearest neighbor search algorithm.
deep: Precompute $\varphi(d_1),\dots,\varphi(d_N)$. At query time compute $\varphi(q)$ and return $$i^\star=\arg\max_i\ \varphi(q)^\top\varphi(d_i)$$ (or the top $k$). Brute force is a loop over stored vectors, without evaluating the network again, a cost of $N$ dot products; for large collections, vector databases and $k$ nearest neighbor search algorithms find the most similar vectors efficiently, which is a purely algorithmic problem the lecturer leaves aside. The same works for images or text. Most newer search systems use ideas like this, and, the lecturer guesses, so does Google to some extent as part of a mix of methods, though nobody outside knows for sure.
say: First I embed every document once and store the vectors. At query time I embed the query with the same model and find the stored vectors with the largest dot product with it. Those documents are my results, the top one or the top ten. I don't need to rerun the big network on the documents, since their vectors are precomputed. For a small collection I can just compute all the dot products, and for a big one I use a vector database or an approximate nearest neighbor search. The same approach works for images, text and audio.
must_mention: embed the query with the same model
vector database or nearest neighbor search at scale

followups.q: Why precompute document embeddings?
followups.a: The expensive network runs only once per document, so queries need only a cheap dot product search.

traps: Embedding the query and the documents with different models.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: What is retrieval augmented generation (RAG), and why use it instead of fine tuning?
plain: A language model from a big lab has never seen your private documents, and you may not want to send them for training. RAG gives the model that information at the moment you ask a question. First you search your own collection for the documents most relevant to the question, often with semantic search, then you put five to ten of them into the model's context together with the question. The model reads both and writes the answer. Nothing about the model changes. Fine tuning on your data is often too expensive, and you may not want to host a huge model yourself.
deep: RAG: given a query, (1) retrieve relevant documents from a corpus (a few, often 5 to 10), (2) place them in the model's context along with the query, and (3) let the model generate a response conditioned on both; no model parameters are modified. Motivation: frontier models are general and cannot see your confidential or fresh data; fine tuning a base model on your small dataset can be too expensive, and you may not want to host or pay for a model with billions or trillions of parameters. RAG is modular: the search stage is almost completely separate from the language model, and it is cheap relative to training. How exactly to search depends on the task and the best way is not known.
say: A model from a big lab hasn't seen my private documents, and I may not want to send them off for training. With retrieval augmented generation, I give the model that information at question time. I search my own collection for the documents most relevant to the question, often using semantic search, then put the top five to ten into the model's context with the question. The model reads both and writes the answer. The model itself doesn't change. It's often much cheaper than fine tuning, and I don't need to host a huge model myself.
must_mention: put them in the context with the query

followups.q: How many documents are typically retrieved?
followups.a: A handful, often about 5 to 10.

traps: Thinking RAG teaches the model new facts permanently.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: What are the advantages of RAG over fine tuning, and what alternatives to semantic search exist for the retrieval step?
plain: Because retrieval is separate from the model, RAG is modular and cheap. You can control who sees what: a user without permission to see a document simply never gets it retrieved. Deleting information is easy, since removing a document from the corpus means it will never be retrieved again, whereas making a trained model forget something is still an open research problem. For retrieval itself, semantic search is not the only choice. Some systems have language models write keyword or pattern searches, which works well for structured data like code, where file trees and exact names make pattern matching effective. Semantic search helps where keywords are hard to define.
deep: Advantages: modularity (the search is almost completely separate from the language model); access control (block users from retrieving documents they may not see, for example a revenue forecast); easy deletion (remove it from the corpus, whereas unlearning data a model was trained on is an open question); and low cost, since the search stage is much cheaper than training. Retrieval options: semantic search with embeddings, or lexical search such as regular expressions or keywords. The lecturer says Anthropic's systems, as publicly understood, use language models to generate regular expressions to search for keyword variations, which works well for code because of its structured trees and strict identifiers; for other data where such patterns are hard to write, semantic search is still valuable, and the two can be combined. He adds that nobody knows exactly which approach is best.
say: RAG has practical advantages because retrieval is separate from the model. It's modular and cheap. I can enforce access control, because a user who isn't allowed to see a document never gets it retrieved. Deleting information is easy, since removing a document from the corpus means it won't be retrieved again, while making a trained model forget something is still an open research problem. For the retrieval step, semantic search isn't the only choice: some systems have language models write regular expressions or keyword searches, which works well for structured data like code. Semantic search is better where keywords are hard to define.
must_mention: keyword or regex search works well for code

followups.q: Why is deleting data easy with RAG but hard with fine tuning?
followups.a: With RAG the data lives in a corpus you control, while fine tuning bakes it into the model weights.

traps: Assuming a retrieval system never leaks documents without access control in the search stage.

topic: CS229 L13: Contrastive learning, search and RAG
q: What is the computational bottleneck of contrastive training, and how big is the batch?
plain: Computing the loss for a batch means filling a B by B grid of dot products, but that part is cheap. The expensive part is getting the embeddings: each of the two B augmented examples has to go through a huge neural network with billions of parameters, so a batch needs two B forward passes. The batch is a subset of the dataset, from 128 up to a few thousand examples, and you take a new subset each time. Fresh random augmentations are generated whenever you pass through the data again, and in practice you do not need many passes.
deep: The loss involves $B^2$ similarity entries, but this is cheap compared with computing the $2B$ embeddings, which requires $2B$ forward passes through a network with billions of parameters; that is the real computational bottleneck. $B$ is a minibatch of the dataset (for example $128$, $1000$ or $4000$), not the entire dataset, and each step takes another set of $B$ examples. More augmentations per image come for free by iterating over the data again with new random augmentations, but you never go through the data more than a few times. Larger $B$ gives more negatives per positive. The composition of the batch also matters for how hard the negatives are (previous cards).
say: The loss itself is cheap: it's a B by B grid of dot products. The expensive part is getting the embeddings, because each of the two B augmented examples has to go through a network with billions of parameters, so a batch needs two B forward passes. B is a minibatch of the dataset, from around a hundred and twenty eight to a few thousand, not the whole dataset, and I take a new subset each step. I get fresh random augmentations whenever I pass over the data again, though in practice I don't make many passes.
must_mention: B is a minibatch of 128 to a few thousand

followups.q: Does a larger batch give more negatives?
followups.a: Yes, each positive is contrasted with B minus 1 negatives, so a larger batch gives more of them.

traps: Counting the B squared similarity computations as the main cost.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: What is an autoregressive language model?
plain: An autoregressive language model generates text one piece at a time, where each new piece depends on everything generated before it. It models the probability of a piece of text as the probability of the first token, times the probability of the second token given the first, and so on. During generation it samples a token, appends it to the text, and uses the longer text to predict the next one. So language is modeled step by step as a sequence. This is the design behind GPT-3 and most large language models used today, as opposed to earlier transformer models that were not autoregressive.
deep: An autoregressive model represents the distribution of a token sequence $x_1,\dots,x_T$ with a sequential model, $p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})$ at each step, and generates by sampling $x_t$, appending it to the context and repeating. This paradigm (autoregressive large language models) started with GPT-3 and is what the lecture covers; earlier non autoregressive transformers are skipped. The model is causal: the distribution at step $t$ depends only on earlier tokens. Training and generation differ: when computing the likelihood the whole sequence is visible, while in generation it must be produced token by token.
say: An autoregressive language model generates text one token at a time, where each new token depends on all the earlier ones. It models the probability of a sequence as the probability of the first token, times the probability of the second given the first, and so on. To generate, it samples a token, appends it to the text, and feeds the longer text back in to predict the next token. So language is modeled sequentially. This is the design behind GPT three and most large language models today, in contrast to earlier transformer models that weren't autoregressive.
must_mention: each token depends on earlier tokens

followups.q: What does the model see at step t?
followups.a: Only tokens before t, not later ones.

traps: Thinking the model sees the whole sequence when generating.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: Why do language models use subword tokens, and how is the vocabulary built?
plain: A model works with numbers, so text has to be cut into units. Characters give far too many steps per sentence. Whole words fail for rare long words: if internationalization is a single token, the model learns nothing about it from internationalize or nation. Subword tokens split rare words into familiar pieces, so a brand new word like a made up technical term is understood through its parts. A tokenizer has a fixed dictionary of subwords, often 100 thousand to 250 thousand entries, built by a greedy frequency based method such as byte pair encoding, and turns text into a list of token IDs.
deep: Tokenization decides the smallest input unit. Characters produce very long sequences (too many steps); whole words make rare, long or new words unseen tokens that share nothing with related forms (internationalization versus internationalized versus nation). Subwords split such words into pieces seen many times, so the meaning of the whole can be composed from parts, which matters for long compounds such as German words or biological terms. The vocabulary $V$ (roughly $10^5$ to $2.5\times10^5$ in open models) is a fixed dictionary built by an algorithm such as byte pair encoding (BPE), a greedy method that finds frequent subwords (the standard version repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols; the lecture only sketches it and says it is not important). Common words, even with a leading space, are single tokens. Each model usually has its own tokenizer, and different tokenizers give different token counts for the same text.
say: Models work with numbers, so I have to cut text into units. Characters make sequences far too long, and whole words handle rare long words badly: if internationalization is one token, the model can't relate it to internationalize or nation. Subword tokens split rare words into familiar pieces, so even a brand new word can be understood from its parts. The tokenizer has a fixed dictionary of subwords, typically around a hundred thousand to a quarter million, built with a greedy frequency based method like byte pair encoding, and it maps text to a list of token IDs. Each model has its own tokenizer.

followups.q: What is BPE in one sentence?
followups.a: A greedy algorithm that builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pieces of text.

traps: Assuming one token is always one word.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: Why do language models factor the sequence probability with the chain rule?
plain: A sequence of T tokens from a vocabulary of V tokens has V to the power T possible values, far too many to give each one its own probability. The chain rule solves this: the probability of the whole sequence equals the probability of the first token, times the probability of the second given the first, times the third given the first two, and so on. Each factor is a distribution over only V options, so a softmax over V numbers is enough to describe it. A single transformer then models all these conditionals, taking the earlier tokens as input and giving the distribution of the next token.
deep: The support of the joint distribution has $V^T$ elements, so a categorical distribution over sequences would need $V^T-1$ parameters. Use the chain rule: $$p_\theta(x_1,\dots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}).$$ Each conditional has only $V$ outcomes, so it can be parameterized by $V$ logits and a softmax. The input of each conditional is the prefix and the output is the distribution of the next token; a transformer models all of them. The decomposition is exact (it assumes nothing), and it enables both maximum likelihood training and sequential generation.
say: A sequence of T tokens from a vocabulary of V tokens has V to the T possible values, so I can't assign each sequence its own probability. The chain rule fixes that: the probability of the whole sequence is the probability of the first token, times the probability of the second given the first, and so on. Each factor is a distribution over just V options, so a softmax over V logits describes it. One transformer then models all the conditionals, taking the prefix as input and returning the next token distribution. The factorization is exact, with no independence assumption.
must_mention: V to the T possible sequences
each conditional is a softmax over V

followups.q: Does the chain rule factorization assume anything?
followups.a: No. It is an identity, exact for any distribution.

traps: Treating the tokens as independent given nothing.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: Walk through how a language model turns token IDs into next token probabilities.
plain: Each token ID picks out one row of a learned embedding table, a vector of D numbers, so the text becomes a sequence of vectors. Often a special beginning of sentence token is added at the front. The sequence of vectors goes through the transformer, a stack of attention and MLP layers, which outputs one vector of V numbers at every position, called logits. The logits at a position describe the next token. Apply softmax to them and you get a probability for each of the V tokens in the dictionary, nonnegative and adding to one. The embeddings are learned parameters, just like the other weights.
deep: Embedding matrix $E\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times D}$ (rows are embeddings, row vectors by the lecture's convention, matching Python code): token $x$ maps to row $E[x]$, equivalent to multiplying a one hot indicator by $E$. A beginning of sentence token $x_0$, one of the reserved special tokens, is often prepended. The transformer $f_\theta$ maps the embedded sequence to logits $u_1,\dots,u_T\in\mathbb{R}^V$ with $u_{t}=f_\theta(x_0,\dots,x_{t-1})$ depending only on earlier tokens, and $p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})=\operatorname{softmax}(u_t)$, a vector in the $V$ dimensional simplex whose entry $j$ is $p_\theta(x_t=j\mid x_{<t})$. The embedding of a token depends only on that token. The causal dependence is guaranteed by the internal design of the transformer, introduced later.
say: Each token ID looks up its row in a learned embedding table, a vector of D numbers, so the text becomes a sequence of vectors. Often a special beginning of sentence token is added at the front. That sequence goes through the transformer, a stack of attention and MLP layers, which outputs a vector of V numbers at every position, the logits. The logits at a position describe the next token, and a softmax turns them into a probability for each of the V tokens in the dictionary. The embeddings are learned parameters like any other weights, and each depends only on its own token.
must_mention: lookup of a learned embedding row

followups.q: What is the shape of the logits at each position?
followups.a: A vector with one entry per token in the vocabulary, V entries.

traps: Thinking embeddings are fixed and not trained.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: How does an autoregressive model generate text from a prompt?
plain: Give the model a prompt, such as a question or instruction, as the first tokens. It computes the probability distribution over the next token, and you pick one, usually by sampling. That token is appended to the text, and the longer text is fed back in to get the distribution for the following token. You keep going until a stop token or a length limit. This feed back loop is why the process is called autoregressive. It differs from computing the likelihood of existing text, where all tokens are already known and can be scored together.
deep: Given a prompt $x_1,\dots,x_k$, repeat for $t=k+1,k+2,\dots$: compute $u_t=f_\theta(x_{<t})$, sample $x_t\sim\operatorname{softmax}(u_t)$, append. The model is fed its own previous outputs, which is the meaning of autoregressive. With no prompt, start from the beginning of sentence token. In contrast, computing the log likelihood of a known sequence sees the whole sequence at once (all conditionals can be evaluated together), whereas generation must create the sequence one token at a time, since the future is unknown.
say: I give the model a prompt as the first tokens. It computes the probability distribution over the next token, I pick one, usually by sampling, and append it to the text. Then I feed the longer text back in to get the distribution for the following token, and keep going until a stop token or a length limit. That feedback loop of the model's own outputs is why it's called autoregressive. It's different from scoring existing text, where all tokens are known and all the conditionals can be evaluated together. In generation the future tokens don't exist yet.
must_mention: sample the next token and append
feed the longer text back in
stop at stop token or length limit

followups.q: How does scoring text differ from generating it?
followups.a: Scoring sees the whole sequence at once, while generation produces one token at a time.

traps: Believing generation produces all tokens in a single forward pass.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: What do temperature and top k do when sampling, and what happens at temperature zero? Give numbers.
plain: Temperature divides the logits by a number tau before the softmax. It does not change which token is most likely, only how sharp the distribution is. With logits 2, 1 and minus 1, the probabilities are about 0.71, 0.26 and 0.04. Make tau small and the biggest logit dominates: at tau 0.5 they become about 0.88, 0.12 and 0.002, and at tau near zero almost all the mass is on the first token. Zero temperature means always pick the most likely token, so generation is deterministic. A temperature above one flattens the distribution for more diversity. Top k keeps only the k most likely tokens and renormalizes.
deep: $$p_\tau(j)=\frac{\exp(u_j/\tau)}{\sum_k\exp(u_k/\tau)}.$$ Dividing by $\tau$ preserves the ordering of logits but changes their scale. Computed for $u=(2,1,-1)$: $\tau=1$ gives $(0.705,0.259,0.035)$; $\tau=0.5$ gives $(0.879,0.119,0.002)$; $\tau=2$ gives $(0.547,0.332,0.122)$; $\tau\to0$ gives $(1,0,0)$, equivalent to taking the arg max (greedy decoding, deterministic). $\tau>1$ flattens the distribution, so more tokens from the long tail are generated, increasing stochasticity and diversity, which is useful for example in reinforcement learning. Top k: keep the $k$ most likely tokens (out of $V\approx250{,}000$), drop the rest and renormalize, so very rare tokens are never produced even though the retained tokens may not carry all the mass. API calls expose temperature.
say: Temperature divides the logits by tau before the softmax. It doesn't change which token is most likely, just how sharp the distribution is. With logits two, one and minus one, the probabilities are about seventy one, twenty six and four percent. At tau point five they sharpen to about eighty eight, twelve and a fraction of a percent, and as tau goes to zero all the mass goes to the top token, so zero temperature means always pick the most likely token, which is deterministic. A temperature above one flattens things for more diversity. Top k keeps only the k most likely tokens and renormalizes.
must_mention: divide logits by tau before softmax
tau zero is the greedy, deterministic choice

followups.q: Why would you want a temperature above one?
followups.a: To sample more diverse outputs from the tail, for example for exploration in reinforcement learning.

traps: Expecting a low temperature to change which token is the most likely.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: What is the training loss of a language model?
plain: The loss for a piece of text is the negative log probability the model assigns to it. Because the probability is a product over positions, the loss is a sum over positions: at each position, look at the model's probability for the token that really came next, take the minus log of it, and add everything up. If the model gives the true next token a high probability, that term is small. This is the same softmax cross entropy used for classification, applied at every position, where the classes are the tokens in the vocabulary. You minimize it with SGD or Adam over many text sequences.
deep: $$-\log p_\theta(x_1,\dots,x_T)=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\Big[\operatorname{softmax}\big(f_\theta(x_0,\dots,x_{t-1})\big)\Big]_{x_t},$$ where the subscript $x_t$ picks the entry of the softmax vector at the index of the token actually observed in the data. This is maximum likelihood (minimize the negative log likelihood), and equals the cross entropy loss at every position with the next token as the label. Averaged over a dataset, it is minimized with an optimizer such as SGD or Adam used as a black box. Check: if the true tokens get probabilities $0.5$, $0.25$ and $0.1$, the loss is $-\log0.5-\log0.25-\log0.1=4.38$ ($1.46$ per token). The sum runs over positions $1$ to $T$.
say: The loss for a sequence is the negative log probability the model assigns to it. Since that probability is a product over positions, the loss is a sum: at each position, I take the model's probability for the token that actually came next, take minus the log, and add up. If the true token gets high probability, that term is small. It's the same softmax cross entropy used for classification, applied at every position, where the classes are the vocabulary tokens. I minimize it with SGD or Adam over lots of text. For example, true token probabilities of point five, point two five and point one give a loss of about four point four.
must_mention: negative log likelihood of the sequence
sum over positions of minus log of the true token probability
softmax cross entropy at each position

followups.q: What is the label at each position?
followups.a: The token that actually appears next in the data.

traps: Averaging probabilities instead of summing log probabilities.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: What is the overall structure of a transformer, and where do positions interact?
plain: A transformer is a stack of layers that alternate between two kinds of blocks. An attention block takes a sequence of vectors and returns a sequence of vectors, letting each position gather information from other positions. An MLP block, a small multilayer perceptron, then processes each position's vector separately. The MLP uses the same weights at every position and does not look at its neighbors. So the only way information flows between different positions is through attention. After enough alternations, a final output gives a vector of logits for each position. The whole stack is trained end to end as one big network with automatic differentiation.
deep: Structure: embedded input $\to$ attention $\to$ MLP $\to$ attention $\to$ MLP $\to\cdots\to$ output vectors $u_1,\dots,u_T$. Attention maps a sequence of vectors to a sequence of vectors by combining information across positions; the MLP (a two or three layer network, possibly with gating or special activations) has shared parameters and is applied independently and in parallel to each position's vector, so there are no dependencies between positions in the MLP. Attention is the only mixing mechanism across time steps. The entire system is one giant neural network trained end to end, and automatic differentiation applies since it is a composition of many elementary operations (many matrix multiplications).
say: A transformer is a stack of layers that alternate between attention blocks and MLP blocks. Attention takes a sequence of vectors and returns a sequence of the same length, letting each position gather information from the others. The MLP is a small multilayer perceptron applied to each position's vector separately, with the same weights at every position, so it doesn't mix information across positions. That means attention is the only place where positions interact. After enough alternations, the final vectors become logits. The whole thing is one big network trained end to end, and automatic differentiation handles the gradients.

followups.q: Where does information flow between tokens?
followups.a: Only through attention layers.

traps: Thinking the MLP combines information from different tokens.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: Explain single head attention with queries, keys and values, including the shapes.
plain: Each input vector is multiplied by three learned matrices, giving a query, a key and a value for that position. The query says what this position is looking for, and the key says what each position offers. To compute the output at position t, take the dot product of its query with the key of every position, giving one score per position. A softmax turns the scores into weights that are positive and add to one, large where query and key match. The output is the weighted average of the value vectors using those weights. A scaling factor is applied to the scores to keep them well behaved.
deep: With row vectors $h_t\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d}$ and learned $W_Q,W_K,W_V\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_h}$: $q_t=h_tW_Q$, $k_t=h_tW_K$, $v_t=h_tW_V\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_h}$. Scores $q_tk_i^\top\in\mathbb{R}$ for $i=1,\dots,T$ form a vector in $\mathbb{R}^T$, then $$p_{ti}=\frac{\exp(q_tk_i^\top/c)}{\sum_j\exp(q_tk_j^\top/c)},\qquad h^{\text{out}}_t=\sum_{i=1}^{T}p_{ti}v_i,$$ where $c$ is a scaling factor (commonly $\sqrt{d_h}$). Each $p_t$ is a probability vector over positions. In matrix form with $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_h}$: $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/c)V$ (row wise softmax). The matrices are trained, so the model learns where to look; if the weights were all zero the network would still be valid but have a poor loss. I checked a toy implementation: each row of $p$ sums to one.
say: Each input vector is multiplied by three learned matrices to give a query, a key and a value for that position. The query says what this position is looking for, and each key says what that position offers. To compute the output at position t, I take the dot product of its query with every position's key, scale it, and apply a softmax, which gives positive weights that add to one. The output is the weighted average of the value vectors with those weights. In matrix form it's softmax of Q K transpose over a scale, times V, and the three projection matrices are learned.
must_mention: query, key and value from learned projections
dot product of query with every key
output is a weighted average of values

followups.q: What is the shape of the score matrix?
followups.a: T by T, one score for each pair of positions.

traps: Applying softmax across the feature dimension instead of across positions.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: Why use attention instead of an MLP on all the tokens, or a giant MLP over the concatenated sequence?
plain: An MLP applied to each token separately has no way to relate tokens, so it cannot understand a sentence from individual words. A giant MLP over all the tokens concatenated could relate them, but it would need enormous weight matrices when sequences are long, even millions of tokens, and its size would depend on the sequence length, so a model trained on 1,000 tokens could not be used on a different length. Attention uses the same small set of parameters whatever the length. It is a compromise: enough structure to be efficient, while still flexible and learned. Convolutional networks also work somewhat but not as well.
deep: Per token MLPs: no interaction between positions, so no chance of modeling dependencies. A giant MLP over the concatenation of all $T$ vectors: the parameter count grows with $T$ (sequences can reach millions of tokens, so matrices become impossibly large), and the parameter count and architecture would change with the sequence length, which is undesirable when training on length 1000 and testing on another length; with attention the number of parameters is independent of the sequence length. With enough compute and data a giant MLP might work but is too expensive. The design principle is to balance structure (to reduce complexity) with flexibility (not to dictate too much, such as simply averaging). Convolutional networks (an MLP with a local receptive field) can work to some extent, though not as well. As the lecturer says, special structures mostly aim at using parameters more efficiently.
say: An MLP applied to each token separately can't relate tokens, so it can't understand a sentence from individual words. A giant MLP over all the concatenated tokens could, but its weight matrices would be enormous for long sequences, and its size would depend on the sequence length, so a model trained on a thousand tokens couldn't handle another length. Attention uses the same small set of parameters regardless of length. It's a compromise between structure and flexibility: enough built in structure to be efficient, while the weights are still learned. Convolutions help a little but not as well.
must_mention: per token MLP cannot relate tokens
giant MLP needs too many parameters
size would depend on the sequence length

followups.q: Could a giant MLP work in principle?
followups.a: With enough data and compute it might, but it would be too expensive.

traps: Saying attention has no parameters.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: Why does a decoder only language model need a causal mask, and how is it implemented?
plain: In the attention formula as written, the output at a position can depend on every position, including later ones. But an autoregressive model must predict the next token without seeing the future, so position t may only look at positions up to t. The fix is a mask: before the softmax, add minus infinity to the scores of all pairs where the key comes later than the query, which is the upper triangle of the score matrix. After the softmax those weights are exactly zero, and the remaining weights still add up to one, so the output is still a weighted average of past values only. Without the mask, the model could cheat during training by reading the answer.
deep: Without masking, $h_t^{\text{out}}=\sum_ip_{ti}v_i$ depends on $v_{T}$ and later inputs, violating the autoregressive property (output at $t$ may only depend on inputs up to $t$). The causal mask $M$ has $M_{ij}=0$ for $j\le i$ and $-\infty$ for $j>i$, so $$\operatorname{Attn}=\operatorname{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{c}+M\Big)V.$$ Adding $-\infty$ turns the upper triangle into $\exp(-\infty)=0$ after softmax, and the remaining entries renormalize to sum to one, a convex combination of $v_1,\dots,v_t$. Equivalent view: drop the invalid terms and renormalize. I verified with a toy implementation that changing the last token's input leaves the outputs of earlier positions unchanged and only changes the last position's output. The mask is needed because during generation future tokens do not exist.
say: As written, attention lets position t look at every position, including later ones, which would break the autoregressive property, and during training the model could simply read the answer. So I add a causal mask: before the softmax I add minus infinity to every score where the key comes after the query, the upper triangle of the score matrix. After the softmax those weights are exactly zero, and the remaining weights still sum to one, so each output is a weighted average of past values only. I checked on a toy example that changing a later token leaves earlier outputs unchanged.
must_mention: position t must not see later tokens
add minus infinity above the diagonal
softmax gives zero weight to masked entries

followups.q: What would go wrong without the mask during training?
followups.a: The model could read the next token it is supposed to predict, so it would learn nothing useful for generation.

traps: Applying the mask after the softmax without renormalizing.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: What is multi head attention and why use it?
plain: Instead of one attention, run several attentions side by side on the same input, each with its own query, key and value matrices. Each one produces its own output vector at every position. Then concatenate the outputs of all the heads for each position and multiply by one more matrix to get a single output vector. Different heads can specialize in different kinds of information, for example one tracking which entity matters and another tracking sentiment. They run in parallel, not one after the other. Big models can have on the order of a hundred heads.
deep: Run $n_h$ single head attentions on the same input $h_1,\dots,h_T$ with different weight matrices $W_Q^{(m)},W_K^{(m)},W_V^{(m)}$ (so they are not literal copies), giving outputs $h_t^{(1)},\dots,h_t^{(n_h)}$ at each position. Combine by concatenating and projecting: $$h_t^{\text{out}}=\big[h_t^{(1)}\,\big|\cdots\big|\,h_t^{(n_h)}\big]W_O.$$ The intuition is that each head acts as a separate attention focusing on a different kind of information, and the results are aggregated into one vector. The heads are parallel within a layer, and each layer has its own number of heads (up to about a hundred in the largest models, per the lecturer's estimate). Parameter check: with $d=4096$ and $32$ heads of $d_h=128$, the heads plus output projection have $4d^2\approx67$ million parameters.
say: Multi head attention runs several attention heads in parallel on the same input, each with its own query, key and value matrices, so each head can look for something different, like which entity matters or what the sentiment is. At each position I concatenate the outputs of all the heads and multiply by one more projection matrix to get a single output vector. The heads run in parallel, not in sequence. It gives the model more ways to combine information in one layer. Large models can use on the order of a hundred heads per layer.
must_mention: separate W_Q, W_K, W_V per head

followups.q: Are the heads sequential?
followups.a: No. They run in parallel on the same input and are then concatenated.

traps: Using the same weight matrices in every head.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: How are residual connections and normalization used around attention and the MLP in a transformer block?
plain: A real transformer block is a bit more than attention followed by an MLP. Around each of them there are two helpers. A normalization layer, often RMSNorm, rescales the vectors so values do not drift. A residual connection adds the block's input back to its output, as in residual networks. So a block computes a normalized version, runs attention or the MLP on it, and adds the original input back. The order matters: normalizing before the sublayer is called pre norm, and after it is post norm. The details are in the lecture notes.
deep: Each sublayer (attention, MLP) is wrapped with normalization (usually RMSNorm, introduced in the neural network section) and a residual connection, as in residual networks. For example, in the pre norm arrangement $h\leftarrow h+\operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{Norm}(h))$ followed by $h\leftarrow h+\operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{Norm}(h))$; in the post norm arrangement, normalization is applied after the residual addition. The lecturer notes there are different ways to add the residuals (before or after attention), called pre norm and post norm, and that the order of normalization, residuals and attention is spelled out in the lecture notes. Residual connections keep a direct path for gradients, and normalization keeps activations from growing, as discussed earlier.
say: A real transformer block wraps attention and the MLP with two helpers. A normalization layer, often RMSNorm, keeps activations at a reasonable scale. A residual connection adds the block's input back to its output, as in residual networks. In the common pre norm arrangement, I normalize the input, run attention, and add the result to the original input, then do the same with the MLP. Post norm applies the normalization after the residual addition instead. The ordering is a design choice, and these pieces keep deep stacks trainable by preserving gradient flow and keeping scales stable.
must_mention: residual adds the block input back
applied around both attention and MLP

followups.q: What is the difference between pre norm and post norm?
followups.a: Where the normalization sits: before the sublayer (pre) or after the residual addition (post).

traps: Forgetting the residual connection and stacking attention and MLP directly.

topic: CS229 L14: Autoregressive LMs and attention
q: What is the computational cost of attention in the sequence length, and how do long context and flash attention relate to it?
plain: For each of the T positions, attention computes a dot product with each of T keys, so the score matrix has T squared entries, and the work is about T squared times the head dimension. Doubling the context quadruples the cost. At a million tokens that would be a trillion score entries, which is why long conversations get compressed. Many variants reduce the dependence on T, though they usually give up some expressiveness. Memory looks like it is also T squared, but flash attention avoids storing the whole score matrix by processing it in blocks against blocks of the values.
deep: Each position computes $T$ dot products of dimension $d_h$, so the score matrix is $T\times T$ and the cost is $O(T^2d_h)$; the dependence on $d_h$ and the number of parameters is roughly linear, and the $T^2$ dependence is the important one. For $T=10^6$ this means $10^{12}$ score entries (about $4$ TB in 32 bit floats for a single matrix), which is impractical, a motivation for context compression in chat systems; real systems use variants with closer to linear dependence on $T$ (the lecturer does not know which are used in practice). Memory is naively $O(T^2)$ for the score matrix, but you can process part of the matrix against the corresponding part of $V$ and never store all of it: this is flash attention. Architectures that improve the $T$ dependence typically lose expressiveness and may lose performance.
say: For each of the T positions, attention computes a dot product with each of T keys, so the score matrix has T squared entries and the work is about T squared times the head dimension. Doubling the context quadruples the cost, and at a million tokens it's a trillion entries, which is why long conversations get compressed. Memory looks like T squared too, but flash attention avoids storing the full score matrix by processing it in blocks against blocks of the values. There are also architectures that reduce the dependence on T, but they usually give up some expressiveness and can lose performance.
must_mention: cost order T squared times d_h
flash attention avoids storing the full matrix

followups.q: Does flash attention reduce the number of operations?
followups.a: Not in this description; it reduces memory by never materializing the full score matrix.

traps: Saying attention cost is linear in the sequence length.

topic: CS229 L15: KV cache, MoE, in context learning, SFT
q: What is the KV cache, and why does it limit batch size during generation?
plain: When a model generates text, each new token's query needs the keys and values of all earlier tokens. Recomputing them every step would be wasteful, so they are stored: that is the KV cache. Only keys and values are stored, not queries, because a query is used only at its own step. The cache grows linearly with the length of the text, and it exists for every head in every layer, so it takes a lot of GPU memory. A hypothetical model with 32 layers, 32 heads, head size 128 and 8,000 tokens needs about 4.2 GB per sequence in 16 bit numbers. That memory limits how many sequences can be processed together, and small batches leave the GPU waiting on memory.
deep: Attention compute scales as $T^2$ but the memory to store the keys and values scales linearly in $T$. During generation only the current query is needed (earlier queries can be discarded), but the keys and values of all previous positions are needed for every later step, so they are cached: $$\text{KV cache}=2\cdot L\cdot n_{kv}\cdot d_h\cdot T\cdot b\ \text{ bytes}.$$ Illustrative arithmetic (a made up configuration): $L=32$, $n_{kv}=32$, $d_h=128$, $T=8000$, $b=2$ bytes gives $4.19$ GB per sequence. Because this occupies most of the GPU memory, you cannot use a large batch during decoding, and without a large batch there is low arithmetic intensity: the GPU is limited by memory bandwidth and waits on the memory system instead of computing, so throughput and utilization (MFU) are poor. This motivates reducing the amount of KV cache stored.
say: During generation, each new token needs the keys and values of all earlier tokens, so I store them instead of recomputing them. That's the KV cache. It holds only keys and values, not queries, because a query is used only at its own step. It grows linearly with the text length and exists for every head in every layer, so it eats a lot of GPU memory. For a hypothetical model with thirty two layers, thirty two heads and eight thousand tokens, it's about four gigabytes per sequence. That limits how many sequences I can batch, and small batches leave the GPU waiting on memory instead of computing.
must_mention: store keys and values of past tokens
grows linearly with length, per head and layer

followups.q: Why does a small batch hurt GPU utilization?
followups.a: Low arithmetic intensity: the GPU waits on memory bandwidth instead of doing enough computation per byte loaded.

traps: Caching queries along with keys and values.

topic: CS229 L15: KV cache, MoE, in context learning, SFT
q: What is grouped query attention, and what does it save?
plain: In standard multi head attention every head has its own queries, keys and values. In grouped query attention you keep all the query heads but share keys and values among groups of heads. With 8 query heads and 2 key and value groups, heads 1 to 4 share the first set and heads 5 to 8 share the second. The attention computation is the same, but there are far fewer keys and values to store, so the KV cache shrinks in proportion: 8 groups instead of 32 heads cuts the cache to a quarter. It saves memory, not computation. Queries are not shared because only the latest query needs to be kept, while keys and values for the whole past must be stored.
deep: With $N_H$ query heads and $N_G<N_H$ key and value groups (usually $N_G$ divides $N_H$), $\tau=N_H/N_G$ query heads share one key and value set. Query head $j$ uses group $g(j)=\lfloor(j-1)/\tau\rfloor+1$: for $N_H=8$, $N_G=2$ the groups are $(1,1,1,1,2,2,2,2)$ (checked). Then $h_j^{\text{out}}=\operatorname{softmax}(Q_jK_{g(j)}^\top/c+M)V_{g(j)}$ with the same number of outputs as before. It saves little time (the number of query key dot products is unchanged), but reduces memory: in the illustrative $4.19$ GB example, $8$ KV groups instead of $32$ gives $1.05$ GB per sequence.
